title: Occamy-1.0: Open Pareto-frontier 35B Intelligence for Co-work
summary: Co-work agents execute complex workflows that combine information gathering, tool use, coding, and file manipulation across many model invocations. Because cost and latency accumulate over the full episode, their practical value depends not only on peak capability but also on how efficiently that capability is delivered. Yet many steps in everyday work emphasize state tracking, coordination, recovery, and follow-through rather than frontier-scale reasoning. We present Occamy-1.0, a cost-efficient co-work model obtained by further training the post-trained Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint. We construct execution-grounded data and environments, capture replayable long-horizon trajectories across multiple harnesses, and use staged post-training to develop and consolidate complementary execution capabilities. Across a broad suite of co-work benchmarks, Occamy-1.0 is consistently among the strongest comparably sized models and remains competitive with substantially larger frontier systems on several tasks. Under our stated evaluation and pricing protocol, its aggregate performance across four representative benchmarks places it at the low-cost knee of the observed cost--performance Pareto frontier. Supporting evaluations in tool calling, coding, and instruction following further show that this specialization preserves broad agentic capability. We release the model weights and a subset of the training data to support research on practical co-work agents and agentic post-training.

AI.tldr: Occamy-1.0 is a cost-efficient co-work model built from a post-trained Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint via execution-grounded data, replayable long-horizon trajectories, and staged post-training; it ranks among the strongest same-sized models and sits at the low-cost knee of the cost-performance Pareto frontier.
AI.motivation: Co-work agents run complex, multi-invocation workflows (information gathering, tool use, coding, file manipulation), so cost and latency accumulate over the full episode. Practical value therefore depends on efficient capability delivery, not just peak capability, and many everyday steps emphasize state tracking, coordination, recovery, and follow-through rather than frontier-scale reasoning.
AI.method: Further training of the post-trained Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint. The authors construct execution-grounded data and environments, capture replayable long-horizon trajectories across multiple harnesses, and apply staged post-training to develop and consolidate complementary execution capabilities.
AI.result: Across a broad suite of co-work benchmarks, Occamy-1.0 is consistently among the strongest comparably sized models and remains competitive with larger frontier systems on several tasks. AI.conclusion: Occamy-1.0 demonstrates that targeted, execution-grounded post-training can yield a cost-efficient co-work agent that balances performance and cost. Model weights and a subset of the training data are released to support research on practical co-work agents and agentic post-training.

title: Reading the Whole Heart: Latent-Attention Masked Autoencoders for Multimodal Cardiac Representation Learning
summary: Cardiovascular diagnosis rests on integrating complementary modalities, like ECG, echocardiography, chest radiographs, and clinical variables, each capturing distinct but correlated aspects of cardiac physiology. Yet most medical foundation models remain modality-specific, combining modalities only for finetuning or post-training. This discards the cross-modal evidence clinicians naturally integrate and ignores the structure within each modality. We introduce Latent-Attention Masked Autoencoders (LAMAE), a multimodal, structure-aware masked autoencoder that jointly learns patient-level representations during self-supervised pretraining. Rather than fusing modalities post hoc, LAMAE exchanges information directly in the latent space through a shared latent-attention module operating over a study-view-entity hierarchy, enabling aggregation of variable observations and graceful handling of missing modalities. Pretrained on over 1.2 million MIMIC-IV hospital stays, LAMAE outperforms modality-specific pretraining and strong contrastive and vision-language baselines across multimodal hospital-stay tasks, such as in-hospital mortality, ICD-10 and DRG coding, and length of stay, while remaining competitive on unimodal tasks. These gains persist even when only a single modality is available at test time, showing that modeling both intra- and inter-modal structure yields more robust, transferable representations.

AI.tldr: LAMAE is a multimodal, structure-aware masked autoencoder that jointly learns patient-level representations during self-supervised pretraining by exchanging information in latent space via a shared latent-attention module over a study-view-entity hierarchy.
AI.motivation: Cardiovascular diagnosis relies on integrating complementary modalities (ECG, echocardiography, chest radiographs, clinical variables), each capturing distinct but correlated aspects of cardiac physiology. However, most medical foundation models remain modality-specific and combine modalities only for finetuning or post-training, discarding the cross-modal evidence clinicians naturally integrate and ignoring the structure within each modality.
AI.method: The authors introduce Latent-Attention Masked Autoencoders (LAMAE), a multimodal, structure-aware masked autoencoder. Rather than fusing modalities post hoc, LAMAE exchanges information directly in the latent space through a shared latent-attention module operating over a study-view-entity hierarchy, enabling aggregation of variable observations and graceful handling of missing modalities. It is pretrained on over 1.2 million MIMIC-IV hospital stays.
AI.result: LAMAE outperforms modality-specific pretraining and strong contrastive and vision-language baselines across multimodal hospital-stay tasks, including in-hospital mortality, ICD-10 and DRG coding, and length of stay, while remaining competitive on unimodal tasks. These gains persist even when only a single modality is available at test time.
AI.conclusion: Modeling both intra- and inter-modal structure yields more robust, transferable representations for cardiovascular and hospital-stay tasks.

title: Scenario-Independent Criticality Assessment and Prediction for Vulnerable Road Users in Autonomous Driving
summary: Increasing safety is the primary objective of automated vehicles. Achieving this goal requires reliable safety metrics that incorporate safety-relevant factors such as object type, velocity, and criticality. A key capability of such metrics is the distinction between critical and non-critical objects, which is addressed through criticality or relevance estimation. Existing criticality metrics are typically designed for specific scenarios and primarily focus on vehicle-to-vehicle interactions. In this paper, we therefore propose a novel criticality metric tailored to vulnerable road users (VRUs), which require special consideration due to their less predictable motion behavior. Furthermore, to avoid the complexity introduced by scenario-specific metrics, we introduce a scenario-independent criticality prediction framework applicable to all traffic participant classes. The effectiveness of both the proposed VRU-centric criticality metric and the criticality prediction framework is evaluated using the DeepAccident dataset, which contains a diverse set of safety-critical traffic scenarios. The proposed VRU-centric criticality metric improves pedestrian criticality classification performance by up to 50 %. In addition, the proposed criticality prediction framework outperforms state-of-the-art metrics by 275 %, achieving an F1-score of 0.96 and enabling scenario-independent criticality assessment across all object classes. These results demonstrate the strong potential of the proposed approaches to enhance criticality assessment for safety evaluation in automated driving systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a VRU-centric criticality metric and a scenario-independent criticality prediction framework to improve safety evaluation for automated vehicles, outperforming state-of-the-art metrics on the DeepAccident dataset.
AI.motivation: Automated vehicles require reliable safety metrics that distinguish critical from non-critical objects. Existing criticality metrics are scenario-specific and focus mainly on vehicle-to-vehicle interactions, neglecting vulnerable road users (VRUs) whose less predictable motion demands special treatment.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel criticality metric tailored to VRUs and a scenario-independent criticality prediction framework applicable to all traffic participant classes, avoiding the complexity of scenario-specific metrics.
AI.result: Evaluated on the DeepAccident dataset, the VRU-centric criticality metric improves pedestrian criticality classification by up to 50%. The criticality prediction framework outperforms state-of-the-art metrics by 275%, achieving an F1-score of 0.96 and enabling scenario-independent criticality assessment across all object classes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approaches show strong potential to enhance criticality assessment for safety evaluation in automated driving systems.

title: Pelican-Sim 1.0: A General World Model Simulator for Embodied Intelligence
summary: In this technical report, we propose Pelican-Sim 1.0, a general world model simulator for embodied intelligence that predicts future observations from visual context and robot actions to support downstream learning and decision making. The model incorporates four key design features: (1) Unified action representation: a 28-dimensional action value space covering most mainstream embodiments, keeping one model valid across heterogeneous devices. (2) Action-visual injection: URDF- and camera-rendered action videos bridge actions and pixels, giving markedly better controllability across embodiments, scenes, and tasks (PSNR +0.904 over alternative fusion baselines). (3) Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE): sparse MoE layers add capacity for heterogeneous dynamics and absorb the action modality while reducing inter-modality conflict (FVD -6.530 vs. the dense backbone). (4) Efficient rollout generation: causal adaptation and few-step distillation yield a four-step autoregressive simulator, achieving a 5.67-fold speedup over the 35-step model. Benefiting from these designs, we train on approximately one million real-world and simulated trajectories and obtain large gains in action controllability and video quality: PSNR improves over the strongest evaluated baselines by 4.636 on AgiBotWorld Beta, 2.080 on RoboMIND, and 10.343 on RoboTwin, with the adapted EWMBench DYN score up 0.426 on RoboTwin. Relying on this, four downstream applications on RoboTwin succeed: 500 generated trajectories added to 50 demonstrations per task raise policy success from 70% to 93%; policy evaluation reaches a Pearson correlation of 0.994 across five checkpoints; and relative success gains reach 47.7% for action selection and 20.3% for policy improvement. Qualitative generalization across trajectory, scene, object, embodiment, and viewpoint shifts highlights its potential as a general-purpose world model simulator.

AI.tldr: Pelican-Sim 1.0 is a general world model simulator for embodied intelligence that predicts future observations from visual context and robot actions, using unified action representation, action-visual injection, sparse MoE, and efficient rollout generation, achieving large gains in controllability and video quality.
AI.motivation: To support downstream learning and decision making in embodied intelligence by building a general-purpose world model simulator that works across heterogeneous devices, scenes, and tasks.
AI.method: Four key design features: (1) a 28-dimensional unified action value space covering mainstream embodiments; (2) action-visual injection with URDF- and camera-rendered action videos bridging actions and pixels; (3) sparse mixture-of-experts layers to add capacity for heterogeneous dynamics and absorb the action modality while reducing inter-modality conflict; (4) causal adaptation and few-step distillation for a four-step autoregressive simulator. Trained on ~1M real-world and simulated trajectories.
AI.result: PSNR gains over strongest baselines: +4.636 on AgiBotWorld Beta, +2.080 on RoboMIND, +10.343 on RoboTwin; adapted EWMBench DYN score up 0.426 on RoboTwin; PSNR +0.904 over alternative fusion baselines; FVD -6.530 vs. dense backbone; 5.67x speedup over 35-step model. Downstream on RoboTwin: policy success 70% to 93% with 500 generated trajectories added to 50 demonstrations per task; policy evaluation Pearson correlation 0.994 across five checkpoints; relative success gains 47.7% for action selection and 20.3% for policy improvement.
AI.conclusion: Qualitative generalization across trajectory, scene, object, embodiment, and viewpoint shifts highlights Pelican-Sim 1.0's potential as a general-purpose world model simulator for embodied intelligence.

title: DU-NO: A Parameter-Efficient Double U-Shaped Neural Operator for Phase-Resolving Wave Modeling
summary: Phase-resolving wave models such as FUNWAVE-TVD are the accuracy standard for nearshore dynamics, resolving the shoaling, refraction, and breaking of individual waves, but their cost rules them out for the ensembles, uncertainty quantification, and real-time warning that operational forecasting demands. Neural operators promise solver-level accuracy at a fraction of that cost, yet on wave-dominated fields the accurate ones are large: hybrid spectral-convolutional operators such as U-FNO (the strongest baseline in our study after DU-NO) buy their fidelity with tens of millions of parameters. We introduce DU-NO (Double U-shaped Neural Operator), a multiscale U-shaped spectral operator that attaches lightweight convolutional U-Net branches only at its two shallowest encoder and decoder levels. The placement follows a sampling argument: high-wavenumber content exists only on fine grids, so the local, full-band pathways go where that content lives, while the coarse, band-limited levels stay purely spectral. A depth-decaying mode schedule holds the model to 3.64M parameters, an order of magnitude below U-FNO. On our publicly released FUNWAVE-TVD benchmark, DU-NO attains the best autoregressive rollout error of six identically trained architectures, improving on U-FNO by 14.9% with 10.8x fewer parameters, and a frequency-band analysis shows the gain holds across all bands, including the high-wavenumber band where truncated-spectral operators collapse. Parameter-matched controls confirm the gain is architectural: rescaled to the same 3.6M budget, the best baseline still trails DU-NO by 28.6%. The advantage carries beyond nearshore waves: DU-NO matches the strongest baselines on 2D Navier-Stokes and wins clearly on PDEBench shallow-water rollouts. Code, trained models, and evaluation artifacts are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/duno-code-5A7B/.

AI.tldr: DU-NO is a 3.64M-parameter multiscale U-shaped spectral neural operator that enables accurate, low-cost autoregressive forecasting of nearshore wave dynamics, outperforming much larger baselines like U-FNO.
AI.motivation: Phase-resolving wave models (FUNWAVE-TVD) are accurate but computationally prohibitive for operational forecasting tasks such as ensembles, uncertainty quantification, and real-time warning. Existing accurate neural operators for wave-dominated fields, such as hybrid spectral-convolutional operators (U-FNO), require tens of millions of parameters, making them costly.
AI.method: The authors propose DU-NO (Double U-shaped Neural Operator), a multiscale U-shaped spectral operator that attaches lightweight convolutional U-Net branches only at the two shallowest encoder and decoder levels. This placement is justified by a sampling argument: high-wavenumber content exists only on fine grids, so local full-band pathways are placed where that content resides, while coarse band-limited levels remain purely spectral. A depth-decaying mode schedule constrains the model to 3.64M parameters.
AI.result: On a publicly released FUNWAVE-TVD benchmark, DU-NO achieves the best autoregressive rollout error among six identically trained architectures, improving on U-FNO by 14.9% with 10.8x fewer parameters. Frequency-band analysis shows gains across all bands, including the high-wavenumber band where truncated-spectral operators collapse. Parameter-matched controls confirm the gain is architectural: at the same 3.6M budget, the best baseline trails DU-NO by 28.6%. DU-NO also matches strongest baselines on 2D Navier-Stokes and wins on PDEBench shallow-water rollouts.
AI.conclusion: DU-NO demonstrates that careful architectural design—placing local convolutional pathways only at fine, high-wavenumber levels—yields solver-level accuracy at an order-of-magnitude lower parameter cost, enabling practical operational forecasting of nearshore wave dynamics while generalizing to other PDE problems.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Conflict Detection Against Operator-Conditioned Weather Hazards
summary: Strategic flight plan validation in Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) environments requires robust methods for predicting aircraft state uncertainty and detecting potential conflicts with dynamic airspace hazards. This paper presents a novel framework for uncertainty-conditioned trajectory prediction combined with polyhedra hazard representation for pre-flight conflict detection. We introduce a closed-form uncertainty estimation method that couples non-uniform rational B-spline (NURBS) curve fitting for kinematic trajectory generation with a Kalman Filter for state covariance propagation. Drawing from the Light Propagation Algorithm (LPA) paradigm, we employ a sigmoid-blended measurement noise model that captures the uncertainty reduction behavior of flight management systems approaching the required time of arrival (RTA) for waypoints. The resulting temporal uncertainty bounds are derived through a velocity-to-time variance transformation, enabling probabilistic assessment of arrival time deviations along the flight path. For hazard representation, we develop an operator-conditioned classification scheme that transforms gridded environmental data, specifically weather phenomena, into three-dimensional polyhedra volumes with intensity-based stratification. These hazard polyhedra incorporate aircraft-specific safety buffers computed from vehicle performance characteristics. Conflict detection is performed through mesh intersection algorithms operating on the spatial uncertainty tube surrounding the mean trajectory against the hazard polyhedra and temporal overlap. The framework enables the continuous strategic validation of flight plans throughout the pre-flight planning time horizon as environmental conditions evolve.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a pre-flight conflict detection framework for Advanced Air Mobility that combines closed-form aircraft state uncertainty prediction with polyhedral hazard representations to validate flight plans against dynamic airspace hazards.
AI.motivation: Strategic flight plan validation in AAM requires robust prediction of aircraft state uncertainty and detection of conflicts with dynamic airspace hazards, which existing approaches insufficiently address.
AI.method: A closed-form uncertainty estimation coupling NURBS curve fitting for kinematic trajectory generation with a Kalman Filter for covariance propagation; a sigmoid-blended measurement noise model inspired by the Light Propagation Algorithm to capture uncertainty reduction near waypoint RTA; velocity-to-time variance transformation for temporal uncertainty bounds; an operator-conditioned classification scheme converting gridded weather data into 3D intensity-stratified hazard polyhedra with aircraft-specific safety buffers; and mesh intersection algorithms testing the spatial uncertainty tube against hazard polyhedra with temporal overlap.
AI.result: The framework yields probabilistic arrival-time deviation bounds and enables conflict detection between the mean trajectory's uncertainty tube and hazard polyhedra, supporting continuous strategic flight plan validation as environmental conditions evolve.
AI.conclusion: The integrated uncertainty-conditioned trajectory prediction and polyhedral hazard representation provide a viable basis for continuous pre-flight conflict detection and strategic flight plan validation in AAM environments.

title: Mined from Scientific Literature: Process Schemas for Atomic Layer Deposition and Etching in Materials Science
summary: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) and atomic layer etching (ALE) are reported heterogeneously across experimental and simulation literature in materials science, hindering comparison and machine-actionable reuse. We present four domain-expert-reviewed JSON Schemas for ALD and ALE experimental and simulation processes. Curated with schema-miner and grounded in QUDT using schema-miner pro, the schemas structure materials, process conditions, configurations , and measured or predicted results. We compare their scope, structure, and semantic grounding, and demonstrate their use for schema-guided literature extraction and publication of structured records through ORKG templates.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces four domain-expert-reviewed JSON Schemas for atomic layer deposition (ALD) and atomic layer etching (ALE) experimental and simulation processes, grounded in QUDT and curated with schema-miner, enabling standardized, machine-actionable reporting and structured literature extraction via ORKG templates.
AI.motivation: ALD and ALE data are reported heterogeneously across experimental and simulation literature in materials science, which hinders comparison and machine-actionable reuse of results.
AI.method: The authors developed four domain-expert-reviewed JSON Schemas covering ALD and ALE experimental and simulation processes. The schemas were curated using schema-miner and grounded in QUDT using schema-miner pro, structuring materials, process conditions, configurations, and measured or predicted results.
AI.result: The paper compares the schemas' scope, structure, and semantic grounding, and demonstrates their application for schema-guided literature extraction and the publication of structured records through ORKG templates.
AI.conclusion: Expert-reviewed, semantically grounded JSON Schemas for ALD and ALE processes support standardized, machine-actionable data representation, facilitating comparison and structured reuse of experimental and simulation literature.

title: Can LLMs in Draft-Verify-Revise Pipelines Resolve Deictic Ambiguity?
comment: 86 pages including supplementary materials, 4 figures, 10 supplementary figures, 17 supplementary tables, 11 supplementary exemplars. Code and data: https://github.com/oekekezie/deictic-ambiguity-companion
summary: Draft-verify-revise is a common LLM orchestration pattern for scaling inference-time compute. One LLM drafts, a second critiques the draft and provides feedback, and a third uses that feedback to revise the draft into the final output. As context cascades between stages, LLMs at different stages can resolve a context-dependent expression such as "previous" differently. When that happens, the expression undergoes a deictic shift, a change in what it refers to. This phenomenon was studied with a synthetic dataset of 10 base examples, each rendered in three conditions. Holding the shared components constant, the conditions varied whether the draft stage LLM (the assistant) or the verify stage LLM (the grader) resolved the expression correctly, and how much independent reasoning the revise stage LLM (the meta-evaluator) needed to determine which reading was correct. Six models from three providers were tested across 21 reasoning effort configurations using e-values for sequential testing, in a primary experiment and an ablation experiment that removed error classification labels from the grader's feedback. A separate LLM analyzed the meta-evaluator's stated rationale for each wrong verdict. Balanced accuracy (the unweighted mean of sensitivity and specificity) ranged from 0.156, below chance, to near-perfect. GPT-5.2 rose from 0.156 without reasoning to 0.942 at its highest reasoning effort level, while Gemini 3 Pro stayed above 0.94 at every level. Gemini 3 Pro at low reasoning effort outscored GPT-5.2 at xhigh reasoning effort for roughly 5% of the cost per trial. When the meta-evaluator erred, it tended to rely on surface cues rather than operational reasoning. Context engineers implementing draft-verify-revise pipelines should be wary of deictic shifts and make the intended referent explicit at each stage.

AI.tldr: Draft-verify-revise LLM pipelines risk "deictic shifts" when context-dependent expressions like "previous" are resolved differently across stages. Using a controlled synthetic dataset of 10 base examples rendered in three conditions, the study found balanced accuracy ranging from 0.156 (below chance) to near-perfect across six models and 21 reasoning-effort configurations.
AI.motivation: Draft-verify-revise is widely used to scale inference-time compute, with one LLM drafting, a second verifying, and a third revising. Because context cascades between stages, each stage may resolve context-dependent expressions differently, causing a deictic shift in what an expression refers to. This failure mode was previously under-examined and needed systematic quantification.
AI.method: A synthetic dataset of 10 base examples, each rendered under three conditions, kept shared components constant while varying whether the draft-stage LLM (assistant) or verify-stage LLM (grader) resolved the expression correctly and how much independent reasoning the revise-stage LLM (meta-evaluator) needed. Six models from three providers were tested across 21 reasoning-effort configurations using e-values for sequential testing, in a primary experiment plus an ablation removing error-classification labels from grader feedback. A separate LLM analyzed the meta-evaluator's stated rationale for each wrong verdict.
AI.result: Balanced accuracy (unweighted mean of sensitivity and specificity) ranged from 0.156, below chance, to near-perfect. GPT-5.2 rose from 0.156 without reasoning to 0.942 at its highest reasoning-effort level, while Gemini 3 Pro stayed above 0.94 at every level. Gemini 3 Pro at low reasoning effort outperformed GPT-5.2 at xhigh reasoning effort for roughly 5% of the cost per trial. When the meta-evaluator erred, it tended to rely on surface cues rather than operational reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Deictic shifts materially impair draft-verify-revise pipelines, with performance driven more by model/effort configuration than by the task itself. Context engineers should be wary of these shifts and make the intended referent explicit at each stage; higher reasoning effort does not uniformly buy robustness, and cheaper models can match or exceed costly high-effort configurations.

title: Multi-Objective Agent-Based Model Predictive Controller for Plug-and-Play Vehicle Control
summary: Functional integration is a growing trend in vehicle control, often involving the coordination of multiple controllers to achieve various objectives simultaneously. The need for flexibility and reliability has led to a "plug-and-play" approach in control system design, which presents challenges for traditional integrated model predictive control (MPC). Agent-based model predictive control (AMPC) has recently emerged as a distributed solution that treats controllers as agents, creating a collaborative framework among them to reach a common goal. However, this approach struggles to manage distributed conflicting objectives when agents are coupled or interdependent. To address this, we propose a novel, practical distributed control scheme called multi-objective AMPC, which adapts the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) into a general control strategy that approximates global optimization while decoupling objectives. We systematically develop three formulations that maintain convergence while addressing control regularization and inequality constraints, applying them to complex vehicle control systems for the first time. The proposed method has been tested on two vehicle control scenarios with a multi-objective topology. Different formulations are compared through simulations, and the most computationally efficient one was implemented on an electric vehicle for real-world evaluations. The results demonstrate that the proposed multi-objective AMPC can converge approximately to the same global optimum as integrated MPC with greater flexibility and the potential to reduce computational costs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes multi-objective AMPC, a distributed scheme that adapts ADMM into a general control strategy to decouple conflicting objectives while approximating global optimization, and validates it on vehicle control systems.
AI.motivation: Functional integration in vehicle control requires coordinating multiple controllers simultaneously, and the plug-and-play design trend challenges traditional integrated MPC. Existing agent-based MPC (AMPC) struggles to manage distributed conflicting objectives when agents are coupled or interdependent.
AI.method: The authors introduce multi-objective AMPC, adapting ADMM into a general distributed control strategy that decouples objectives while approximating global optimization. They systematically develop three formulations that preserve convergence while handling control regularization and inequality constraints, then apply them to complex vehicle control systems.
AI.result: The method was tested on two vehicle control scenarios with a multi-objective topology. Simulations compared the three formulations, and the most computationally efficient one was deployed on an electric vehicle for real-world evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Multi-objective AMPC converges approximately to the same global optimum as integrated MPC, while offering greater flexibility and the potential to reduce computational costs.

title: GLARE: Generative Learning via Adversarial Reward Estimation For Social Dynamics Forecasting
summary: Meeting continuation requires tracking the agenda, speaker roles, participant intentions, and disagreement across long multi-party discussions. We introduce the Meeting Dynamic Forecasting Benchmark (MDFB), constructed from 2,207 real-world meetings and 24,794 future-facing queries. Given a transcript prefix and an active question, a model generates a plausible multi-turn continuation in one call. We evaluate utility---progress toward the question---and human-likeness---plausible conversational flow and role consistency---without requiring exact reproduction of the observed future. We further present GLARE, an adaptation of adversarial imitation learning to conditional language generation. A discriminator ranks the observed continuation above samples from the current actor, and its score supplies a KL-regularized policy reward; retraining on current-policy negatives allows the reward landscape to evolve with the actor. GLARE attains average human-evaluated win rates of 0.66 on utility and 0.70 on human-likeness, outperforming SFT and SPIN while remaining below the observed human continuation. We also demonstrate MDFB as a social reasoning arena for comparing general-purpose models, including closed-source systems, through reference-assisted judgments. Together, these studies illustrate the benchmark's use for both task-specific learning and output-based evaluation of meeting behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MDFB, a benchmark of 2,207 real meetings and 24,794 future-facing queries for multi-turn meeting continuation, and GLARE, an adversarial imitation learning method that reaches 0.66 utility and 0.70 human-likeness win rates.
AI.motivation: Meeting continuation demands tracking agendas, speaker roles, intentions, and disagreement over long multi-party discussions, yet existing evaluation requires exact reproduction of observed futures and lacks a benchmark for utility and human-likeness.
AI.method: MDFB gives a transcript prefix and active question; the model generates a multi-turn continuation in one call, evaluated on utility and human-likeness. GLARE adapts adversarial imitation learning to conditional generation: a discriminator ranks observed continuations above actor samples, its score provides a KL-regularized policy reward, and retraining on current-policy negatives evolves the reward landscape.
AI.result: GLARE achieves average human-evaluated win rates of 0.66 on utility and 0.70 on human-likeness, outperforming SFT and SPIN while remaining below observed human continuation. MDFB also serves as a social reasoning arena for comparing general-purpose and closed-source models via reference-assisted judgments.
AI.conclusion: MDFB supports both task-specific learning and output-based evaluation of meeting behavior, demonstrating its dual use as a training benchmark and a comparison arena.

title: A Data-Driven Distributed Control Scheme: Learning Multi-Objective Agent-Based MPC for Path-Tracking
comment: 7 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Author accepted manuscript of a paper published in IEEE ITSC 2024
summary: Agent-based model predictive control (AMPC) has recently been proposed for vehicle systems with various controllers, such as differential braking and torque vectoring, where controllers are regarded as distributed agents contributing to the same objective. However, this scheme is challenging in handling multiple conflicting objectives with coupled agents. A common approach for such tasks is the integrated MPC, where all objectives and agents are stacked together in one optimization. Nevertheless, as more agents and objectives are involved, the integrated MPC will face challenges like computational burdens and maintenance difficulties in practice. To this end, this paper proposes a learning multi-objective AMPC that can improve design flexibility and computing efficiency. First, under the assumption of information exchange, a multi-objective AMPC tailored from the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is proposed to decouple the system and achieve the same performance as the integrated scheme iteratively. Second, a learning-based method for initializing iterations is proposed to accelerate convergence. In addition, a data management method is proposed for real-time efficiency, and an authentication module is designed for learning reliability. We compare the proposed scheme against the integrated scheme via a combined path-tracking simulation for autonomous vehicles with various controllers. The proposed scheme achieves the same control performance as the integrated one while reducing the computational time by 43.5%. Furthermore, the learning-based method saves 88.6% more computational time than without learning, making it suitable for real-time implementation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a learning multi-objective agent-based MPC (AMPC) that decouples coupled agents and objectives via ADMM to match integrated MPC performance, and uses learning-based initialization plus data management and an authentication module to achieve real-time efficiency.
AI.motivation: Agent-based MPC handles distributed controllers as agents sharing one objective, but struggles with multiple conflicting objectives and coupled agents. Integrated MPC stacks all objectives and agents into a single optimization, yet scales poorly—suffering computational burden and maintenance difficulties as agents and objectives grow. A method is needed that retains integrated-MPC performance while improving design flexibility and computing efficiency.
AI.method: The authors first formulate a multi-objective AMPC derived from the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), assuming information exchange, to decouple the system and iteratively achieve the same performance as the integrated scheme. They then introduce a learning-based initialization of iterations to accelerate convergence, a data management method for real-time efficiency, and an authentication module for learning reliability. Validation uses a combined path-tracking simulation for autonomous vehicles with various controllers.
AI.result: The proposed scheme matches the control performance of the integrated MPC while reducing computational time by 43.5%. The learning-based initialization saves an additional 88.6% computational time compared with the no-learning case, supporting real-time implementation.
AI.conclusion: The learning multi-objective AMPC preserves integrated-MPC control performance while substantially cutting computation, and the learning-based initialization makes it suitable for real-time deployment.

title: Soft Symbol Grounding for Prototypical Concepts
comment: 20th Conference on Neurosymbolic Learning and Reasoning (NeSy 2026)
summary: Neuro-symbolic models are usually trained with supervision only on final labels, leaving the intermediate concepts unobserved. Since many concept assignments are consistent with a given label, training can predict labels correctly while recovering the wrong concepts, a failure known as a reasoning shortcut. Prototypical networks reduce shortcuts by anchoring each concept to a few labeled examples, but existing methods still couple perception and reasoning through a hand-crafted, task-specific differentiable loss that must be redesigned for every task. We introduce \textbf{Soft-PNet}, which removes this loss: it reframes concept grounding as a Metropolis walk over a precomputed cache of feasible symbolic solutions, guided by a prototype distribution built from a single labeled anchor per concept, and trains against one KL objective between the prototype-weighted cache and the network's concept predictions. The objective is identical across tasks and remains applicable when the solution space cannot be enumerated. On \texttt{MNIST-EvenOdd}, Visual Sudoku, and \texttt{Kand-Logic} under scarce supervision, Soft-PNet matches loss-engineered prototypical networks at the concept and label levels and recovers concepts that soft-grounding baselines miss, with no loss engineering and lower training time.

AI.tldr: Soft-PNet replaces hand-crafted, task-specific differentiable losses in prototypical neuro-symbolic networks with a unified KL objective, reframing concept grounding as a Metropolis walk over a precomputed cache of feasible symbolic solutions guided by a prototype distribution from one labeled anchor per concept.
AI.motivation: Neuro-symbolic models trained only on final labels leave intermediate concepts unobserved. Many concept assignments can yield the correct label while recovering wrong concepts, a failure called reasoning shortcut. Prototypical networks mitigate this by anchoring concepts to labeled examples, but existing methods couple perception and reasoning via hand-crafted, task-specific differentiable losses that must be redesigned for every task. The authors aim to remove this loss engineering.
AI.method: Soft-PNet reframes concept grounding as a Metropolis walk over a precomputed cache of feasible symbolic solutions, guided by a prototype distribution built from a single labeled anchor per concept. Training uses one KL objective between the prototype-weighted cache and the network's concept predictions. The objective is identical across tasks and remains applicable when the solution space cannot be enumerated.
AI.result: On MNIST-EvenOdd, Visual Sudoku, and Kand-Logic under scarce supervision, Soft-PNet matches loss-engineered prototypical networks at both concept and label levels and recovers concepts that soft-grounding baselines miss, with no loss engineering and lower training time.
AI.conclusion: A single task-agnostic KL objective over a prototype-guided Metropolis walk enables competitive concept and label accuracy without per-task differentiable loss design, while also reducing training time and improving concept recovery over soft-grounding baselines.

title: Battery-Aware Predictive Trajectory Planning and Control for Multirotors Under Disturbances
summary: This paper presents a battery-aware predictive trajectory-planning and control framework for multirotors operating under spatially localized disturbances. Candidate trajectories are evaluated through closed-loop vehicle--motor--battery propagation, allowing disturbance-induced control demand, electrical energy, battery evolution, and terminal-voltage-dependent actuator capability to enter the planning process. % A reduced-order battery model is numerically benchmarked against an independently implemented Simscape equivalent-circuit reference, with a power NRMSE of $0.64\%$ and a cumulative-energy discrepancy below $0.7\%$. % In a $150$-s, $640$-m mission containing three disturbance regions, the selected trajectory reduces electrical energy consumption by $7.46\%$ and position-tracking RMSE by approximately $72\%$ relative to the disturbance-aware fixed-reference baseline. % Planner ablations show that battery-dependent terms are nonbinding at nominal SOC but alter the selected trajectory under a depleted-battery stress condition. % Execution with multiple feedback controllers further demonstrates that controller selection changes the tradeoff among tracking accuracy, energy consumption, and actuator utilization. % The results demonstrate the benefit of accounting for predicted closed-loop energetic and battery--actuator consequences during trajectory selection.

AI.tldr: A battery-aware predictive trajectory-planning and control framework for multirotors under spatially localized disturbances, where candidate trajectories are evaluated via closed-loop vehicle–motor–battery propagation, reducing energy use by 7.46% and tracking RMSE by ~72% versus a disturbance-aware fixed-reference baseline.
AI.motivation: Multirotors operating under spatially localized disturbances face increased control demand that stresses actuator capability and electrical energy, yet conventional trajectory planning typically ignores closed-loop energetic and battery–actuator consequences. The paper motivates incorporating these effects into planning so that disturbance-induced demand, energy, battery evolution, and terminal-voltage-dependent actuator limits inform trajectory selection.
AI.method: The framework evaluates candidate trajectories through closed-loop vehicle–motor–battery propagation. A reduced-order battery model is numerically benchmarked against an independently implemented Simscape equivalent-circuit reference. Planning includes battery-dependent terms and is tested via planner ablations and execution with multiple feedback controllers.
AI.result: The reduced-order battery model achieved a power NRMSE of 0.64% and cumulative-energy discrepancy below 0.7% versus the Simscape reference. In a 150-s, 640-m mission with three disturbance regions, the selected trajectory cut electrical energy consumption by 7.46% and position-tracking RMSE by ~72% relative to a disturbance-aware fixed-reference baseline. Ablations showed battery-dependent terms are nonbinding at nominal SOC but alter trajectory selection under depleted-battery stress; controller selection changes the tradeoff among tracking accuracy, energy consumption, and actuator utilization.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for predicted closed-loop energetic and battery–actuator consequences during trajectory selection benefits multirotor operation under localized disturbances, and battery-dependent planning becomes consequential under depleted-battery conditions.

title: Learning Symbolic Constraint Representations from Examples: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach
summary: Learning user-defined concepts as constraint networks has been extensively studied in the constraint acquisition (CA) literature. However, existing approaches typically rely on intensive interactions with a human oracle, making the learning process costly in terms of time and number of queries. In this paper, we propose a neuro-symbolic framework for automatic CA that significantly reduces user involvement by introducing neural Oracle Transformer models which learn to emulate user responses and to generalize conceptual knowledge. Trained on previously available examples, the learned oracle interacts with a dedicated CA engine, FastCA, which systematically refines the oracle's responses into a sound, consistent, and interpretable constraint network. This neuro-symbolic interaction enables the recovery of structured symbolic models from data without prior domain knowledge. Our results demonstrate that this neuro-symbolic interplay effectively aligns data-driven pattern recognition with symbolic reasoning, offering a robust approach to automating model construction in combinatorial domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a neuro-symbolic framework for automatic constraint acquisition that uses neural Oracle Transformer models to emulate user responses, replacing costly human interaction while a CA engine (FastCA) refines responses into interpretable constraint networks.
AI.motivation: Existing constraint acquisition approaches rely on intensive interactions with a human oracle, making learning costly in time and number of queries. The authors aim to reduce user involvement while still recovering structured symbolic models.
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic framework introduces neural Oracle Transformer models trained on previously available examples to emulate user responses and generalize conceptual knowledge. The learned oracle interacts with a dedicated CA engine, FastCA, which systematically refines the oracle's responses into a sound, consistent, and interpretable constraint network.
AI.result: The neuro-symbolic interplay effectively aligns data-driven pattern recognition with symbolic reasoning, enabling recovery of structured symbolic models from data without prior domain knowledge. It offers a robust approach to automating model construction in combinatorial domains.
AI.conclusion: By combining neural oracle emulation with symbolic CA refinement, the framework automates constraint model construction with significantly reduced user involvement, bridging data-driven and symbolic reasoning.

title: Robust Prototypical Networks for Few-Shot Sensor Fault Diagnosis
summary: Industrial fault diagnosis often operates with only a handful of labeled fault examples, making few-shot learning attractive for sensor monitoring. Standard prototypical networks are simple and effective; however, their class prototypes may become unstable in the very-low-shot regime because each decision relies on a small support set. We propose \emph{Multi-Episode Prototypical Networks} (MEPN), which aggregate prototypes from multiple disjoint support episodes and use their mean as the final class representative, reducing prototype variance without changing the encoder architecture. We evaluate MEPN on the DeFACTO sensor dataset using five-way fault classification with synthetic bias, drift, spike, and noise faults injected into real industrial measurements. Over 100 independent runs, MEPN reaches \textbf{\SensorOneShotGcpn\%} in the per-episode one-shot setting ($K\!=\!1$ shot, aggregated over $N_{\text{agg}}\!=\!10$ support episodes), substantially above single-episode baselines. Under an equal 10-sample support budget, MEPN and ProtoNet at $K\!=\!10$ are statistically indistinguishable, confirming prototype accumulation as the mechanism rather than superior fixed-budget learning.

AI.tldr: MEPN aggregates prototypes across multiple disjoint support episodes to stabilize class representations in very-low-shot industrial fault diagnosis, reaching high accuracy in one-shot DeFACTO classification.
AI.motivation: Industrial fault diagnosis typically has only a handful of labeled fault examples, so few-shot learning is attractive for sensor monitoring. Standard prototypical networks are simple and effective, but their class prototypes can be unstable in the very-low-shot regime because each decision relies on a small support set.
AI.method: Multi-Episode Prototypical Networks (MEPN) aggregate prototypes from multiple disjoint support episodes and use their mean as the final class representative, reducing prototype variance without changing the encoder architecture.
AI.result: Evaluated on the DeFACTO sensor dataset with five-way fault classification and synthetic bias, drift, spike, and noise faults injected into real industrial measurements. Over 100 independent runs, MEPN reaches high accuracy in the per-episode one-shot setting (K=1 shot, aggregated over N_agg=10 support episodes), substantially above single-episode baselines. Under an equal 10-sample support budget, MEPN and ProtoNet at K=10 are statistically indistinguishable.
AI.conclusion: MEPN improves very-low-shot fault diagnosis by prototype accumulation, not by superior fixed-budget learning; the equal-budget comparison confirms prototype accumulation as the operative mechanism.

title: Do Influence-Derived Data Perturbations Enable Machine Unlearning? A Controlled Study of Three Plausible Roles
summary: We evaluate Deep Perturbation Learning (DPL), which perturbs training images and labels along influence-derived directions, in three roles in which prior work has positioned it for machine unlearning: a direct deletion signal (the strongest claim), a utility-preserving regularizer, and a warm start for adversarial unlearning. Evidence for the weaker roles has been used to support the stronger one, so we test each role separately under a matched protocol with exact-seed retraining baselines. An audit of the public implementation identifies two correctness issues: image directions are computed on augmented, normalized tensors but applied to raw images, and the label perturbation falls below float32 resolution, leaving labels unchanged. After correcting the image-perturbation pipeline, DPL fails the direct-deletion criterion on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 in all three paired seeds. Its utility effects are inconsistent in sign across seeds, and once direction-computation time is counted it underperforms simple warm-start baselines. A one-seed Tiny ImageNet check likewise does not favor DPL as a regularizer or warm start; preprocessing inconsistencies in the released code make the direct comparison there inconclusive. These results cover random instance deletion only and do not rule out influence-based methods in other deletion regimes. We release a role-matched evaluation protocol and an audit checklist for perturbation-based deletion claims.

AI.tldr: This paper audits Deep Perturbation Learning (DPL) for machine unlearning, uncovers two correctness bugs in its public implementation, and shows that after fixing the image-perturbation pipeline, DPL fails as a direct deletion signal and offers no consistent advantage as a regularizer or warm start.
AI.motivation: Prior work positions DPL in three increasingly weaker roles (direct deletion signal, utility-preserving regularizer, warm start for adversarial unlearning), yet evidence for the weaker roles has been used to support the strongest claim. The authors aim to test each role separately under a matched, exact-seed retraining protocol, since such role conflation can lead to overclaimed deletion capability.
AI.method: The authors evaluate DPL in three roles under a matched protocol with exact-seed retraining baselines. They audit the public implementation and identify two correctness issues: image directions are computed on augmented, normalized tensors but applied to raw images, and the label perturbation falls below float32 resolution, leaving labels unchanged. They then correct the image-perturbation pipeline and conduct paired-seed experiments on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 plus a one-seed Tiny ImageNet check, comparing DPL against simple warm-start baselines with direction-computation time counted. They also release a role-matched evaluation protocol and an audit checklist.
AI.result: After correcting the image-perturbation pipeline, DPL fails the direct-deletion criterion on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 in all three paired seeds. Its utility effects are inconsistent in sign across seeds, and once direction-computation time is counted, it underperforms simple warm-start baselines. The one-seed Tiny ImageNet check also does not favor DPL as a regularizer or warm start; preprocessing inconsistencies in the released code make that direct comparison inconclusive.
AI.conclusion: DPL does not substantiate the strong direct-deletion claim and provides no consistent benefit in the weaker regularizer or warm-start roles. These findings cover random instance deletion only and do not rule out influence-based methods in other deletion regimes. The authors contribute a role-matched evaluation protocol and an audit checklist for perturbation-based deletion claims.

title: Pneumatic neurons for soft robots enable inflate-and-fire networks for rhythmic motion
summary: Animals coordinate their movements through distributed neural circuits, but soft robots still typically depend on external, centralized electronics for control. Building soft robots that operate without centralized electronic controllers while remaining responsive to their environment remains a frontier challenge in soft robotics. In this work we introduce a soft-robot control architecture inspired by leaky integrate-and-fire models of biological neural circuits. The Pneumatic neuron (Pneu-ron) is a soft actuator that unifies energy conversion, logic, and actuation in one component. Each module combines a low-boiling-point fluid (LBF), a heater, and a mechanical switch into a self-excitable unit. Boiling the LBF inflates the module and triggers excitation and inhibition of adjacent modules in a process we call "inflate-and-fire". When interconnected into excitatory-inhibitory rings, Pneu-rons generate stable, sequential oscillations whose frequency emerges from the material dynamics and environmental conditions. By harnessing the inflation of Pneu-rons for actuation these networks can drive oscillatory locomotion of soft robots. Pneu-ron networks sustain oscillation under mechanical load and thermal variations, adapting through material physics rather than computation. Dynamical modeling of these networks reveals a dimensionless bifurcation diagram that dictates the network's oscillatory behavior. Encoding logic and actuation into material-level modules presents a new avenue for adaptive, electronics controller-free, soft robots.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "Pneu-ron," a soft actuator module inspired by leaky integrate-and-fire neural models that unifies energy conversion, logic, and actuation in a single component, enabling electronics-free oscillatory control and locomotion in soft robots.
AI.motivation: Soft robots typically rely on external, centralized electronic controllers for coordination, which limits their autonomy and responsiveness. Building soft robots that operate without centralized electronics while still responding to their environment remains a frontier challenge in soft robotics, motivating a bio-inspired, material-level control architecture.
AI.method: The Pneu-ron combines a low-boiling-point fluid (LBF), a heater, and a mechanical switch into a self-excitable unit. Boiling the LBF inflates the module, triggering excitation and inhibition of adjacent modules via an "inflate-and-fire" process. These modules are interconnected into excitatory-inhibitory rings to generate sequential oscillations, and the authors develop dynamical modeling yielding a dimensionless bifurcation diagram characterizing network oscillatory behavior.
AI.result: When interconnected into excitatory-inhibitory rings, Pneu-rons produce stable, sequential oscillations whose frequency emerges from material dynamics and environmental conditions. Harnessing Pneu-ron inflation for actuation drives oscillatory locomotion of soft robots. The networks sustain oscillation under mechanical load and thermal variations, adapting through material physics rather than computation.
AI.conclusion: Encoding logic and actuation into material-level modules offers a new avenue for adaptive, electronics controller-free soft robots. The dimensionless bifurcation diagram provides a design framework governing the network's oscillatory behavior.

title: AnchorVLN: Geometry-Anchored Vision-Language Grounding Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Navigation
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) in unseen indoor environments is useful in real-world robotics, where an agent must follow natural-language instructions, locate objects, and answer spatial questions without a pre-built map or fixed object vocabulary. Multimodal vision-language models (VLMs) provide strong open-vocabulary grounding and zero-shot reasoning, but struggle to emit reliable metric quantities such as range, bearing, and comparative spatial relations directly from images. Existing approaches address this by folding geometry into hand-engineered pipelines or asking models to output waypoints, requiring changes to the control stack for different robots, tasks, or vocabularies. We introduce AnchorVLN, an open-vocabulary VLN system built on a simple rule: the VLM proposes semantics; geometry decides metrics. It is realised as EMBODIED-NAV-MCP, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server driven by a VLM agent through a compact set of callable tools. Since no tool accepts distance in metres or bearing in radians, the schema enforces the semantic-geometry boundary without modifying the downstream autonomy stack. We benchmark both tasks of the CMU Vision-Language Navigation Challenge 2026: 30 instruction-following questions over 15 scenes and a frozen 45-question object-reference set. The full system achieves 64.4 percent on instruction following, dropping by 13.3 percentage points without controller modeling (t = 2.77). On object reference, geometric anchoring clears the challenge overlap threshold on 10 of 45 questions, versus 0 of 45 for direct coordinate estimation, reducing median center error from 3.37 m to 2.48 m.

AI.tldr: AnchorVLN is an open-vocabulary vision-language navigation system built on the principle "the VLM proposes semantics; geometry decides metrics," implemented as an MCP server with callable tools whose schema forbids metric outputs, achieving 64.4% on CMU VLN Challenge instruction following and improving object-reference geometric anchoring over direct coordinate estimation.
AI.motivation: Unseen indoor VLN is valuable for real-world robotics, requiring agents to follow natural-language instructions, locate objects, and answer spatial questions without a pre-built map or fixed object vocabulary. Multimodal VLMs offer strong open-vocabulary grounding and zero-shot reasoning but are unreliable at emitting metric quantities (range, bearing, comparative spatial relations) directly from images. Existing fixes fold geometry into hand-engineered pipelines or make models output waypoints, forcing control-stack changes across robots, tasks, and vocabularies.
AI.method: AnchorVLN enforces a semantic-geometry boundary: the VLM proposes semantics while geometry computes metrics. It is realized as EMBODIED-NAV-MCP, a Model Context Protocol server driven by a VLM agent through a compact set of callable tools. No tool accepts distance in metres or bearing in radians, so the schema enforces the boundary without modifying the downstream autonomy stack.
AI.result: Benchmarked on both CMU Vision-Language Navigation Challenge 2026 tasks (30 instruction-following questions over 15 scenes; frozen 45-question object-reference set): full system reaches 64.4% on instruction following, dropping 13.3 percentage points without controller modeling (t = 2.77). On object reference, geometric anchoring clears the challenge overlap threshold on 10/45 questions versus 0/45 for direct coordinate estimation, reducing median center error from 3.37 m to 2.48 m.
AI.conclusion: Separating semantics (VLM) from metric reasoning (geometry) via schema-constrained tools yields reliable open-vocabulary VLN without altering the autonomy stack, and geometric anchoring substantially outperforms direct coordinate estimation on object reference.

title: Affective Agent: On-Device Personalized Intervention Reasoning for Wearable Systems
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Internet Computing, Special Issue on Wearable Computing (Sep/Oct 2026). 4 figures, 2 tables
summary: Affective computing has advanced wearable state inference, but on-device reasoning about whether, when, and how to intervene remains challenging. We present Affective Agent, a three-layer reference architecture for personalized intervention reasoning under uncertainty on wearable-class hardware. It combines a compact sub-billion-parameter language model with physiological evidence, context, and user history to decide whether, when, and how to intervene, without cloud dependency or per-user retraining. The architecture is organized into three interacting layers (perception, personalization, and reasoning), adapting to individual users through host-managed structured memory evolution rather than per-user weight updates. We instantiate Affective Agent in indoor environmental quality control and evaluate it on held-out, simulator-generated longitudinal scenarios spanning physiological variation, context, signal quality, and intervention history. Results show that memory-driven personalization and two-pass structured reasoning improve intervention decisions within this synthetic evaluation. By moving the decision layer on-device, this work demonstrates a path from wearable state inference toward closed-loop, personalized intervention on wearable-class hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Affective Agent, a three-layer reference architecture (perception, personalization, reasoning) enabling personalized, uncertainty-aware intervention decisions on wearable-class hardware using a sub-billion-parameter language model and structured memory, without cloud dependency or per-user retraining.
AI.motivation: Affective computing has advanced wearable state inference, but on-device reasoning about whether, when, and how to intervene remains challenging. Existing approaches typically rely on cloud dependency or per-user retraining, which limits practical, personalized, closed-loop intervention on wearable-class hardware.
AI.method: The authors propose Affective Agent, a three-layer reference architecture combining a compact sub-billion-parameter language model with physiological evidence, context, and user history. It organizes computation into perception, personalization, and reasoning layers, achieving personalization through host-managed structured memory evolution instead of per-user weight updates. The architecture is instantiated in indoor environmental quality control and evaluated on held-out, simulator-generated longitudinal scenarios covering physiological variation, context, signal quality, and intervention history.
AI.result: Results show that memory-driven personalization and two-pass structured reasoning improve intervention decisions within this synthetic evaluation.
AI.conclusion: By moving the decision layer on-device, the work demonstrates a path from wearable state inference toward closed-loop, personalized intervention on wearable-class hardware, without cloud dependency or per-user retraining.

title: LoRA-RC: Reservoir Computing with Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: Reservoir computing (RC) trains only a linear readout over a fixed recurrent layer, making it fast and data-efficient for online prediction. However, a static reservoir degrades under system drift, readout-only adaptation is then insufficient, and unconstrained reservoir adaptation can destroy the echo-state and incremental stability properties that make RC reliable. This paper proposes LoRA-RC, which adapts the recurrent matrix through a low-rank correction driven by streaming prediction errors. The base reservoir and adaptation bases are fixed offline; a small core matrix is adapted online, projected onto a spectral-norm ball, and low-pass filtered at each step. The projection guarantees that every applied recurrent matrix remains within a certified contraction set, and an incremental input-to-state stability bound is established for the reservoir along each online adaptation path, with path-independent rate and gain. On a Lorenz system with an abrupt parameter drift, LoRA-RC cuts post-drift prediction error by 56% versus a fixed RC and 51% versus readout-only adaptation; ablations over 20 seeds show that removing the projection inflates this error by more than a factor of 40.

AI.tldr: LoRA-RC adapts a reservoir's recurrent matrix online via a low-rank correction driven by streaming prediction errors; a spectral-norm-ball projection keeps every adapted reservoir inside a certified contraction set while preserving incremental input-to-state stability, cutting post-drift error by 56% over a fixed reservoir and 51% over readout-only adaptation on a drifting Lorenz system.
AI.motivation: A static reservoir is fast and data-efficient for online prediction but degrades under system drift. Readout-only adaptation is then insufficient, while unconstrained reservoir adaptation destroys the echo-state and incremental stability properties that make reservoir computing reliable.
AI.method: LoRA-RC applies a low-rank correction to the recurrent matrix, driven by streaming prediction errors. The base reservoir and adaptation bases are fixed offline, while a small core matrix is adapted online, projected onto a spectral-norm ball, and low-pass filtered at each step. The projection guarantees every applied recurrent matrix stays within a certified contraction set, and an incremental input-to-state stability bound is established along each online adaptation path with path-independent rate and gain.
AI.result: On a Lorenz system with an abrupt parameter drift, LoRA-RC reduces post-drift prediction error by 56% versus a fixed reservoir and 51% versus readout-only adaptation. Ablations over 20 seeds show that removing the projection inflates this error by more than a factor of 40.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank, constrained online adaptation of the recurrent matrix enables reservoir computing to track system drift while retaining the contraction and incremental stability guarantees of a fixed reservoir, with projection being essential to stability and performance.

title: DATAFARM: Distribution-Aligned Task and Motion Planning for Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Collecting high-quality robot data remains a fundamental challenge for training robot foundation models. Task and motion planning (TAMP) offers a scalable way to generate demonstrations, but our experiments show that raw TAMP trajectories provide surprisingly little benefit when used to fine-tune pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models, despite successfully solving the target tasks. We hypothesize that this failure arises from a behavioral distribution mismatch between planner-generated trajectories and the data used to pretrain the VLA. To address this mismatch, we introduce DATAFARM: Distribution-Aligned Task And motion planning for Fine-tuning A Robot foundation Model, an approach that incorporates the pretraining distribution directly into TAMP trajectory generation. DATAFARM aligns generated trajectories with the pretraining data in robot joint configurations, motion style, and temporal execution profiles. We evaluate DATAFARM on three tabletop manipulation tasks that TAMP can perform and a cloth-folding task beyond the capability of TAMP. DATAFARM achieves an average success rate of 56.7%, substantially outperforming raw TAMP (8.3%) while approaching human teleoperation (61.7%). On Deformable Object Manipulation, which is outside the fine-tuning distribution, the fine-tuned model retains 85% success, compared with 90% for the pretrained model. These results show that aligning planner-generated demonstrations with the pretraining distribution can make TAMP an effective source of data for VLA fine-tuning. Website and code: https://prpl-group.com/datafarm/

AI.tldr: Raw TAMP trajectories poorly fine-tune pretrained VLAs due to behavioral distribution mismatch; DATAFARM aligns TAMP-generated trajectories with the pretraining distribution, boosting success from 8.3% to 56.7% and preserving 85% on out-of-distribution deformable tasks.
AI.motivation: Collecting high-quality robot data for training robot foundation models is a fundamental challenge. TAMP is a scalable way to generate demonstrations, but the authors experimentally observe that raw TAMP trajectories provide surprisingly little benefit for fine-tuning pretrained VLA models, even when the trajectories successfully solve the target tasks. They hypothesize this failure stems from a behavioral distribution mismatch between planner-generated trajectories and the data used to pretrain the VLA.
AI.method: DATAFARM (Distribution-Aligned Task And motion planning for Fine-tuning A Robot foundation Model) incorporates the pretraining distribution directly into TAMP trajectory generation. It aligns generated trajectories with pretraining data along three axes: robot joint configurations, motion style, and temporal execution profiles.
AI.result: Evaluated on three tabletop manipulation tasks performable by TAMP and a cloth-folding task beyond TAMP's capability. DATAFARM achieves 56.7% average success, versus 8.3% for raw TAMP, approaching human teleoperation (61.7%). On Deformable Object Manipulation, outside the fine-tuning distribution, the fine-tuned model retains 85% success vs. 90% for the pretrained model.
AI.conclusion: Aligning planner-generated demonstrations with the pretraining distribution makes TAMP an effective data source for VLA fine-tuning, overcoming the behavioral distribution mismatch that limits naive TAMP-based fine-tuning.

title: DWMP: Leveraging Dual World Models for Humanoid Obstacle Traversal
summary: Humanoid robots must traverse cluttered obstacle fields using onboard proprioceptive and visual observations, yet existing methods usually process multimodal observations without explicitly considering their different characteristics: proprioceptive observations are low-dimensional but governed by highly nonlinear robot dynamics, while egocentric visual observations are high-dimensional, noisy, and redundant. We propose DWMP (Dual World Model Policy), a framework that provides the actor with separate but complementary world-model representations for humanoid obstacle traversal. A Koopman-based dynamics world model lifts proprioceptive observations into a latent space where their temporal evolution is approximately linear, making the dynamics features easier for the actor to learn from. An RSSM-based visual world model compresses egocentric depth observations into compact stochastic states while preserving obstacle-related geometry. The student policy receives the fused latent representation for action generation, combining linearized proprioceptive dynamics with compressed visual perception. Experiments in simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show that DWMP improves obstacle traversal performance over baselines and supports real-world deployment under randomized obstacle layouts.

AI.tldr: DWMP is a dual world-model policy for humanoid obstacle traversal that processes proprioceptive and visual observations through separate, complementary world models—a Koopman-based dynamics model and an RSSM-based visual model—fusing them for a student policy.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid obstacle traversal methods process multimodal observations without explicitly accounting for their distinct characteristics: proprioceptive observations are low-dimensional but governed by highly nonlinear dynamics, whereas egocentric visual observations are high-dimensional, noisy, and redundant.
AI.method: The framework employs a Koopman-based dynamics world model that lifts proprioceptive observations into a latent space with approximately linear temporal evolution, and an RSSM-based visual world model that compresses egocentric depth observations into compact stochastic states preserving obstacle geometry. The student policy receives the fused latent representation to generate actions.
AI.result: Experiments in simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved obstacle traversal performance over baselines and successful real-world deployment under randomized obstacle layouts.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling the distinct characteristics of proprioceptive and visual observations via separate, complementary world models yields better humanoid obstacle traversal and supports real-world deployment.

title: BlueLM-GUI Technical Report: A Real-Device-Centric Flywheel for Self-Improving Mobile GUI Agents
summary: Mobile GUI agents are shifting from multi-module frameworks to native models trained end-to-end, yet industrial deployment faces three persistent gaps. Sandbox training produces a distribution mismatch with production environments; expensive real-device failures remain underutilized; and fixed benchmarks saturate, losing the power to guide iteration. We present BlueLM-GUI, a 35B-A3B mobile GUI agent built as a real-device-centric flywheel that closes these gaps through three principles. Every Sample Matters: a dual-track pipeline with Heterogeneous Triple-System Consensus evaluation and an Error Correction \& Derivation Module salvages every trajectory into usable supervision. Every Rollout Is Real: a three-stage recipe---continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and agentic reinforcement learning on hundreds of real phones---grounds every rollout in real production environments, so the capability the model learns transfers directly to deployment. Every Query Evolves: a quota-driven benchmark methodology with three orthogonal axes enables precise attribution and allows the benchmark to be systematically upgraded as the model improves. BlueLM-GUI achieves 87.4 on MobileGUI-VBench, surpassing the best closed-source model by 5.1 points, and 84.9 on AndroidWorld, the best result among open-source models and competitive with closed-source models. These results demonstrate that grounding model training and iterative improvement in both real devices and the three Every principles yields strong, robust, and transferable mobile GUI capability.

AI.tldr: BlueLM-GUI, a 35B-A3B mobile GUI agent, uses a real-device-centric flywheel built on three "Every" principles (Every Sample Matters, Every Rollout Is Real, Every Query Evolves) to close sandbox-to-production gaps, and achieves 87.4 on MobileGUI-VBench and 84.9 on AndroidWorld.
AI.motivation: Mobile GUI agents are transitioning from multi-module frameworks to native end-to-end models, but industrial deployment faces three persistent gaps: (1) sandbox training causes distribution mismatch with production environments; (2) costly real-device failures are underutilized as training signal; and (3) fixed benchmarks saturate and lose their ability to guide iteration.
AI.method: A three-principle, real-device-centric flywheel: Every Sample Matters—a dual-track pipeline with Heterogeneous Triple-System Consensus evaluation and an Error Correction & Derivation Module that converts every trajectory into usable supervision; Every Rollout Is Real—a three-stage recipe of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and agentic reinforcement learning conducted on hundreds of real phones; Every Query Evolves—a quota-driven benchmark methodology with three orthogonal axes enabling precise attribution and systematic benchmark upgrading.
AI.result: BlueLM-GUI scores 87.4 on MobileGUI-VBench, exceeding the best closed-source model by 5.1 points, and 84.9 on AndroidWorld, the top result among open-source models and competitive with closed-source models.
AI.conclusion: Grounding model training and iterative improvement in both real devices and the three "Every" principles yields strong, robust, and transferable mobile GUI capability, validating the real-device-centric flywheel as an effective paradigm for industrial mobile GUI agent deployment.

title: A Deployable Architecture for Robot-Mediated Tasks (DART): Evaluation in Socially Assistive Robot-Guided Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Exercises
summary: Socially assistive robots (SARs) can support structured health and well-being interventions, but hardware and cost constraints limit interaction complexity and longitudinal real-world deployments. We present DART: Deployable Architecture for Robot-Mediated Tasks, an architecture that extends SARs through a web application and cloud infrastructure, enabling visual content, user input, remote computation, and persistent data storage synergistically with the robot's physical embodiment, speech, and movement. We evaluated DART by instantiating it in an interatively-developed full-stack HRI system for helping university students with elevated generalized anxiety to complete cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) homework exercises. The resulting system, which used the low-cost open-source Blossom robot platform, was refined and evaluated through a participatory design process and multiple user studies, and finally evaluated in an in-lab study with 103 participants, and then a six-week in-home deployment with four participants. In the in-lab evaluation, participants showed significant within-session reductions in stress, state anxiety, and negative affect, and gave the platform a mean System Usability Scale score of 78.89. In the home deployment, the mean System Usability Scale score was 87.5, with positive qualitative feedback on usability. Participants across both groups identified speech input, visual presentation, and web-robot synchronization as priorities for improvement. These findings validate DART as an effective architecture for extending the capabilities of a low-cost SAR in both in-lab single-session and in real-world longitudinal deployments.

AI.tldr: DART is a web-and-cloud architecture that extends low-cost socially assistive robots, validated via a CBT-homework HRI system on the Blossom robot in a 103-participant lab study and a six-week in-home deployment.
AI.motivation: SARs can support structured health and well-being interventions, but hardware and cost constraints limit interaction complexity and longitudinal real-world deployment. The authors aim to overcome these limitations with a deployable architecture that augments a low-cost robot rather than relying on expensive hardware.
AI.method: The authors propose DART (Deployable Architecture for Robot-Mediated Tasks), which extends SARs through a web application and cloud infrastructure, synergistically combining visual content, user input, remote computation, and persistent data storage with the robot's physical embodiment, speech, and movement. DART was instantiated as a full-stack HRI system, developed iteratively, to help university students with elevated generalized anxiety complete CBT homework exercises. The system used the low-cost open-source Blossom robot and was refined via participatory design and multiple user studies, then evaluated in an in-lab study (N=103) and a six-week in-home deployment (N=4).
AI.result: In the in-lab evaluation, participants showed significant within-session reductions in stress, state anxiety, and negative affect, with a mean System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 78.89. In the home deployment, the mean SUS score was 87.5, accompanied by positive qualitative feedback on usability.
