Across both groups, participants prioritized speech input, visual presentation, and web-robot synchronization for improvement.
AI.conclusion: The findings validate DART as an effective architecture for extending the capabilities of a low-cost SAR in both in-lab single-session and real-world longitudinal deployments.

title: Is Gaussian Splatting Becoming Neural Again? A Taxonomy and Controlled Study of Learned Parameterization
summary: Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) combines explicit primitives with efficient rasterization, yet recent systems increasingly use neural networks to generate or share Gaussian parameters. We characterize this trend along five axes: attribute decoding, spatial sharing, view-conditioned decoding, topology generation, and amortized inference. An analysis of 19 representative methods shows that these choices address different limitations and cannot be reduced to a binary neural label. We also isolate three forms of neural parameterization in a controlled mip-NeRF 360 study. Sharing appearance and opacity improves reconstruction quality, while decoding geometric structure offers no further gain. The evidence favors selective neuralization: shared functions help when they capture reusable correlations without sacrificing the local geometric freedom of explicit splats.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes neural parameterization in 3D Gaussian Splatting across five axes, analyzes 19 methods, and shows through a controlled study that selectively "neuralizing" shared appearance/opacity helps while decoding geometric structure does not.
AI.motivation: Recent 3DGS systems increasingly use neural networks to generate or share Gaussian parameters, but this trend is often treated as a simplistic binary (neural vs. non-neural) distinction. The paper argues this obscures the varied roles neural components actually play and the different limitations they address.
AI.method: The authors characterize the trend along five axes: attribute decoding, spatial sharing, view-conditioned decoding, topology generation, and amortized inference. They survey 19 representative methods to show these choices address distinct limitations. They then isolate three forms of neural parameterization in a controlled mip-NeRF 360 study.
AI.result: Sharing appearance and opacity improves reconstruction quality, while decoding geometric structure offers no further gain.
AI.conclusion: The evidence favors selective neuralization: shared functions help when they capture reusable correlations without sacrificing the local geometric freedom of explicit splats. Neural parameterization cannot be reduced to a binary label.

title: READ: Learning Risk-Informed Fields for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving requires more than recognizing what is present in a scene: a planner must determine how road structure, surrounding agents, and their motion states should influence a future maneuver. Existing learning-based planners can capture these influences through latent scene features and trajectory decoders, but the relationship between environmental factors and candidate actions often remains implicit. This limits the ability to inspect, diagnose, or refine how scene context affects the safety of a predicted trajectory. Classical safety fields provide an explicit spatial representation of this relationship, but their risk shapes and relative weights are prescribed in advance and do not adapt to each scene. We introduce READ, a framework that learns an explicit, planning-aligned risk representation from complementary geometric and behavioral constraints. READ instantiates this representation as a continuous spatiotemporal field, enabling differentiable queries along candidate trajectories. The learned field connects scene understanding with action selection by encouraging predicted trajectories to align with low-risk regions, while retaining a differentiable interface for trajectory evaluation and refinement. READ integrates with both end-to-end planners and Vision-Language-Action models. Experiments on NAVSIM show consistent gains across matched end-to-end backbones and strong performance in a VLA setting; READ also achieves competitive results on NAVSIM v2. These results establish learned spatial risk as an explicit, adaptable representation for safe planning.

AI.tldr: READ learns an explicit, planning-aligned spatiotemporal risk field from geometric and behavioral constraints, providing a continuous, differentiable interface that guides and evaluates trajectories, yielding gains on NAVSIM and NAVSIM v2 with both end-to-end and VLA planners.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based planners capture scene influences only implicitly via latent features and decoders, obscuring how environmental factors shape candidate actions and limiting inspection, diagnosis, and refinement of safety. Classical safety fields are explicit but use prescribed, non-adaptive risk shapes and weights that do not adapt per scene.
AI.method: READ learns an explicit, planning-aligned risk representation from complementary geometric and behavioral constraints, instantiated as a continuous spatiotemporal field supporting differentiable queries along candidate trajectories. It connects scene understanding to action selection by encouraging trajectories to align with low-risk regions while retaining a differentiable interface for trajectory evaluation and refinement; it integrates with both end-to-end planners and Vision-Language-Action models.
AI.result: On NAVSIM, READ shows consistent gains across matched end-to-end backbones and strong performance in a VLA setting; it also achieves competitive results on NAVSIM v2.
AI.conclusion: Learned spatial risk serves as an explicit, adaptable representation for safe planning, bridging scene understanding and action selection while enabling differentiable trajectory evaluation and refinement.

title: Niching Agents in The Core
summary: The Core is a unique competitive co-evolution algorithm that allows agents to evolve autonomous control without utilizing a traditional fitness function. The agents evolve via local interactions through tournament selection, crossover, and mutation, producing offspring by evolving better controllers. Previous works have shown The Core's ability to evolve agents capable of combat and navigation in the Xpilot video game. This research expands upon that premise by niching agents to specific subsets of the original environment The Core was tested in. Our results demonstrate the niched agents capacity for success over agents niched to the entire system and agents niched to different sub-environments.

AI.tldr: This paper extends The Core, a competitive co-evolution algorithm, by niching agents to specific sub-environments of the Xpilot game, showing that specialized agents outperform those evolved for the full or other sub-environments.
AI.motivation: The Core eliminates the need for a traditional fitness function by relying on local interaction-driven co-evolution, and this research aims to further its premise by exploring whether niching agents into subsets of the original environment improves their evolutionary outcomes.
AI.method: Niching agents to specific subsets of the original Xpilot environment, leveraging The Core's tournament selection, crossover, and mutation mechanisms for autonomous controller evolution.
AI.result: Niched agents demonstrated a capacity for success over agents niched to the entire system and agents niched to different sub-environments.
AI.conclusion: Niching within The Core enhances agent performance, validating the benefit of environment specialization for competitive co-evolution.

title: Understanding Whole-Body Robot Teleoperation Strategies Under Diverse Task Objectives and Constraints
summary: This work investigates the control strategies of complex whole-body robot teleoperation that coordinate active perception, bimanual manipulation, and navigation. We developed a hybrid control framework, combining the free-form and constrained control, for the whole-body teleoperation of the TIAGo mobile manipulator. We conducted a user study to explore people's control strategies under different task constraints such as limited time and low tolerance of errors. Our results highlight the effective use of coordinated control in improving task efficiency and reducing the risk of reaching individual joint limits. We discuss our results and their implications for designing future whole-body robot teleoperation systems.

AI.tldr: This work develops a hybrid control framework (free-form + constrained) for whole-body teleoperation of the TIAGo mobile manipulator, and a user study examines control strategies under task constraints, showing coordinated control improves efficiency and reduces joint-limit risk.
AI.motivation: Whole-body teleoperation of mobile manipulators must simultaneously coordinate active perception, bimanual manipulation, and navigation. How human operators manage these coupled degrees of freedom under task constraints is not well understood, motivating the design of better teleoperation systems.
AI.method: A hybrid control framework combining free-form and constrained control was developed for whole-body teleoperation of the TIAGo mobile manipulator. A user study then explored participants' control strategies under varying task constraints, such as limited time and low error tolerance.
AI.result: Results indicate that coordinated control effectively improves task efficiency and reduces the risk of reaching individual joint limits.
AI.conclusion: The findings inform the design of future whole-body robot teleoperation systems, highlighting the benefits of coordinated control strategies.

title: OneLA: Scaling Linear-Attention Decoding to Large Beams in Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) relies on large-beam decoding to generate hundreds of candidate items, creating a new scaling challenge for recurrent linear attention. Existing linear attention serving systems either materialize a full recurrent state for every beam or repeatedly replay shared history, incurring substantial memory and traffic overhead. To address this, we present OneLA, a linear-attention decoding framework that exploits the shared prompt and short divergent suffixes of GR workloads. Specifically, OneLA represents all beam states using a single shared prompt-derived state and compact, append-only records of their divergent transitions. Using this representation, OneLA computes only the state information required at each decoding step, without reconstructing a full recurrent state for every beam. Furthermore, OneLA uses a lightweight ancestry index to track the transition records that make up each beam's history, allowing beams to be updated without moving or copying existing records. A fused GPU kernel further reuses the shared state across beams. Our analysis shows that OneLA achieves 1.54-2.46x end-to-end decode speedups while substantially reducing recurrent-state memory use and data movement.

AI.tldr: OneLA is a linear-attention decoding framework for generative recommendation that exploits shared prompts and short divergent suffixes across beams, using a single shared prompt state plus append-only divergent transition records to avoid full per-beam states, achieving 1.54-2.46x decode speedups.
AI.motivation: Generative recommendation relies on large-beam decoding to generate hundreds of candidate items, posing a scaling challenge for recurrent linear attention. Existing linear-attention serving systems either materialize a full recurrent state for every beam or repeatedly replay shared history, causing substantial memory and data traffic overhead.
AI.method: OneLA represents all beam states with a single shared prompt-derived state plus compact, append-only records of their divergent transitions. It computes only the state information needed at each decoding step without reconstructing a full recurrent state per beam. A lightweight ancestry index tracks the transition records forming each beam's history, enabling beam updates without moving or copying records. A fused GPU kernel reuses the shared state across beams.
AI.result: OneLA achieves 1.54-2.46x end-to-end decode speedups while substantially reducing recurrent-state memory use and data movement.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the shared prompt and short divergent suffixes typical of GR workloads enables efficient large-beam linear-attention decoding, mitigating the memory and traffic bottlenecks of per-beam state materialization.

title: FoldNet++: a Large-Scale Synthetic Dataset for Robotic T-Shirt Folding and Unfolding
summary: Due to the highly deformable nature of garments, training a generalizable policy for robotic T-shirt folding and unfolding remains a significant challenge. In this work, we present a large-scale synthetic dataset for robotic T-shirt folding and unfolding, covering 6 robotic embodiments, 1K T-shirts, 1K environmental assets, and 120K episodes with rich annotations, which can be used to train a wide range of manipulation policies. We first follow the FoldNet pipeline to generate a large-scale dataset of physically simulatable T-shirts with diverse appearances and annotated semantic keypoints. Based on these semantic keypoints, we then generate manipulation demonstrations for different robotic embodiments through a unified rule-based framework. We use these demonstrations to train visuomotor policies, and experimental results demonstrate that models trained solely on our synthetic data can achieve over 90\% end-to-end task success rates when directly deployed to unseen real-world environments and previously unseen T-shirts from arbitrary initial configurations. Project URL: https://pku-epic.github.io/FoldNetXX/.

AI.tldr: This work introduces a large-scale synthetic dataset (6 embodiments, 1K T-shirts, 1K environmental assets, 120K annotated episodes) for robotic T-shirt folding and unfolding, and shows that visuomotor policies trained solely on it achieve over 90% success in unseen real-world settings.
AI.motivation: Garments are highly deformable, making it difficult to train generalizable policies for robotic T-shirt folding and unfolding. Existing approaches lack large-scale, diverse, and well-annotated data spanning multiple embodiments and environments.
AI.method: The authors follow the FoldNet pipeline to generate physically simulatable T-shirts with diverse appearances and annotated semantic keypoints. Using these keypoints, they produce manipulation demonstrations for different robotic embodiments via a unified rule-based framework. The resulting demonstrations train visuomotor policies.
AI.result: Models trained only on the synthetic data attain over 90% end-to-end task success rates when directly deployed to unseen real-world environments and previously unseen T-shirts from arbitrary initial configurations.
AI.conclusion: A large-scale, richly annotated synthetic dataset with multi-embodiment demonstrations enables generalizable garment manipulation policies that transfer zero-shot to real-world T-shirt folding and unfolding.

title: Decentralized Evolution of Hexapod Gaits with Independent Leg Controllers
summary: This paper presents a novel approach to hexapod locomotion by evolving each leg's gait independently through a decentralized evolutionary algorithm. Using the Webots simulator and the Mantis hexapod robot, we optimize individual leg controllers without centralized coordination, allowing emergent behaviors to drive the development of efficient, coordinated locomotion. Our decentralized method is benchmarked against cooperative coevolution, demonstrating improved efficacy in generating stable and adaptive gaits while showing interesting emergent coordination. By enabling independent evolution of leg controllers, this method reduces the complexity of gait optimization and highlights the potential of decentralized strategies for scalable and adaptive robotic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper evolves each hexapod leg's gait independently using a decentralized evolutionary algorithm, optimizing leg controllers without centralized coordination to yield efficient and adaptive locomotion.
AI.motivation: Centralized gait optimization for hexapod locomotion is complex and scales poorly. The authors aim to reduce gait-optimization complexity and explore scalable, adaptive control strategies by decentralizing the evolution process.
AI.method: Individual leg controllers of the Mantis hexapod in the Webots simulator are evolved independently via a decentralized evolutionary algorithm, with no centralized coordination, permitting emergent coordination. The approach is benchmarked against cooperative coevolution.
AI.result: The decentralized method outperforms cooperative coevolution, generating more stable and adaptive gaits and exhibiting interesting emergent coordination.
AI.conclusion: Independent evolution of leg controllers simplifies gait optimization and demonstrates the potential of decentralized strategies for scalable, adaptive robotic locomotion.

title: IMPLY: Physically Anchored Consistency for World-Model Rollouts
summary: A world model asked what happens if an object is pushed at several speeds produces several futures. If the model has the object in mind, those futures agree about it: each implies the same mass and friction. The consistency checks now used to vet world-action models ask whether a model's futures agree with each other, and none of them knows any physics. We show that this is not enough, and what to do instead. IMPLY reads the physics each rollout implies by inverting a simulator and scores a set of rollouts by how well one object explains all of them, anchored to two calibration pushes the model has observed. In a controlled setting, self-consistency gives a perfect score to a model that ignores the object and always predicts a typical push; anchoring exposes it (AUROC 0.70 versus 1.00). On a real model, V-JEPA 2-AC adapted to the scene, the same thing happens. Given its own calibration pushes the model tracks the object (per-object correlation with the truth 0.91); given another object's, it does not (0.05). Self-consistency cannot tell these apart, preferring the right evidence on 52% of objects, chance level, while anchored disagreement prefers it on 73% and correlates 0.92-0.99 with the rollouts' error. Used to choose among candidate rollout sets, it comes within 0.003 of an oracle that sees the truth. A model that has internalised the wrong object is exactly as self-consistent as one that has internalised the right one; consistency has to be anchored to evidence.

AI.tldr: Self-consistency checks for world-action models are insufficient because a model that internalises the wrong object is just as self-consistent as one that internalises the right one. IMPLY instead reads the physics each rollout implies by inverting a simulator and scores rollouts by how well one object explains all of them, anchored to observed calibration pushes.
AI.motivation: World-action models that predict multiple futures for a scene should agree about a persistent object across those futures, but existing consistency checks only test whether futures agree with each other and incorporate no physics. The authors argue this is not enough: consistency must be anchored to evidence, otherwise a model that internalises an incorrect object passes.
AI.method: IMPLY inverts a simulator to read the physics that each rollout implies, then scores a set of rollouts by how well a single object explains them, anchored to two calibration pushes the model has observed. It is evaluated in a controlled setting and on V-JEPA 2-AC adapted to the scene, comparing self-consistency against anchored disagreement using AUROC, per-object correlation with ground truth, rollout error correlation, and oracle-based rollout set selection.
AI.result: In the controlled setting, self-consistency gives a perfect score to a model that ignores the object and always predicts a typical push, while anchoring exposes it (AUROC 0.70 versus 1.00). On the real model (V-JEPA 2-AC), with its own calibration pushes it tracks the object (per-object correlation 0.91) but with another object's it does not (0.05). Self-consistency cannot distinguish these, preferring the right evidence on 52% of objects (chance level), whereas anchored disagreement prefers it on 73% and correlates 0.92-0.99 with rollout error. For selecting among candidate rollout sets, it comes within 0.003 of an oracle with ground truth access.
AI.conclusion: A model with the wrong internalised object is exactly as self-consistent as one with the right object, so consistency alone cannot validate world-action models. Consistency must be anchored to evidence, and IMPLY's anchored physics inference provides a practical scoring method that approaches oracle performance.

title: Beyond ID Embeddings: Process-Grounded Language Modeling for Cognitive Diagnosis
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 20 pages, including references and appendices
summary: Cognitive Diagnosis Models (CDMs) play a pivotal role in personalized online learning. Traditional CDMs rely on discrete, ID-based embeddings to represent students, exercises, and concepts. This paradigm diverges from the nature of learner cognition, where knowledge is not stored and retrieved as isolated symbols. As a result, CDMs suffer from semantic limitations when new exercises or concepts appear. In this paper, we propose a Process-aware Language Cognitive Diagnosis (PLCD) framework that uses language-derived structures as cognitive priors and response records to calibrate student posterior states. PLCD leverages large language models (LLMs) to construct concept schemas and cognitive process graphs, and uses target-conditioned semantic memory to retrieve historical responses that are relevant to each target exercise. A process-grounded Language-to-Cognition Mapper with DA-MoE experts and process-level contrastive learning then maps the textual evidence into a unified cognitive space. Experimental results show that PLCD not only outperforms traditional baselines in predicting student performance but also exhibits strong cognitive transfer capabilities. These results connect the computational power of LLMs with the psychometric goal of measuring latent knowledge states, suggesting that structured language priors calibrated by response records can improve cold-start robustness and cognitive grounding.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PLCD, a Process-aware Language Cognitive Diagnosis framework that replaces discrete ID-based embeddings with LLM-derived language structures (concept schemas, cognitive process graphs) as cognitive priors, calibrated by response records via a process-grounded Language-to-Cognition Mapper, achieving better performance prediction and cognitive transfer.
AI.motivation: Traditional CDMs rely on discrete, ID-based embeddings for students, exercises, and concepts, which diverges from the nature of learner cognition where knowledge is not stored as isolated symbols. This causes semantic limitations when new exercises or concepts appear (cold-start problems).
AI.method: PLCD uses LLMs to construct concept schemas and cognitive process graphs, and employs target-conditioned semantic memory to retrieve historical responses relevant to each target exercise. A process-grounded Language-to-Cognition Mapper with DA-MoE experts and process-level contrastive learning maps textual evidence into a unified cognitive space, using language-derived structures as cognitive priors and response records to calibrate student posterior states.
AI.result: PLCD outperforms traditional baselines in predicting student performance and exhibits strong cognitive transfer capabilities, improving cold-start robustness and cognitive grounding.
AI.conclusion: The results connect the computational power of LLMs with the psychometric goal of measuring latent knowledge states, suggesting that structured language priors calibrated by response records can improve cold-start robustness and cognitive grounding.

title: PATH: Continuous Target Sensing among Autonomous Cooperative Drones
summary: Continuous target sensing by uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) is constrained by limited flight endurance, motivating the transfer of tracking responsibility between cooperating UAVs. Such a handoff requires the receiver to identify the same physical target currently tracked by the sender despite differences in viewpoint, scale, and target appearance. Existing approaches based on global target localization or appearance-based cross-view association are limited by positioning uncertainty or ambiguous visual features. This paper presents Perspective Alignment \& Tracking Handoff (\textbf{PATH}), a platform-agnostic, geometry-assisted sensing and verification framework for target handoff between two moving UAVs. The sender reconstructs the tracked target as a metric 3D point using RGB-D sensing, while the receiver estimates its relative pose from a fiducial observation and projects the transmitted target point into its own image as a spatial prior for target acquisition. The receiver-generated candidate is then returned to the sender and verified through a cross-view Mutual Agreement Handshake before tracking responsibility is transferred. Real-world UAV experiments show mean relative-position and target-position errors of 0.047~m and 0.030~m, respectively. Under visually ambiguous conditions, PATH achieves 96.0\% frame-level receiver-side target acquisition accuracy, with 2.0\% false-positive and 2.0\% false-negative rates. A sensor-error sensitivity analysis shows that relative-pose uncertainty is the dominant contributor to receiver-view projection error. The implementation operates at video rate with compact inter-UAV communication below 16~kB/s at 60~Hz, demonstrating the feasibility of lightweight geometry-assisted target handoff on resource-constrained UAV platforms.

AI.tldr: PATH is a platform-agnostic, geometry-assisted framework enabling continuous target tracking handoff between two moving UAVs, combining RGB-D 3D target reconstruction, fiducial-based relative pose estimation, spatial-prior projection, and a cross-view Mutual Agreement Handshake for verification.
AI.motivation: UAV-based continuous target sensing is limited by flight endurance, so tracking responsibility must be transferred between cooperating UAVs. This handoff is difficult because the receiving UAV must re-identify the same physical target under viewpoint, scale, and appearance changes. Global localization approaches suffer from positioning uncertainty, while appearance-based cross-view association fails under ambiguous visual features.
AI.method: The sender reconstructs the tracked target as a metric 3D point using RGB-D sensing. The receiver estimates its relative pose from a fiducial observation and projects the transmitted target point into its own image as a spatial prior for target acquisition. The receiver-generated candidate is sent back to the sender and verified via a cross-view Mutual Agreement Handshake before tracking responsibility transfer.
AI.result: Real-world UAV experiments yielded mean relative-position and target-position errors of 0.047 m and 0.030 m. Under visually ambiguous conditions, PATH reached 96.0% frame-level receiver-side acquisition accuracy with 2.0% false-positive and 2.0% false-negative rates. Sensitivity analysis identified relative-pose uncertainty as the dominant contributor to receiver-view projection error. The system runs at video rate with inter-UAV communication under 16 kB/s at 60 Hz.
AI.conclusion: PATH demonstrates the feasibility of lightweight, geometry-assisted target handoff on resource-constrained UAV platforms, offering accurate and verifiable tracking transfer without relying on global localization or unambiguous appearance features.

title: VRL-Bench: Benchmarking agents on computer control tasks under finite trial budgets
summary: Learning from trial and error is a promising way to improve language agents on complex tasks such as computer control. Reflexion introduced verbal reinforcement learning, which turns failed trials into text that guides later attempts without updating model parameters. We introduce VRL-Bench, a harness for fair evaluation of trial-and-error learning under finite trial budgets. Across three models on MiniWoB and WebShop, we evaluate updates from several prominent verbal-memory methods spanning Reflexion and later work: each improves observed success over memory-free retry in some settings but reduces it in others. Replay experiments show that using reflection can reduce success rates, revealing a trade-off between exploiting experience and continued exploration. We propose VEX$^2$, a verbal exploration--exploitation scheduler that uses a language model to jointly select policies and allocate the remaining trial budget. VEX$^2$ is the only evaluated update to achieve positive observed success-rate gains over retry in all six settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VRL-Bench, a harness for fair evaluation of trial-and-error learning in language agents under finite trial budgets, and proposes VEX², a verbal exploration–exploitation scheduler that is the only evaluated update to yield positive success-rate gains over retry across all six settings tested.
AI.motivation: Trial-and-error learning, exemplified by Reflexion's verbal reinforcement learning, is promising for improving language agents on complex tasks like computer control. However, prior verbal-memory methods are not fairly compared under finite trial budgets, and it is unclear whether turning failed trials into guiding text reliably improves success.
AI.method: The authors build VRL-Bench, a harness enabling fair evaluation of trial-and-error learning under finite trial budgets. They evaluate prominent verbal-memory updates (Reflexion and later work) across three models on MiniWoB and WebShop. They also run replay experiments and propose VEX², a verbal exploration–exploitation scheduler where a language model jointly selects policies and allocates the remaining trial budget.
AI.result: Each evaluated verbal-memory method improves observed success over memory-free retry in some settings but reduces it in others. Replay experiments show that using reflection can reduce success rates, revealing a trade-off between exploiting experience and continued exploration. VEX² is the only evaluated update achieving positive observed success-rate gains over retry in all six settings.
AI.conclusion: Verbal-memory updates do not uniformly help; reflection can harm performance due to an exploration–exploitation trade-off. Explicitly scheduling exploration and exploitation via a language model, as in VEX², provides consistent gains over retry, suggesting that budget-aware scheduling is key to effective trial-and-error learning for language agents.

title: SoK: Rethinking Jailbreaking in the Era of Agentic AI: Attacks, Defenses, and Practical Consideration
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into agentic AI systems that reason, plan, invoke tools, maintain persistent memory, communicate with other agents, and execute multi-step tasks. At the same time, modern models exhibit substantially stronger native safety alignment than earlier generations on which many jailbreak attacks and defenses were originally studied. This shift raises a fundamental question: \textit{which established jailbreak-security findings remain valid in the era of modern LLMs and agentic AI?} We address this question through a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) that reframes jailbreak security around the full agentic execution pipeline. We develop unified taxonomies of attacks and defenses spanning user interaction, planning and reasoning, memory, tool use, and inter-agent communication, and introduce a security--utility--efficiency evaluation framework that separates native harmful-prompt safety, adversarial jailbreak robustness, and agent-level security outcomes. We further conduct a controlled empirical study of representative attacks and defenses within a common agentic framework. Our results reveal three important gaps. First, strong native alignment does not imply robustness to adversarial jailbreaks. Second, defense effectiveness is highly model-, attack-, and component-dependent and can come at substantial cost in over-refusal, utility, and latency. Third, low final-response attack success can mask severe intermediate compromise: planning, memory, and tool interactions may remain unsafe even when the final response is successfully filtered. These findings motivate a shift from response-centric jailbreak defense toward cross-layer, execution-aware security that protects agent state, component transitions, and external actions while preserving practical utility and efficiency.

AI.tldr: This SoK reframes jailbreak security around the full agentic execution pipeline (interaction, planning, memory, tools, inter-agent communication), providing unified attack/defense taxonomies and a security-utility-efficiency evaluation framework. A controlled empirical study shows native alignment ≠ adversarial robustness, defense effectiveness is highly context-dependent, and low final-response attack success can mask severe intermediate compromise.
AI.motivation: LLMs are evolving from conversational assistants into agentic AI systems (reasoning, planning, tool invocation, persistent memory, inter-agent communication, multi-step execution), while modern models have substantially stronger native safety alignment than the earlier generations on which most jailbreak attacks and defenses were studied. This raises the question of which established jailbreak-security findings still hold, motivating a re-examination of jailbreak security across the full agentic pipeline.
AI.method: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) that reframes jailbreak security around the full agentic execution pipeline. The authors develop unified taxonomies of attacks and defenses spanning user interaction, planning and reasoning, memory, tool use, and inter-agent communication, and introduce a security-utility-efficiency evaluation framework separating native harmful-prompt safety, adversarial jailbreak robustness, and agent-level security outcomes. They then conduct a controlled empirical study of representative attacks and defenses within a common agentic framework.
AI.result: Three gaps emerge: (1) strong native alignment does not imply robustness to adversarial jailbreaks; (2) defense effectiveness is highly model-, attack-, and component-dependent and can incur substantial costs in over-refusal, utility, and latency; (3) low final-response attack success can mask severe intermediate compromise—planning, memory, and tool interactions may remain unsafe even when the final response is successfully filtered.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate a shift from response-centric jailbreak defense toward cross-layer, execution-aware security that protects agent state, component transitions, and external actions while preserving practical utility and efficiency.

title: Communication-Constrained Multi-Robot Exploration With Adaptive Communication Windows
summary: Exploring unknown environments with multi-robot teams can improve efficiency by allowing robots to explore in parallel. However, realizing these gains requires effective information sharing. When communication is intermittent, robots must balance the benefits of sharing information against the cost of diverting from exploration to establish communication. This paper introduces MACE, a decentralized exploration framework that actively evaluates whether establishing communication is worthwhile. At scheduled communication windows, robots estimate the cost of reaching previously identified communication locations. By formulating this decision as a variant of the Vehicle Orienteering Problem, robots evaluate routes based on the travel required to establish communication and the exploration that can be completed along the way. This approach enables robots to communicate more frequently than under purely opportunistic strategies while reducing the unnecessary travel associated with fixed rendezvous strategies. Across a set of simulated environments with varying size and geometry, we demonstrate that MACE reduces the total exploration time by up to 23% compared to existing communication-constrained exploration strategies.

AI.tldr: MACE is a decentralized multi-robot exploration framework that decides whether establishing communication is worthwhile by formulating the decision as a Vehicle Orienteering Problem variant, reducing total exploration time by up to 23% over existing communication-constrained strategies.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot teams can improve exploration efficiency through parallel exploration, but this requires effective information sharing. Under intermittent communication, robots face a trade-off: sharing information versus diverting from exploration to establish communication. Existing opportunistic and fixed rendezvous strategies are suboptimal—the former communicates too rarely, the latter incurs unnecessary travel.
AI.method: MACE actively evaluates whether establishing communication is worthwhile. At scheduled communication windows, robots estimate the cost of reaching previously identified communication locations. The decision is formulated as a variant of the Vehicle Orienteering Problem, where routes are evaluated based on the travel required to establish communication and the exploration that can be completed along the way.
AI.result: Across simulated environments with varying size and geometry, MACE reduces total exploration time by up to 23% compared to existing communication-constrained exploration strategies. It enables more frequent communication than purely opportunistic strategies while reducing unnecessary travel compared to fixed rendezvous strategies.
AI.conclusion: MACE demonstrates that actively reasoning about the trade-off between communication and exploration, via a Vehicle Orienteering Problem formulation, yields a more effective decentralized communication-constrained exploration policy than opportunistic or fixed-rendezvous baselines.

title: Hierarchical Belief Modeling for Zero-Shot Opponent Adaptation in Partially Observable Multi-Agent Navigation
summary: Lux AI Season 3 requires agents to act under partial observability, randomized episode level dynamics, and a best of five match structure that rewards both tactical execution and fast adaptation. We present HORIZON, a hierarchical agent that combines symmetry aware spatial perception, dual memory belief tracking, relic centric graph attention, information gain driven exploration, and an opponent conditioned policy mixture. HORIZON separates short horizon control from cross match meta reasoning, while auxiliary belief and world model objectives stabilize learning. Trained with PPO in a large scale JAX simulator, the resulting agent explicitly infers hidden game parameters and opponent style. Experiments show consistent gains in match win rate, episode win rate, adaptation gain, and league rating over strong recurrent and feed forward baselines.

AI.tldr: HORIZON is a hierarchical agent for Lux AI Season 3 that combines spatial perception, dual memory belief tracking, relic graph attention, information gain exploration, and an opponent conditioned policy mixture to win under partial observability and randomized dynamics.
AI.motivation: Lux AI Season 3 demands agents act under partial observability, randomized episode level dynamics, and a best of five match structure rewarding both tactical execution and fast adaptation.
AI.method: Combines symmetry aware spatial perception, dual memory belief tracking, relic centric graph attention, information gain driven exploration, and an opponent conditioned policy mixture. Separates short horizon control from cross match meta reasoning with auxiliary belief and world model objectives. Trained with PPO in a large scale JAX simulator.
AI.result: Consistent gains in match win rate, episode win rate, adaptation gain, and league rating over strong recurrent and feed forward baselines.
AI.conclusion: The agent explicitly infers hidden game parameters and opponent style, showing hierarchical meta reasoning plus belief/world model auxiliary objectives yield superior adaptation and competitive performance.

title: Autonomous Precision Milling of Biological Structures via Generic Anatomical Priors and Active Boundary Perception
comment: 18 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO) for possible publication
summary: Autonomous precision milling of biological structures is challenged by incomplete knowledge of target geometry, local material thickness, and critical internal boundaries. Subject-specific preoperative models can address geometric and thickness variations, but static models cannot determine boundary status encountered during execution, while repeated target-specific imaging limits scalability. This article presents an uncertainty-aware autonomous milling framework that assigns complementary roles to generic anatomical priors and active boundary perception. A generic anatomical prior provides conservative global guidance and is transformed through semantic-guided registration and hybrid vision-force calibration into robot-executable guidance for individual targets. As milling approaches uncertain boundaries, the robot actively probes the remaining structure and uses relative stiffness changes to estimate boundary status and structural detachability. A state-adaptive controller governs transitions between active perception and spatially selective incremental refinement, repeating this cycle until the termination criterion is satisfied. Hierarchical experiments on biological surrogates and in vivo mouse cranial window creation demonstrate accurate anatomical prior transfer, reliable boundary adaptation, and autonomous precision milling of biological structures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an uncertainty-aware autonomous milling framework that combines generic anatomical priors with active boundary perception for precise milling of biological structures.
AI.motivation: Autonomous precision milling of biological structures is difficult due to incomplete knowledge of target geometry, local material thickness, and critical internal boundaries. Subject-specific models handle geometric variation but cannot assess boundary status during execution, and repeated target-specific imaging is not scalable.
AI.method: The framework assigns complementary roles to generic anatomical priors and active boundary perception. A generic prior offers conservative global guidance, which is converted into robot-executable guidance via semantic-guided registration and hybrid vision-force calibration. Near uncertain boundaries, the robot actively probes remaining structure and estimates boundary status and detachability from relative stiffness changes. A state-adaptive controller manages transitions between active perception and spatially selective incremental refinement, iterating until the termination criterion is met.
AI.result: Hierarchical experiments on biological surrogates and in vivo mouse cranial window creation show accurate anatomical prior transfer, reliable boundary adaptation, and autonomous precision milling of biological structures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed uncertainty-aware framework enables autonomous precision milling of biological structures by integrating generic anatomical priors with active boundary perception and adaptive control.

title: LifeFuse-Mem: Lifecycle-Aware State Fusion Against Temporary Overwriting for Long-Term Memory
summary: Long-running LLM agents require memory mechanisms that maintain coherent internal states across interactions. We study a lifecycle-labeled memory setting in which write episodes provide lifecycle metadata during training, and phase-aware readout is used during evaluation. This setting reflects the need to distinguish information that should remain influential across future interactions from information that should affect only the current context. A mismatch between these lifecycles can cause temporary information to overwrite durable knowledge, leading to behavioral drift in persistent agents. Within this setting, we introduce \textbf{LifeFuse-Mem}, a lifecycle-aware neural memory framework that separates information according to its temporal commitment. LifeFuse-Mem uses dedicated memory components and lifecycle-aware updates to allow stable and transient knowledge to evolve locally without converting temporary context into durable state. On the controlled anti-overwrite benchmark, LifeFuse-Mem improves acquisition-controlled retention and reduces temporary overwrite; on two public long-memory benchmarks, it remains broadly competitive. These results suggest that explicit lifecycle signals can help diagnose and mitigate overwrite in compact online memory.

AI.tldr: LifeFuse-Mem is a lifecycle-aware neural memory framework for long-running LLM agents that separates stable from transient knowledge using dedicated memory components and lifecycle-aware updates, reducing temporary overwrite and behavioral drift.
AI.motivation: Long-running LLM agents need memory mechanisms that maintain coherent internal states across interactions. A key challenge is that a mismatch between the lifecycles of different information types can cause temporary information to overwrite durable knowledge, leading to behavioral drift in persistent agents.
AI.method: The paper studies a lifecycle-labeled memory setting where write episodes provide lifecycle metadata during training and phase-aware readout is used during evaluation. Within this setting, the authors introduce LifeFuse-Mem, which uses dedicated memory components and lifecycle-aware updates so that stable and transient knowledge evolve locally without converting temporary context into durable state.
AI.result: On a controlled anti-overwrite benchmark, LifeFuse-Mem improves acquisition-controlled retention and reduces temporary overwrite. On two public long-memory benchmarks, it remains broadly competitive.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that explicit lifecycle signals can help diagnose and mitigate overwrite in compact online memory.

title: STAR: Sparse Tactile Representation Learning in Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Models for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Dexterous manipulation requires coordinated multi-finger control and effective tactile feedback, yet learning these capabilities remains challenging due to the lack of large-scale real-world data and the difficulty of extracting effective representations from sparse tactile signals. We build a robot platform and teleoperation system to collect a 200-hour bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with synchronized visual, tactile, and language annotations, comprising 10,576 trajectories across 65 tasks, 69.5% of which involve dexterous multi-finger manipulation. We further propose STAR, an integrated training recipe for vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) models that addresses the spatial, temporal, and informational sparsity of tactile signals through visual-tactile joint pre-training, sparse-global tactile token representation, and sparse future tactile prediction. Trained on this dataset, STAR achieves a 61% average success rate across four real-world tasks with 100 post-training trajectories per task, demonstrating dexterous performance under task-specific post-training.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a 200-hour bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with synchronized vision, tactile, and language data, plus an integrated VTLA training recipe (STAR) that handles tactile sparsity and reaches 61% average success on four real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation requires coordinated multi-finger control and effective tactile feedback, but progress is constrained by the absence of large-scale real-world data and the difficulty of extracting useful representations from sparse tactile signals.
AI.method: The authors build a robot platform and teleoperation system to collect a 200-hour bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset (10,576 trajectories, 65 tasks, 69.5% involving multi-finger manipulation) with synchronized visual, tactile, and language annotations. They propose STAR, a training recipe for vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) models comprising visual-tactile joint pre-training, sparse-global tactile token representation, and sparse future tactile prediction, addressing spatial, temporal, and informational sparsity in tactile signals.
AI.result: Trained on the collected dataset, STAR achieves a 61% average success rate across four real-world tasks, with 100 post-training trajectories per task, demonstrating dexterous performance under task-specific post-training.
AI.conclusion: Combining large-scale real-world multimodal data with a sparsity-aware VTLA training recipe enables effective dexterous manipulation and provides a foundation for vision-tactile-language-action learning.

title: Do LLMs Trust the Accuser or the Accusation? Measuring Belief Shifts in Werewolf
comment: Accepted by the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026 Main Conference)
summary: Social-deduction games such as Werewolf are increasingly used to evaluate LLM agents, but existing evaluations often rely on final game outcomes. We propose a belief-shift evaluation benchmark in Werewolf for analyzing communication skills through belief updating. Using LLM-played games, we annotate suspicion and accusation messages and measure how an observing village-side model's beliefs change after each message. We evaluate 40 open-weight LLM configurations on 1,224 annotated messages. Our results show that larger models better distinguish true wolves from villagers based on game history, but accusations still strongly influence their beliefs. Models become more suspicious of the accused target and less suspicious of the accuser, especially when the accuser is trusted, even if the accuser is wolf-aligned. Larger models better resist accusations from accusers they already distrust. Overall, our findings suggest that current open-weight LLMs up to 120B parameters still struggle to integrate accusation content with source trust in strategic communication. Our benchmark and code are available at https://rlg.iis.sinica.edu.tw/papers/werewolf-accusation-benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a belief-shift evaluation benchmark for Werewolf that measures how an observing LLM's beliefs update after suspicion/accusation messages, rather than relying on final game outcomes. Evaluating 40 open-weight LLM configurations on 1,224 annotated messages, it finds that larger models better distinguish wolves from villagers but remain strongly swayed by accusations, often trusting accusers even when wolf-aligned.
AI.motivation: Social-deduction games like Werewolf are increasingly used to evaluate LLM agents, yet existing evaluations mostly rely on final game outcomes, which are coarse and fail to capture the underlying communication skills. The authors aim to analyze communication skills more directly through belief updating.
AI.method: They build a belief-shift evaluation benchmark in Werewolf. Using LLM-played games, they annotate suspicion and accusation messages, then measure how an observing village-side model's beliefs change after each message. They evaluate 40 open-weight LLM configurations across 1,224 annotated messages.
AI.result: Larger models better distinguish true wolves from villagers based on game history, but accusations still strongly influence their beliefs: models become more suspicious of the accused and less suspicious of the accuser, especially when the accuser is trusted, even if the accuser is wolf-aligned. Larger models better resist accusations from already-distrusted accusers.
AI.conclusion: Current open-weight LLMs up to 120B parameters still struggle to integrate accusation content with source trust in strategic communication. The benchmark and code are publicly released.

title: A Hierarchical Coverage Path Planning Algorithm for Unknown Environments
summary: This paper presents an online coverage path planning algorithm for unknown environments. During navigation, the initially unknown search area is progressively decomposed into disconnected subareas as new obstacle information is acquired and coverage proceeds. These subareas are organized in an incrementally constructed decomposition tree that preserves their hierarchical parent-child relationships. Based on this tree, a global coverage tour is maintained and updated online by prioritizing newly generated child subareas according to their exploration states and distances from the robot. A local planner then generates coverage motions within each selected subarea, allowing the robot to adapt its trajectory as the environment is gradually revealed. Its performance is evaluated via high-fidelity simulations in complex scenarios. The results show improved coverage efficiency in terms of path length and overlap ratio in comparison to three baseline algorithms.

AI.tldr: An online coverage path planning algorithm for unknown environments that incrementally decomposes the search area into subareas organized in a decomposition tree, maintains a global coverage tour, and uses a local planner within each subarea.
AI.motivation: Coverage path planning in initially unknown environments is challenging because the search area is not fully known in advance; the environment is revealed progressively as the robot moves.
AI.method: The unknown search area is progressively decomposed into disconnected subareas as new obstacle information is acquired and coverage proceeds. These subareas are organized in an incrementally constructed decomposition tree preserving hierarchical parent-child relationships. A global coverage tour is maintained and updated online, prioritizing newly generated child subareas by their exploration states and distances from the robot. A local planner generates coverage motions within each selected subarea, adapting the trajectory as the environment is revealed.
AI.result: High-fidelity simulations in complex scenarios show improved coverage efficiency in terms of path length and overlap ratio compared to three baseline algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed decomposition-tree-based online coverage planning approach effectively improves coverage efficiency in unknown environments relative to existing baselines.

title: EvoRS: On-Policy Self-Evolution of Reward Systems for Open-Ended Reinforcement Learning
summary: Open-ended reinforcement learning often relies on rubric-based rewards for tasks without directly verifiable answers. Yet the policy and reward system form a dynamic feedback loop: as the policy optimizes the current reward, an initially useful reward system may become unreliable due to reward hacking or reduced response discriminability. The reward system should therefore evolve rather than remain fixed during training. Existing dynamic-rubric methods adapt evaluation criteria, but reward failures can also arise from scoring mechanisms or signal composition. We introduce EvoRS, a self-evolving RL framework that evolves the reward system from on-policy experience, representing it as an executable Reward-DAG. Specifically, an agentic designer updates this system from on-policy rollouts and reward traces to maintain train-time reliability. Across writing and roleplay, EvoRS achieves the best quality under all three judges, outperforming the policy by \(2.107\) and \(4.767\) points, respectively, while reducing reward hacking and coverage failures and preserving reward informativeness. Ablations confirm that a comprehensive fixed reward system cannot remain reliable in open-ended tasks and must evolve throughout training.

AI.tldr: EvoRS is a self-evolving RL framework that represents the reward system as an executable Reward-DAG and iteratively updates it from on-policy rollouts and reward traces, maintaining reward reliability and improving open-ended task quality.
AI.motivation: Open-ended RL often lacks directly verifiable answers and relies on rubric-based rewards. Since policy and reward form a dynamic feedback loop, a reward system that is initially useful can become unreliable as the policy optimizes it, due to reward hacking or reduced response discriminability. Existing dynamic-rubric methods only adapt evaluation criteria, but failures can also stem from scoring mechanisms or signal composition. Hence the reward system should evolve rather than stay fixed.
AI.method: EvoRS evolves the reward system from on-policy experience, representing it as an executable Reward-DAG. An agentic designer updates this system based on on-policy rollouts and reward traces to maintain train-time reliability.
AI.result: Across writing and roleplay, EvoRS achieves the best quality under all three judges, outperforming the policy by 2.107 and 4.767 points respectively, while reducing reward hacking and coverage failures and preserving reward informativeness. Ablations confirm a comprehensive fixed reward system cannot remain reliable in open-ended tasks and must evolve throughout training.
AI.conclusion: Evolving the reward system during training is necessary and effective for open-ended RL; EvoRS improves quality, mitigates reward hacking and coverage failures, and preserves reward informativeness, validating that fixed reward systems are insufficient.

title: Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration
summary: As enterprises modernize legacy monolithic systems to microservices, Large Language Models (LLMs) are heavily utilized for automated code translation. However, traditional vector-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Standard RAG) struggles to capture topological relationships. It fetches isolated chunks that sever inheritance chains, leading to high compilation failure rates. This paper introduces a Hierarchical Context-Resident Graph (HCRG) methodology to resolve these limitations. Our pipeline uses tree-sitter for Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) extraction, maps architectural edges into a Google Cloud Spanner Property Graph, and serializes this structure into a Gemini Context Cache for topological, parent-first code translation. We shift evaluation from naive text-overlap to a custom 7-metric Software Engineering framework. Traditional metrics like CodeBLEU (which scored 91% for both methods) effectively masked Standard RAG's structural failures behind syntactically plausible but broken code. Empirically, Graph RAG decisively mitigates dependency loss: API hallucination rates dropped from 56.4% to 16.2%, Dependency Resolution Quality improved from 34.8% to 65.9%, and Parent-Child Consistency rose from 26.7% to 45.5%. However, Graph RAG introduces specific trade-offs. The dense global context causes defensive over-engineering by the LLM, reducing Cyclomatic Complexity Consistency from 71.6% to 46.7%, and slightly degrades Docstring Preservation (67.0% to 61.0%). Ultimately, while trading code complexity for reduced hallucinations, Graph RAG provides a substantially more viable, architecturally sound path for automated enterprise codebase modernization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HCRG, a Graph RAG pipeline (tree-sitter AST + Spanner Property Graph + Gemini Context Cache) for legacy-to-microservices code translation, showing large reductions in API hallucination and gains in dependency resolution and parent-child consistency over Standard RAG, at the cost of higher code complexity and slightly lower docstring preservation.
AI.motivation: As enterprises migrate legacy monolithic systems to microservices, LLMs are used for automated code translation, but Standard vector-based RAG retrieves isolated chunks that sever topological relationships such as inheritance chains, causing high compilation failure rates. The authors argue evaluation also needs to move beyond naive text-overlap metrics.
AI.method: A Hierarchical Context-Resident Graph (HCRG) methodology: tree-sitter extracts the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST); architectural edges are mapped into a Google Cloud Spanner Property Graph; the structure is serialized into a Gemini Context Cache to enable topological, parent-first code translation. Evaluation is shifted from text-overlap to a custom 7-metric Software Engineering framework.
AI.result: Graph RAG decisively mitigates dependency loss: API hallucination 56.4% -> 16.2%; Dependency Resolution Quality 34.8% -> 65.9%; Parent-Child Consistency 26.7% -> 45.5%. Trade-offs: dense global context causes defensive over-engineering, reducing Cyclomatic Complexity Consistency from 71.6% to 46.7%, and Docstring Preservation degrades slightly from 67.0% to 61.0%. CodeBLEU scored 91% for both methods, masking Standard RAG's structural failures.
AI.conclusion: Graph RAG trades code complexity for reduced hallucinations and provides a substantially more viable, architecturally sound path for automated enterprise codebase modernization than Standard RAG.

title: ProClosure: Hierarchical Room-Object Assignment using Progressive Boundary Closure from Monocular Video
summary: A 3D scene graph groups objects into rooms. When a robot is asked to fetch an object from the kitchen, that grouping is what tells it where to look. An object recorded in the wrong room is not retrievable by a query naming the correct room. We introduce Progressive Boundary Closure, which recovers room layer from a monocular RGB video. A SLAM front end and an open-vocabulary segmenter supply a structural point cloud, camera trajectory and object tracks. The cloud is rasterised into a top-down map, rooms are recovered from it, and each object takes the room holding most of its extent. The difficulty lies in the map itself. Walls are recorded only where the camera looked, so a gap in the boundary may be a doorway or a stretch of wall that was never observed; nothing distinguishes the two. Prior methods treat both as passages, merging rooms that should remain separate. We observe that both require the same treatment: a room should not extend across either, so both are closed and need not be distinguished. Such an opening closes under a small amount of boundary growth, and few sightlines cross it, so points in different rooms rarely see one another. We use the first to recover rooms and the second to assign objects to them. Rooms are obtained by Progressively thickening the boundary inward and freezing each free-space region once it becomes enclosed, so every opening seals at its own scale rather than at a radius fixed in advance. Camera poses are used as seeds, which removes the sampling heuristic and makes the segmentation deterministic. Over 10 floors of 6 HM3D-Semantics scenes, scored against HOV-SG on identical top-down maps, we recover 74 rooms for 72 annotated regions (HOV-SG: 44), raising room F_1 from 0.741 to 0.890 at IoU 0.25 at some cost in precision, and object-to-room ARI from 0.488 to 0.696 (p=0.002, ahead on every floor).

AI.tldr: Progressive Boundary Closure recovers room layer from monocular RGB video by closing all boundary gaps and assigning objects via sightline visibility, improving room F1 (0.741→0.890) and object-to-room ARI (0.488→0.696) over HOV-SG on HM3D-Semantics.
AI.motivation: 3D scene graphs need correct room labels for object retrieval; objects in wrong rooms become unretrievable. Prior methods cannot distinguish unobserved wall stretches from doorways, so they treat both as passages and wrongly merge rooms.
AI.method: SLAM front end + open-vocabulary segmenter produce structural point cloud, camera trajectory, and object tracks. Cloud is rasterised to top-down map. Rooms recovered by progressively thickening boundaries inward and freezing each free-space region once enclosed (openings seal at their own scale). Camera poses used as seeds, making segmentation deterministic. Objects assigned to the room holding most of their extent, using sightline visibility (few sightlines cross openings).
AI.result: Over 10 floors of 6 HM3D-Semantics scenes vs HOV-SG on identical top-down maps: 74 rooms recovered for 72 annotated regions (HOV-SG: 44); room F1 0.741→0.890 at IoU 0.25 (slight precision cost); object-to-room ARI 0.488→0.696 (p=0.002, better on every floor).
AI.conclusion: Treating doorways and unobserved wall stretches identically (closing both) avoids erroneous room merging and yields substantially better room segmentation and object-to-room assignment than prior art.

title: TripPattern: A Pattern-based Text Watermarking Method for Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to Findings of AACL-IJCNLP 2026. 16 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables
summary: Text watermarking techniques have gained significant attention for identifying machine-generated text and mitigating risks from large language models (LLMs). Existing methods typically divide an LLM's vocabulary into green and red tokens, but encouraging generation toward green tokens can reduce text quality and naturalness. To address this, we propose TripPattern, a watermarking framework that formulates text watermarking as a pattern-based matching task using three vocabulary partitions. TripPattern divides the vocabulary into one neutral group and two pattern groups. During generation, the model alternates token selection between the two pattern groups to embed detectable patterns, while neutral tokens are selected independently to improve flexibility and preserve naturalness. For detection, TripPattern uses pattern-based statistical tests that provide interpretable p-values by measuring how often adjacent tokens alternate between the pattern groups. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations on four multilingual datasets show that TripPattern maintains LLM generation quality while achieving robust watermark detectability.

AI.tldr: TripPattern is a text watermarking framework that reformulates watermarking as a pattern-based matching task with three vocabulary partitions (one neutral, two pattern groups), enabling robust, interpretable watermark detection while preserving LLM generation quality across multilingual datasets.
AI.motivation: Text watermarking helps identify machine-generated text and mitigate LLM risks. Existing methods split the vocabulary into green and red tokens, but biasing generation toward green tokens degrades text quality and naturalness. There is a need for a watermarking approach that retains detectability without compromising generation quality.
AI.method: TripPattern divides the vocabulary into one neutral group and two pattern groups. During generation, the model alternates token selection between the two pattern groups to embed detectable alternation patterns, while neutral tokens are selected independently to preserve flexibility and naturalness. For detection, it applies pattern-based statistical tests that yield interpretable p-values by measuring how often adjacent tokens alternate between the pattern groups. Theoretical analysis supports the design.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations on four multilingual datasets demonstrate that TripPattern maintains LLM generation quality while achieving robust watermark detectability, with interpretable p-values.
AI.conclusion: TripPattern offers an effective watermarking solution that balances generation quality and watermark robustness, providing interpretable detection statistics and validated multilingual performance.

title: When Does AI Augment Work? A Workflow-Level Framework for Human-Agent Collaboration
comment: 8 pages. Whitepaper from the CIVIC-AI 2026 workshop
summary: We aim to characterise the value of artificial intelligence in the workplace. Current studies largely measure this value in terms of the current automation capabilities and public adoption of AI. However, such metrics ignore the greater impacts of human--agent collaboration in transforming the nature of work. To account for this, we must expand the scope of our analysis beyond atomised tasks of today, and instead focus on how AI can augment entire workflows of the future. To ground this analysis, we establish a precise definition of AI augmentation comprising six conditions, spanning durable net value, meaningful human control, accountability and recovery, and long-term human development through learning, career pathways, and job purpose. We elaborate on these conditions and apply the framework in a case study of AI-mediated social surveys. We conclude by outlining how organisations, researchers, and government leaders can use this framework to make sense of the future of work.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI's workplace value should be measured not by current automation capabilities or adoption rates, but by AI augmentation of entire future workflows, defined through six precise conditions and illustrated via a case study of AI-mediated social surveys.
AI.motivation: Existing studies assess AI's workplace value mainly through current automation capabilities and public adoption, metrics that overlook the larger effects of human-agent collaboration in reshaping the nature of work. The authors seek a framework that captures AI augmentation at the workflow level rather than at atomised tasks.
AI.method: The authors establish a precise definition of AI augmentation comprising six conditions covering durable net value, meaningful human control, accountability and recovery, and long-term human development through learning, career pathways, and job purpose. They elaborate these conditions and apply the framework in a case study of AI-mediated social surveys.
AI.result: The framework yields a structured account of AI augmentation across the six conditions and demonstrates its applicability through the AI-mediated social survey case study, showing how augmentation differs from narrow automation-focused assessment.
AI.conclusion: Organisations, researchers, and government leaders can use the proposed framework to make sense of the future of work and to evaluate AI's value through augmentation of workflows rather than current task automation.

title: Confidence-Gated Transductive Test Generation for Code Reranking
summary: Test case synthesis is crucial for evaluating and ranking programs generated by large language models (LLMs). However, constructing high-quality test cases remains challenging because reliable expected outputs are often difficult to obtain. We propose Confidence-Gated Transductive Test Generation (CoTT), which first uses an efficient inductive procedure and invokes transductive generation only when inductive confidence is low. This adaptive design improves output reliability while allocating extra computation only when needed. On code reranking benchmarks, CoTT outperforms prior baselines across the reported metrics while reducing cost relative to applying transductive generation to every input. These results show that confidence-based allocation of test-time computation provides a favorable efficiency-effectiveness trade-off with a single efficient LLM.

AI.tldr: CoTT is a confidence-gated transductive test generation method that uses an efficient inductive procedure and only triggers transductive generation when inductive confidence is low, improving reliability and reducing cost for LLM code reranking.
AI.motivation: Test case synthesis is essential for evaluating and ranking LLM-generated programs, but constructing high-quality test cases is hard because reliable expected outputs are difficult to obtain.
AI.method: CoTT first applies an efficient inductive procedure and invokes transductive generation only when inductive confidence is low, adaptively allocating extra computation only when needed.
AI.result: On code reranking benchmarks, CoTT outperforms prior baselines across reported metrics while reducing cost compared with applying transductive generation to every input.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-based allocation of test-time computation offers a favorable efficiency-effectiveness trade-off using a single efficient LLM.

title: Driving Context-guided Model Predictive Planning and Control for Autonomous Car Racing at the Limit and Beyond
comment: Accepted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots & Systems - IROS 2026
summary: This paper presents a Model Predictive Control-based motion planning and control pipeline for autonomous car racing capable of adapting to different driving contexts, such as overtaking, nominal driving, and countersteering. A Cost Blending state machine manages the identification of different driving contexts and the selection of their predefined weights to be applied to the Model Predictive Planning (MPP) and Control (MPC) modules. The two optimization-based solutions share the same problem formulation and model, differing only in horizon length, rate, tuning, and in their open-loop versus closed-loop approach to maximize the effectiveness of their interaction. The work is validated on the fully autonomous open-wheel racecar Superformula EAV-25, with a lap time achieved that is within 2% of the best human driver reference. The results demonstrate the capability of the solution in driving at the limit of handling, smoothly executing overtaking maneuvers, and quickly reacting to high oversteering conditions to recover the vehicle stability.

AI.tldr: A Model Predictive Control-based planning and control pipeline enables an autonomous racecar to adapt to overtaking, nominal driving, and countersteering contexts, achieving lap times within 2% of the best human reference.
AI.motivation: Autonomous racing requires a controller that can handle distinct driving contexts—overtaking, nominal driving, and countersteering—within a single algorithmic framework rather than relying on separate, context-specific solutions.
AI.method: The pipeline couples a Model Predictive Planning (MPP) module and a Model Predictive Control (MPC) module that share an identical problem formulation and model, differing only in horizon length, update rate, tuning, and open-loop versus closed-loop behavior. A Cost Blending state machine identifies the current driving context and selects predefined weights applied to both modules.
AI.result: Validated on the fully autonomous open-wheel racecar Superformula EAV-25, the solution achieved a lap time within 2% of the best human driver reference, drove at the limit of handling, executed smooth overtaking maneuvers, and recovered vehicle stability quickly under high oversteering conditions.
AI.conclusion: Cost Blending over a unified MPP/MPC formulation provides an effective and adaptive motion planning and control strategy for autonomous car racing across multiple driving contexts.

title: Information Specialization and Constrained Synthesis in Multi-Agent LLM Forecasting: A Prospective Live-Study of the 2026 FIFA World Cup
summary: Large language models are being organized into multi-agent systems with specialized roles, but whether such specialization produces distinct forecasts and whether subsequent synthesis improves utility remains unclear. In this study, we carried out a live, prospective evaluation over the final 56 matches of the information-dense 2026 FIFA World Cup, keeping a frontier foundation model constant while assigning two primary forecasting agents contrasting specialist roles: a quantitative specialist focusing on structured performance statistics and a news specialist focusing on current injuries, tactics and information from press conferences. Their forecasts were then reviewed by a separate critic before being combined by a meta-agent, resulting in a sequential four-agent model. Forecasts from the betting market served as an external benchmark. The news specialist obtained the highest mean probability-weighted Top-3 utility and matched the betting market in Top-3 exact-score hits. Nevertheless, the two specialist forecasters agreed on at least two of the three scorelines in 50 out of 56 matches, and the meta-agent never generated more than one scoreline outside the specialists' forecast set. These findings show that rapidly changing, unstructured information can provide a valuable forecasting signal alongside structured statistics, whereas adding critic and meta-agent stages does not necessarily create complementary information or improve on the strongest specialist.

AI.tldr: A live prospective study of the 2026 FIFA World Cup's final 56 matches used a four-agent LLM system with specialist forecasters, a critic, and a meta-agent. The news specialist achieved the best probability-weighted Top-3 utility and matched betting-market exact-score hits, but specialists showed high overlap and the meta-agent added no complementary information.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly assign specialized roles, yet it is unclear whether such specialization yields genuinely distinct forecasts and whether subsequent critic/meta-agent synthesis improves forecasting utility.
AI.method: Live prospective evaluation over 56 matches of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, holding a frontier foundation model constant. Two forecasting agents took contrasting roles: a quantitative specialist using structured performance statistics and a news specialist using current injuries, tactics, and press-conference information. A separate critic reviewed their forecasts, then a meta-agent combined them, forming a sequential four-agent pipeline. Betting-market forecasts served as an external benchmark.
AI.result: The news specialist achieved the highest mean probability-weighted Top-3 utility and matched the betting market in Top-3 exact-score hits. However, the two specialists agreed on at least two of three scorelines in 50 of 56 matches, and the meta-agent never produced more than one scoreline outside the specialists' forecast set.
AI.conclusion: Rapidly changing unstructured information can provide a valuable forecasting signal alongside structured statistics. Adding critic and meta-agent stages does not necessarily generate complementary information or outperform the strongest specialist.

title: From Collaboration to Capability: Internalizing Routed LLM Experts into Compact Reasoners
summary: A compact controller can coordinate stronger experts by selecting whom to consult, formulating requests, and integrating their responses. We study whether learning from both the controller's decisions and the experts' reasoning and code improves its generation after expert removal. We introduce \textsc{Rivet} for \emph{collaboration internalization}: expert-augmented reinforcement learning applies a shared outcome signal to controller decisions and returned expert spans, and verified trajectory internalization consolidates complete successful interactions through format-aware supervised training. The deployed controller generates reasoning, code, and interaction structure with local Python execution and no external LLM. Across seven competition-mathematics benchmarks, RIVET-1.7B and RIVET-4B achieve average accuracies of $28.25\%$ and $44.16\%$; Stage~II improves RIVET-4B's accuracy after expert removal by $6.49$ points, and GPQA-Diamond results provide evidence of generalization to scientific reasoning. Ablations show gains from ordinary trajectory supervision and additional format weighting, supporting the effectiveness of training on the content and structure of verified collaborations.
