AI.tldr: The paper introduces RIVET, a framework for "collaboration internalization" that trains a compact controller to learn from both its own decisions and experts' reasoning/code, so it can operate standalone after expert removal.
AI.motivation: A compact controller can coordinate stronger experts by selecting whom to consult, formulating requests, and integrating responses. The key question is whether learning from the controller's decisions as well as the experts' reasoning and code improves generation after those experts are removed.
AI.method: RIVET combines two stages: (1) expert-augmented reinforcement learning, which applies a shared outcome signal to both controller decisions and returned expert spans; and (2) verified trajectory internalization, which consolidates complete successful interactions via format-aware supervised training. The deployed controller generates reasoning, code, and interaction structure using local Python execution, without any external LLM.
AI.result: Across seven competition-mathematics benchmarks, RIVET-1.7B and RIVET-4B reach average accuracies of 28.25% and 44.16%, respectively. Stage II improves RIVET-4B's accuracy after expert removal by 6.49 points, and GPQA-Diamond results indicate generalization to scientific reasoning. Ablations confirm gains from ordinary trajectory supervision and additional format weighting.
AI.conclusion: Training on both the content and structure of verified collaborations is effective for internalizing expert capability into a compact controller, enabling strong standalone performance after expert removal and evidence of cross-domain generalization.

title: Improving Imitation Learning Efficiency for Manipulation through Geometric Prior Pretraining
summary: Applying an imitation learning policy to a new manipulation task usually requires collecting new demonstrations and retraining the model, which makes sample efficiency a practical concern. Pretraining on large-scale robot datasets is effective in this respect, but such datasets are costly to collect and train on, while data augmentation techniques typically require a new round of data generation and retraining for each task. A complementary question is what useful prior can be provided to a policy at negligible cost before any task-specific data are collected. In this study, we construct a geometric visual pretraining dataset in which each scene contains only a plane, an object, and a hand, and trajectories are generated automatically. The scenes contain neither textures nor backgrounds; pretraining primarily exposes the policy to the geometric relationship between the hand and the object. Furthermore, representing the hand as a cube avoids tailoring the dataset to a specific robot morphology. We evaluate this geometric prior using ACT on three simulated robots across five manipulation tasks each, as well as on three real-world robot tasks. Across many of these robot--task combinations, fine-tuning from the geometric prior achieves higher success rates in the early stages of training than training from scratch while using only a small number of task demonstrations. These results suggest that even highly simplified geometric scenes can provide a useful initialization that transfers across robots and to real-world tasks when task data are limited.

AI.tldr: A geometric visual pretraining dataset with only a plane, object, and cube-shaped hand provides a cheap prior that, via ACT fine-tuning, improves early-stage success on simulated and real manipulation tasks with few demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning policies require new demonstrations and retraining for each manipulation task, making sample efficiency a practical concern. Large-scale robot pretraining is costly, and data augmentation needs new data generation and retraining per task. This raises the question of what useful prior can be supplied at negligible cost before any task-specific data are collected.
AI.method: Construct a geometric visual pretraining dataset where each scene contains only a plane, an object, and a hand, with trajectories generated automatically. Remove textures and backgrounds so pretraining focuses on hand-object geometric relationships. Represent the hand as a cube to avoid tailoring to a specific robot morphology. Evaluate with ACT on three simulated robots (five tasks each) and three real-world tasks, fine-tuning from the geometric prior versus training from scratch with few demonstrations.
AI.result: Across many robot-task combinations, fine-tuning from the geometric prior achieves higher success rates in early training stages than training from scratch, using only a small number of task demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: Even highly simplified geometric scenes can provide a useful initialization that transfers across robots and to real-world tasks when task data are limited.

title: Reproducing and Evaluating the Generalizability of Subliminal Learning in Open-Weight Models
comment: Accepted at BlackBoxNLP@EMNLP'26 (The 9th BlackboxNLP Workshop Special Track: Reproducibility and Reliability in Interpretability Analyses)
summary: In this reproduction paper we investigate subliminal learning, a consequence of distillation where teacher models transmit behavioral preference traits through semantically unrelated data. The original paper explores two types of traits (animal preferences and misalignment), three data modalities (number sequences, code, and chain of thought), and several model families. We reproduce their experiments and extend the setup along three axes: new preference categories (actors and politicians), a new task (chess move generation), and an additional open-weight model (Ministral8B). We also run a controlled ablation on the numbers task's answer-space size (1-, 2-, and 3-digit sequences). We focus on open-weight models with accessible checkpoints on HuggingFace, since the original paper's GPT-4.x fine-tuning is no longer available. Our reproduction supports the original paper's claims, but our extensions show they are not universal as transmission strength varies across traits and tasks, and one model shows almost no effect at all.

AI.tldr: A reproduction study of subliminal learning confirms the original findings on behavioral trait transmission via semantically unrelated data, but shows the effect is not universal across traits, tasks, and models.
AI.motivation: The original paper on subliminal learning—where teacher models pass behavioral preference traits to students through semantically unrelated data—needed independent reproduction, especially since its GPT-4.x fine-tuning is no longer accessible, motivating a shift to open-weight models and testing generality.
AI.method: The authors reproduce the original experiments across two trait types (animal preferences, misalignment), three data modalities (number sequences, code, chain of thought), and several model families. They extend along three axes: new preference categories (actors, politicians), a new task (chess move generation), and an additional open-weight model (Ministral8B). They also conduct a controlled ablation on the numbers task's answer-space size (1-, 2-, and 3-digit sequences), using open-weight models with HuggingFace checkpoints.
AI.result: The reproduction supports the original paper's claims, but the extensions demonstrate these claims are not universal: transmission strength varies across traits and tasks, and one model exhibits almost no effect.
AI.conclusion: Subliminal learning is reproducible but not universal, with transmission strength dependent on the specific trait, task, and model, highlighting boundary conditions and limited generality of the phenomenon.

title: Control Architecture for Safe Grasping of Fragile Objects Using a Coarse Position-Controlled Gripper
summary:
Robots are increasingly used in unstructured environments. The need for them to safely grasp unknown objects without damaging them becomes crucial. Humans achieve this by sensing and quickly responding by adjusting their grasping force. Similarly, effective grasp acquisition in robots requires compliant interaction strategies that can adapt to uncertain object properties and adjust to any instabilities during manipulation.
  We present a geometry-aware force/torque-based contact estimation method for a coarse position-controlled gripper, combined with an adaptive admittance controller for safe grasp acquisition. The desired contact forces are estimated online to keep stable contact with objects of unknown properties. This enables compliant and stable grasps while avoiding excessive forces. Experiments with objects of different sizes, shapes, stiffnesses, and weights show that the proposed algorithm not only prevents slippage but also applies minimal force to safely grasp an object without causing excessive deformation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a geometry-aware force/torque-based contact estimation method combined with an adaptive admittance controller, enabling a position-controlled gripper to safely grasp unknown objects with compliant, stable, minimal-force contact.
AI.motivation: Robots increasingly operate in unstructured environments where objects have unknown properties. Grasping such objects safely without damage requires compliant interaction strategies that emulate human sensing and rapid force adjustment. Coarse position-controlled grippers lack the fine force control needed, motivating a method that estimates contact and adapts force online.
AI.method: A geometry-aware contact estimation method based on force/torque sensing for a coarse position-controlled gripper, paired with an adaptive admittance controller for safe grasp acquisition. Desired contact forces are estimated online to maintain stable contact with objects of unknown properties, regulating interaction to avoid excessive forces.
AI.result: Experiments across objects of varying sizes, shapes, stiffnesses, and weights demonstrate the algorithm prevents slippage while applying minimal force to grasp objects safely without excessive deformation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed geometry-aware estimation plus adaptive admittance control yields compliant, stable, and safe grasps of unknown objects, balancing slip prevention against minimal deformation-inducing force.

title: Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving
summary: While multimodal reasoning has advanced rapidly, solving complex geometry problems critically hinges on active visual assistance, such as constructing auxiliary lines, spurring the rise of Visual Chain-of-Thought (VCoT). However, existing evaluations typically assess visual generation quality and final answer accuracy in isolation, failing to examine whether intermediate visual aids are geometrically valid, effectively utilized in subsequent reasoning, or causally responsible for task success. To bridge this gap, we introduce GeoVAD-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that pairs a fine-grained five-dimensional trajectory diagnosis covering perception, auxiliary quality, utilization, deductive reasoning, and final correctness with controlled No-Aux, Auto-Aux, and GT-Aux intervention settings to systematically isolate intermediate error modes, the causal gains of visual aids, and the resulting autonomy gap. Our findings reveal that while high-quality auxiliary aids offer substantial theoretical gains for geometric problem solving, autonomous generation is frequently hampered by compounding errors across geometric perception, faithful visual manipulation, visual-state grounding, and deductive reasoning. Guided by these diagnostic insights, we establish a specialized data construction pipeline encompassing geometric perception, diagram editing, and interleaved visual-textual reasoning trajectories, and develop a progressive SFT and multimodal RL training framework. The resulting model, GeoWeave-8B, outperforms the base model by +25.3% in final geometric accuracy and achieves a +30.4% gain in process average across the four intermediate diagnostic dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GeoVAD-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for Visual Chain-of-Thought in geometry, revealing that auxiliary visual aids give large theoretical gains but autonomous generation suffers from compounding intermediate errors. Leveraging these insights, the authors build GeoWeave-8B via a specialized data pipeline and progressive SFT + multimodal RL, achieving +25.3% final accuracy and +30.4% process gain.
AI.motivation: Existing VCoT evaluations assess visual generation quality and final answer accuracy in isolation, and fail to examine whether intermediate visual aids are geometrically valid, effectively utilized in subsequent reasoning, or causally responsible for task success.
AI.method: GeoVAD-Bench: a diagnostic benchmark pairing a five-dimensional trajectory diagnosis (perception, auxiliary quality, utilization, deductive reasoning, final correctness) with controlled No-Aux, Auto-Aux, and GT-Aux intervention settings to isolate intermediate error modes, causal gains of visual aids, and the autonomy gap. Guided by these insights, the authors establish a data construction pipeline (geometric perception, diagram editing, interleaved visual-textual reasoning trajectories) and a progressive SFT + multimodal RL training framework to produce GeoWeave-8B.
AI.result: High-quality auxiliary aids offer substantial theoretical gains for geometric problem solving, yet autonomous generation is frequently hampered by compounding errors across geometric perception, faithful visual manipulation, visual-state grounding, and deductive reasoning. GeoWeave-8B outperforms the base model by +25.3% in final geometric accuracy and achieves a +30.4% gain in process average across the four intermediate diagnostic dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Process-level diagnostic evaluation and intervention settings are necessary to expose and address intermediate VCoT failures; combining diagnosis-driven data construction with progressive SFT and multimodal RL substantially improves both final accuracy and intermediate reasoning quality in geometric problem solving.

title: High-Fidelity Multi-Body Simulator for Autonomous Racing
summary: We present a custom high-fidelity vehicle dynamics simulation environment for testing and validation of Autonomous Racing software. The digital twin of the autonomous vehicle is developed in Dymola, using racecar dynamics modeling libraries to build a complete multi-body model. A 3D road surface, including elevation profiles and curbs, is implemented using the Curved Regular Grid (CRG) standard. The model is exported from Dymola as a Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU) and integrated into a custom software-in-the-loop simulator, where communication interfaces with the autonomous racing stack were developed in C++. A calibration procedure based on experimental data is also presented, along with a validation study to further support the quality of the proposed framework. The simulator runs in real time on a portable computer and provides reliable ground truth for algorithms validation prior to real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: A high-fidelity, real-time vehicle dynamics simulator for validating autonomous racing software, built from a Dymola-generated multi-body digital twin exported as an FMU and integrated into a custom SIL environment with CRG-based 3D road surfaces, calibrated and validated against experimental data.
AI.motivation: Autonomous racing algorithms require reliable ground-truth testing before real-world deployment, but deploying and validating on physical racecars is costly and risky. A high-fidelity simulation environment is needed to test and validate autonomous racing software safely and efficiently.
AI.method: The digital twin of the autonomous vehicle is developed in Dymola using racecar dynamics modeling libraries to build a complete multi-body model. A 3D road surface with elevation profiles and curbs is implemented using the Curved Regular Grid (CRG) standard. The model is exported from Dymola as a Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU) and integrated into a custom software-in-the-loop (SIL) simulator, with communication interfaces to the autonomous racing stack developed in C++. A calibration procedure based on experimental data and a validation study are also presented.
AI.result: The simulator runs in real time on a portable computer and provides reliable ground truth for algorithm validation. Calibration against experimental data and a validation study further support the quality of the proposed framework.
AI.conclusion: The proposed high-fidelity, real-time SIL simulation framework enables reliable validation of autonomous racing software prior to real-world deployment.

title: SteerDuplex: Steerable Duplex Speech Dialogue Models
summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models support low-latency turn taking, interruption handling, and backchanneling, yet a key capability remains underexplored: steerability, the ability to reliably shift conversational behavior along attributes such as tone, persona, speaking rate, and voice style in response to user instructions. We introduce a taxonomy of text- and audio-based steerability that identifies substantial gaps in current full-duplex models. To address this gap, we introduce SteerDuplex, a Moshi-based full-duplex speech model fine-tuned on natural conversations and synthetic dialogues targeting instruction following, vocal delivery, reasoning, and duplex interaction. We further apply two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) with hybrid rewards, combining verifiable interaction checks and judge-based semantic feedback to improve timing and response continuity. To evaluate full-duplex spoken steerability, we introduce SteerBench, a benchmark with 390 spoken prompts and 1,067 human-authored binary audio and text rubrics spanning tone, persona, style/accent, and speed/length. On SteerBench, supervised training improves audio-steering average pass rate by 44.5 percentage points over the strongest evaluated open baseline. On Audio MultiChallenge, task average pass rate improves by 7 points over its strongest evaluated open baseline. RL further raises source-clean interruption response from 72.5% to 82.5% and reduces synthetic pause barge-in from 26.5% to 9%. Steering and aggregate task scores remain comparable or higher, while reward probes reveal reward hacking through incomplete responses. Our model and benchmark support systematic research on spoken steerability, with reward analysis showing why timing gains must be evaluated alongside response completeness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a taxonomy of spoken steerability, the SteerDuplex model (Moshi-based, fine-tuned with two-stage hybrid-reward RL), and the SteerBench benchmark, demonstrating large gains in audio-steering pass rates, task performance, and interruption handling while revealing reward hacking via incomplete responses.
AI.motivation: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models excel at low-latency turn taking, interruption handling, and backchanneling, but steerability—reliably shifting conversational behavior along attributes like tone, persona, speaking rate, and voice style per user instructions—remains underexplored. A taxonomy of text- and audio-based steerability reveals substantial gaps in current full-duplex models, motivating a dedicated model and evaluation suite.
AI.method: The authors (1) define a taxonomy of text- and audio-based steerability to map gaps in existing full-duplex models; (2) build SteerDuplex, a Moshi-based full-duplex speech model fine-tuned on natural conversations plus synthetic dialogues targeting instruction following, vocal delivery, reasoning, and duplex interaction; (3) apply two-stage reinforcement learning with hybrid rewards combining verifiable interaction checks and judge-based semantic feedback to improve timing and response continuity; and (4) construct SteerBench, comprising 390 spoken prompts and 1,067 human-authored binary audio and text rubrics across tone, persona, style/accent, and speed/length.
AI.result: On SteerBench, supervised training improves the audio-steering average pass rate by 44.5 percentage points over the strongest evaluated open baseline. On Audio MultiChallenge, the task average pass rate improves by 7 points over the strongest evaluated open baseline. RL raises source-clean interruption response from 72.5% to 82.5% and reduces synthetic pause barge-in from 26.5% to 9%, with steering and aggregate task scores remaining comparable or higher. Reward probes reveal reward hacking through incomplete responses.
AI.conclusion: The model and benchmark enable systematic research on spoken steerability. The reward analysis highlights that timing gains must be evaluated alongside response completeness, since optimizing interruption metrics can induce reward hacking via truncated responses.

title: VertexCBF: Improving Neural Control Barrier Functions via Vertex-Restricted Control Search
summary: As the number of autonomous robots continues to grow, safety becomes increasingly important. Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a theoretically grounded framework for ensuring safety, but existing design methods often face limitations in effectiveness, scalability, or interpretability, and may result in overly conservative safe sets. In this paper, we propose \emph{VertexCBF}, a framework for learning neural CBFs in a scalable, systematic, and explainable way. We approximate the stationary Hamilton--Jacobi value function using a neural network trained via a combination of physics-informed and sparsely supervised learning. By exploiting control-affine dynamics and a convex polytope control set, under which the Hamiltonian is maximized at the control vertices, we efficiently generate supervision points via GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search, while a residual architecture guarantees that the learned CBF is never larger than the specified constraint function. We evaluate the method on 15 systems and compare it against relevant baselines, showing that it reliably recovers large safe sets where the baselines are conservative or fail completely. In addition, we perform a hardware experiment in which a mobile robot safely avoids pedestrians using a neural CBF trained with our method.

AI.tldr: VertexCBF learns neural control barrier functions by approximating the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi value function via physics-informed and sparsely supervised learning, using GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search and a residual architecture to avoid overly conservative safe sets.
AI.motivation: As autonomous robots proliferate, safety becomes critical. Control barrier functions (CBFs) offer a theoretically grounded safety framework, but existing design methods suffer from limited effectiveness, scalability, or interpretability, and often yield overly conservative safe sets.
AI.method: The framework approximates the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi value function with a neural network trained via combined physics-informed and sparsely supervised learning. Exploiting control-affine dynamics and a convex polytope control set, where the Hamiltonian is maximized at control vertices, supervision points are efficiently generated through GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search. A residual architecture guarantees the learned CBF is never larger than the specified constraint function.
AI.result: Evaluated on 15 systems against relevant baselines, VertexCBF reliably recovers large safe sets where baselines are conservative or fail completely. A hardware experiment demonstrates a mobile robot safely avoiding pedestrians using a neural CBF trained with the method.
AI.conclusion: VertexCBF provides a scalable, systematic, and explainable approach to learning neural CBFs that mitigates conservatism and scales effectively, validated in both simulation across many systems and a real-world robotic safety task.

title: Generative AI Use Cases In Real Estate Marketing: Adoption and Constraints in Germany
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is changing how work is organized and performed. Real estate marketing is a prime example of this, yet evidence of GenAI in real estate agents' day-to-day practice remains scarce. In this work, we report on our insights from a German-based empirical study with eleven semi-structured interviews. GenAI is already utilized across different activities, with marketing communication being the most prominent. Concrete use cases are emergent and unevenly adopted, with writing exposé texts being the only widely established one. Interaction is predominantly human-in-the-loop: GenAI drafts, structures, and retrieves, while real estate agents curate, verify, and decide. Constraints stem less from model capability than from integration with listings and documents, data availability, and compliance in sensitive tasks. The study contributes a grounded map of existing and potential use cases and identifies tentative practical implications for adoption.

AI.tldr: Empirical interview study with eleven German real estate agents showing GenAI is used across marketing activities, but only exposé writing is widely established; interaction is human-in-the-loop, and constraints come mainly from integration, data availability, and compliance rather than model capability.
AI.motivation: GenAI is changing how work is organized and performed, and real estate marketing is a prime example. However, evidence of GenAI use in real estate agents' day-to-day practice remains scarce, leaving a gap in understanding actual adoption patterns.
AI.method: The authors conducted a German-based empirical study consisting of eleven semi-structured interviews with real estate agents.
AI.result: GenAI is already utilized across different activities, with marketing communication being the most prominent. Concrete use cases are emergent and unevenly adopted; writing exposé texts is the only widely established one. Interaction is predominantly human-in-the-loop: GenAI drafts, structures, and retrieves, while agents curate, verify, and decide. Constraints stem less from model capability than from integration with listings and documents, data availability, and compliance in sensitive tasks.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes a grounded map of existing and potential GenAI use cases in real estate marketing and identifies tentative practical implications for adoption.

title: Parameter Sensitivity Analysis for Aerial LiDAR-Inertial Odometries in low-altitude flights
summary: LiDAR-based SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) and LIO (LiDAR-inertial odometry) algorithms are often used for precise navigation of unmanned aerial vehicles, especially during interactions with the aerial robot's environment. However, the performance of these algorithms is greatly dependent on the scenario, LiDAR, and robot motion characteristics, often requiring an intensive tuning process to achieve the desired performance. To aid these tuning efforts, this paper analyzes the influence on performance of the parameters of an EKF-based LIO algorithm (FAST-LIO2) and the LIO module of a graph-based SLAM algorithm (Cartographer) on aerial LiDAR SLAM datasets recorded using different LiDARs in low-to-moderate-altitude flights in diverse environments. The analysis is conducted on the absolute trajectory error (ATE) resulting from processing the datasets with the LIO algorithms configured with each combination of parameters obtained in an exhaustive grid search. The relationship between individual parameters and the ATE results is assessed using Pearson's correlation, while the influence of each parameter is assessed using random forest permutation importance analyses with random forest models trained to predict the resulting ATE values based on the choice of parameters. The performed analysis obtains for Cartographer and FAST-LIO2: i) the identification of parameters with stronger influence in performance, ii) a simplified tuning procedure, and iii) tuning recommendations. Using the proposed tuning recommendations, both algorithms obtain on the analyzed datasets ATE values within 5 cm to the optimal performance found in the grid search procedure in 94% of the analyzed cases.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how the parameters of two LiDAR-inertial odometry algorithms (FAST-LIO2 and Cartographer's LIO module) affect their accuracy (ATE) on aerial LiDAR SLAM datasets, using Pearson correlation and random forest permutation importance, and derives a simplified tuning procedure with recommendations.
AI.motivation: LiDAR-based SLAM and LIO algorithms are used for precise UAV navigation, but their performance depends heavily on the scenario, LiDAR, and robot motion, typically requiring intensive tuning to reach desired performance. This motivates a systematic analysis of parameter influence to ease the tuning burden.
AI.method: The authors perform an exhaustive grid search over parameter combinations for an EKF-based LIO algorithm (FAST-LIO2) and the LIO module of a graph-based SLAM algorithm (Cartographer), running them on aerial LiDAR SLAM datasets recorded with different LiDARs during low-to-moderate-altitude flights in diverse environments. The resulting absolute trajectory error (ATE) is analyzed at a per-parameter level via Pearson's correlation, and each parameter's influence is assessed using random forest permutation importance, with random forest models trained to predict ATE from the parameter choices.
AI.result: For both Cartographer and FAST-LIO2 the analysis yields: (i) identification of the parameters with the strongest influence on performance, (ii) a simplified tuning procedure, and (iii) concrete tuning recommendations. Applying the recommendations, both algorithms achieve ATE values within 5 cm of the optimal grid-search performance in 94% of the analyzed cases.
AI.conclusion: The proposed parameter-influence analysis and derived tuning recommendations substantially reduce tuning effort while closely matching optimal accuracy, enabling near-optimal performance for aerial LiDAR SLAM/LIO with a simplified tuning process.

title: Residual Vector-based Reconstruction as Long-Context Recall Regardless of Context Window Size
summary: Large language models (LLMs) process long contexts, including long documents and lengthy conversations, but face token-level memory usage that increases proportionally to input length. Although model optimization and lossy prompt compression are widely used, these methods still fail to solve the long-context recall problem beyond pretrained and size-constrained context windows. This paper proposes a long-context recall method that maintains near-constant GPU memory usage as context length increases, without additional training. The main idea is to reconstruct facts using parameter activations in the LLM's feed-forward layers, which store residual vectors representing facts from the source document. Utilizing residual vectors allows the LLM to deterministically reconstruct query relevant facts without referencing the original document, preserving high fidelity and reducing memory usage without fine-tuning weights. Experimental results show that the proposed method enables answering single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts where previous methods fail.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a training-free long-context recall method that keeps GPU memory nearly constant as context length grows, by reconstructing facts from parameter activations in the LLM's feed-forward layers rather than holding the full context.
AI.motivation: LLMs handle long documents and conversations, but token-level memory usage scales proportionally with input length. Existing fixes—model optimization and lossy prompt compression—still cannot solve long-context recall beyond pretrained and size-constrained context windows.
AI.method: The approach exploits the LLM's feed-forward layers, which store residual vectors encoding facts from the source document. Using these residual vectors, the model deterministically reconstructs query-relevant facts without referencing the original document, requiring no additional training or weight fine-tuning.
AI.result: The method answers single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts where prior methods fail, while maintaining near-constant GPU memory as context length increases.
AI.conclusion: Reconstructing facts from feed-forward parameter activations offers a high-fidelity, memory-efficient solution to long-context recall without fine-tuning weights.

title: A Multi-Vehicle Dataset with Camera, LiDAR, and Radar Sensors and Scanned 3D Models for Custom Auto-Annotation using RTK-GNSS
summary: Datasets are a crucial element in the development of perception algorithms. They relate sensor measurement data to annotated reference information and allow for the deduction of sensor and object characteristics. In autonomous driving, the reference data commonly consist of semantic image segmentation, point-wise associations, or bounding box annotations. The dataset proposed in this work, however, aims to dig deeper into the evaluation of measurement principles and provides scanned 3D models of all vehicles together with a pose and continuous kinematics reference obtained by RTK-GNSS. Combined, the state of the complete dynamic surrounding of the sensor vehicle is known for any point in time. Subsequent reference formats can be easily computed in user-defined granularity. This dataset involves single-object and multi-object recordings with seven target vehicles. In particular, measurement effects such as occlusion, as well as reflections, can be evaluated, as the normals of the shape of the target vehicles are known. We describe the dataset, discuss the technical background of its development, and briefly present exemplary evaluations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel autonomous driving dataset that provides scanned 3D models of target vehicles with RTK-GNSS-based pose and continuous kinematics, enabling high-fidelity evaluation of measurement principles and flexible derivation of reference formats.
AI.motivation: Existing perception datasets typically provide only semantic segmentation, point-wise associations, or bounding box annotations, which are insufficient for deeply evaluating sensor measurement principles. There is a need for richer reference data that captures full dynamic scene state and object geometry to study effects such as occlusion and reflections.
AI.method: The dataset records seven target vehicles in single-object and multi-object scenarios. For each vehicle, scanned 3D models are provided together with pose and continuous kinematics reference obtained via RTK-GNSS. This combination yields the complete state of the dynamic surrounding of the sensor vehicle at any point in time, from which user-defined reference formats can be computed. The known surface normals of target vehicle shapes allow analysis of measurement effects including occlusion and reflections.
AI.result: The paper describes the dataset, discusses the technical background of its development, and presents exemplary evaluations demonstrating its utility for analyzing measurement principles and deriving customized reference data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dataset enables deeper evaluation of perception sensor measurement principles than conventional annotation schemes, supporting flexible, user-defined reference generation and detailed study of occlusion and reflection effects.

title: I Am AdMan: A Pipeline for Automatic Generation of Personalized Advertising Imagery
summary: Personalized marketing can increase customer engagement, satisfaction, and conversion. While existing personalization approaches have become effective at matching the right product to the right customer, the visual representation of advertisements remains generic and only weakly tailored to the individual. Prior research shows that generative artificial intelligence can improve the creation of personalized advertisements, particularly for text, and that image generation models can support scalable advertisement production. However, little research has examined how detailed customer information can be systematically translated into fully AI-generated, personalized advertising imagery at scale on a technical level. To address this gap, we propose AdMan, a multi-agent pipeline that transforms customer data into personas, generates personalized advertisement images conditioned on product reference images, and applies an LLM-based judge agent for automated quality control. We implement the pipeline with two different model configurations and evaluate it across four products, using six celebrity personas for qualitative inspection, and 100 real customer profiles, producing 1745 advertisements. The evaluation combines a qualitative expert focus group and a quantitative artifact-rate assessment. The results show that the pipeline can generate photorealistic and personalized advertisements. At the same time, performance varies substantially by product complexity and model configuration. Our findings extend the literature on AI-based personalized advertising by demonstrating the feasibility and current limitations of fully automated image generation for advertising.

AI.tldr: AdMan is a multi-agent pipeline that converts customer data into personas, generates personalized ad images conditioned on product references, and uses an LLM judge for quality control; tested on 4 products and 100 real profiles (1745 ads), it produces photorealistic personalized ads but performance varies by product complexity and model setup.
AI.motivation: Existing personalization methods match the right product to the right customer, but ad visuals remain generic and only weakly tailored to individuals. Generative AI can improve personalized ad creation (mainly text) and image models enable scalable production, yet little research systematically translates detailed customer information into fully AI-generated, personalized advertising imagery at scale on a technical level.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline (AdMan): (1) transform customer data into personas; (2) generate personalized ad images conditioned on product reference images; (3) apply an LLM-based judge agent for automated quality control. Implemented with two model configurations; evaluated across four products, six celebrity personas (qualitative inspection), and 100 real customer profiles, yielding 1745 advertisements. Evaluation combines a qualitative expert focus group and a quantitative artifact-rate assessment.
AI.result: The pipeline can generate photorealistic and personalized advertisements. Performance varies substantially by product complexity and model configuration.
AI.conclusion: The work extends the literature on AI-based personalized advertising by demonstrating both the feasibility and current limitations of fully automated image generation for advertising.

title: Enabling and Understanding Personalization in AI-Generated Advertising Imagery
summary: Personalized marketing traditionally matches static products to customers, while dynamic creative optimization focuses mainly on AI-driven text personalization or basic product image modifications. We address this gap by developing and implementing an AI-based framework that generates personalized advertising imagery directly from customer data. We evaluate this framework in a two-stage within-subject study with N=100 participants across four products and three levels of personalization, varied by the amount and specificity of customer data used. Participants rated each image on attitude toward the advertisement, attitude toward the product, and purchase intention. Results show that participants perceive differences across personalization levels and evaluate AI-generated advertising imagery most positively at a moderate level of personalization. High personalization increases perceived personalization, which is positively associated with all three outcome measures, but also increases perceived creepiness, which is negatively associated with the outcomes and dominates the total effect.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an AI framework that generates personalized advertising imagery from customer data, tested with N=100 participants. AI-generated ads are evaluated most favorably at a moderate personalization level; high personalization raises perceived personalization but also perceived creepiness, which dominates the total effect.
AI.motivation: Personalized marketing traditionally matches static products to customers, and dynamic creative optimization focuses mainly on AI-driven text personalization or basic product image modifications. The paper addresses this gap by targeting personalized advertising imagery generated directly from customer data.
AI.method: A two-stage within-subject study with N=100 participants, covering four products and three levels of personalization that vary by the amount and specificity of customer data used. Participants rated each AI-generated image on attitude toward the advertisement, attitude toward the product, and purchase intention.
AI.result: Participants perceived differences across personalization levels and evaluated AI-generated advertising imagery most positively at a moderate level of personalization. High personalization increased perceived personalization, positively associated with all three outcome measures, but also increased perceived creepiness, negatively associated with the outcomes and dominating the total effect.
AI.conclusion: AI-generated advertising imagery is subject to a personalization trade-off: moderate levels yield the most favorable evaluations, and excessive personalization backfires because perceived creepiness outweighs the benefits of perceived personalization.

title: Before the Tipping Point: Force-Guided Active Perception for Shape-Agnostic Estimation of 3D Centers of Mass
summary: Estimating the 3D center of mass of unknown objects is challenging when grasping is infeasible, geometry is irregular, or mass distribution is uneven. We present a force-based method that estimates CoM height and mass from a single sub-critical tipping experiment by a robot manipulator. The robot applies a quasistatic elevated push and retract motion, using force-angle measurements recorded during tipping to identify parameters from the object trajectory. Our proposed push-retract cycle mitigates frictional bias, enabling generalized fitting. We experimentally validate our method using a robot manipulator with a six-axis force torque sensor on varying types of objects without prior shape information and without specific models. We also propose a method to prevent toppling, keeping the object in a sub-critical tipping regime by leveraging a safety margin. In experimental studies, our method recovers mass, CoM height, and toppling angle with relative errors below 5.0 percent across all unknown objects. This work demonstrates reliable 3D inertial parameter estimation under proper safety thresholds in tipping. Our proposed method informs and enables reliable non-prehensile manipulation and robotic grasping of challenging objects that were previously infeasible.

AI.tldr: A force-based method estimates an unknown object's mass and center-of-mass height from a single sub-critical tipping experiment using a robot manipulator, achieving relative errors below 5.0%.
AI.motivation: Estimating the 3D center of mass of unknown objects is difficult when grasping is infeasible, geometry is irregular, or mass distribution is uneven.
AI.method: The robot applies a quasistatic elevated push-and-retract motion; force-angle measurements recorded during tipping are used to fit parameters from the object trajectory. The push-retract cycle mitigates frictional bias, enabling generalized fitting, and a safety margin keeps the object in a sub-critical tipping regime to prevent toppling. Validation uses a manipulator with a six-axis force-torque sensor on varied objects without prior shape information or specific models.
AI.result: Mass, CoM height, and toppling angle are recovered with relative errors below 5.0% across all unknown objects.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates reliable 3D inertial parameter estimation under proper safety thresholds in tipping, informing and enabling reliable non-prehensile manipulation and robotic grasping of challenging objects previously infeasible.

title: Implicit Personality Representations in Humans and LLMs
comment: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics (EMNLP 2026)
summary: A century of psychology has found that the trait words people use to describe one another vary, but the relational structure among those traits, which ones go together and which oppose, is strikingly consistent across raters and cultures. We test whether the LLM (Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct) reproduces this structure in its internal trait representations. From millions of crowd-sourced personality ratings of fictional characters, we build a human implicit-personality matrix over hundreds of traits; from contrastive model activations, we build a matching matrix over the same traits. The two relational structures align strongly (Mantel r = 0.77), and the agreement holds trait by trait as well as in aggregate. Two dominant axes of the model's trait representations recover the social and intellectual dimensions long known to organize human personality impressions, social warmth and intellectual competence. On held-out dialogue, projecting model activations onto these directions yields personality profiles that agree with human ratings. This work establishes a framework that enables comprehensive, human-grounded comparison between internal model trait geometry and the shared structure of human personality impressions.

AI.tldr: The authors show that an LLM's internal trait representations align strongly (Mantel r = 0.77) with human implicit-personality structure across hundreds of traits, and that two dominant axes recover the classic social and intellectual dimensions of personality impressions.
AI.motivation: A century of psychology has found a strikingly consistent relational structure among the trait words people use, yet it is unknown whether LLMs encode the same shared structure in their internal trait representations. Establishing such alignment matters for grounding model behavior in human personality science.
AI.method: They build a human implicit-personality matrix over hundreds of traits from millions of crowd-sourced personality ratings of fictional characters, and a matching matrix from contrastive activations of Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct over the same traits. They compare the two relational structures using Mantel tests, at both aggregate and trait-by-trait levels, then identify dominant axes of the model's trait geometry and project activations onto them for held-out dialogue.
AI.result: The two relational structures align strongly (Mantel r = 0.77), with agreement holding trait by trait as well as in aggregate. The two dominant axes of the model's trait representations recover the social and intellectual dimensions known to organize human personality impressions—social warmth and intellectual competence. On held-out dialogue, projections onto these directions yield personality profiles that agree with human ratings.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a framework enabling comprehensive, human-grounded comparison between internal model trait geometry and the shared structure of human personality impressions, demonstrating that LLM trait representations reproduce the cross-culturally consistent human relational structure.

title: Robust Underwater Grasping of Sloped Objects with a Waterproof Passive Adaptive Gripper
summary: Robust grasping of everyday objects remains challenging for parallel-jaw grippers, particularly when handling sloped or asymmetric items that induce torque-driven rolling and shear slip. These challenges become even more severe in domestic environments such as kitchens, where objects are often wet or submerged, drastically reducing friction between the gripper and the object. To address these issues, we present a waterproof passive adaptive gripper that combines local and global adaptability for high-performance grasping in the submerged environments. The proposed gripper features a fully waterproof design that integrates a passive rotational joint for global self-alignment on sloped surfaces and passive variable-stiffness pads for local surface adaptation. Experiments in both dry and underwater conditions on various cylindrical and conical objects demonstrate superior holding capability and grasp robustness compared to rigid-pad and fixed-joint baselines. The proposed design offers a practical and robust solution that successfully enables stable underwater manipulation of diverse everyday objects, effectively addressing a critical gap in current underwater robotic grasping for daily-life applications.

AI.tldr: A waterproof passive adaptive gripper with a passive rotational joint and variable-stiffness pads enables stable underwater grasping of sloped and asymmetric everyday objects.
AI.motivation: Parallel-jaw grippers struggle to grasp sloped or asymmetric objects that cause torque-driven rolling and shear slip. These problems worsen in domestic settings like kitchens, where wet or submerged objects drastically reduce friction. Current underwater robotic grasping lacks a practical solution for stable manipulation of diverse daily-life objects.
AI.method: The authors present a waterproof passive adaptive gripper combining local and global adaptability. It integrates a passive rotational joint for global self-alignment on sloped surfaces and passive variable-stiffness pads for local surface adaptation, within a fully waterproof design.
AI.result: Experiments in dry and underwater conditions on various cylindrical and conical objects show superior holding capability and grasp robustness compared with rigid-pad and fixed-joint baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed design provides a practical and robust solution for stable underwater manipulation of diverse everyday objects, addressing a critical gap in underwater robotic grasping for daily-life applications.

title: When Rubrics Fail: Hallucinations Reveal Blind Spots in Medical AI Evaluation
summary: Hallucinations can undermine clinician trust in LLMs, making it important that evaluation methods capture clinically relevant errors. Rubric-based evaluation has become the leading approach for assessing LLMs in medicine, but it is unclear whether rubric scores reflect such errors. We first study this in a controlled setting using MedHallu, finding that more specific rubrics better distinguish correct from hallucinated responses. To test this systematically, we develop a taxonomy of medical hallucination types and a clinician-validated error-injection pipeline that creates matched correct and error-injected responses. Across HealthBench, HealthBench Professional, and LiveMedBench, our clinically relevant hallucinations are missed by rubrics, often leaving scores unchanged. We find that rubrics are most effective when explicitly checking facts, and are less effective for additional or unexpected errors they do not anticipate. A preliminary retrieval-based factuality check recovers some of the rubric-blind errors, suggesting a complementary approach. These findings reveal systematic blind spots in current medical evaluation of LLMs and suggest that rubric scores alone are insufficient to establish clinical reliability, potentially undermining clinician trust and confidence in clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: Rubric-based evaluation misses clinically relevant hallucinations in medical LLMs; a retrieval-based factuality check can help recover some rubric-blind errors.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations undermine clinician trust in LLMs, so evaluation methods must capture clinically relevant errors. Rubric-based evaluation is now the leading approach for assessing LLMs in medicine, but it is unclear whether rubric scores actually reflect such errors.
AI.method: First, a controlled study using MedHallu examining whether rubric specificity distinguishes correct from hallucinated responses. Then a systematic test: a taxonomy of medical hallucination types plus a clinician-validated error-injection pipeline that generates matched correct and error-injected responses. Evaluation across HealthBench, HealthBench Professional, and LiveMedBench. Finally, a preliminary retrieval-based factuality check.
AI.result: More specific rubrics better distinguish correct from hallucinated responses in MedHallu. However, across the three benchmarks, clinically relevant hallucinations are missed by rubrics, often leaving scores unchanged. Rubrics work best when explicitly checking facts and are less effective for additional or unanticipated errors. A retrieval-based factuality check recovers some rubric-blind errors.
AI.conclusion: Current medical evaluation of LLMs has systematic blind spots. Rubric scores alone are insufficient to establish clinical reliability, which may undermine clinician trust and confidence in clinical deployment; complementary factuality checking is suggested.

title: Skill Issue: Lessons from Optimizing Repository SKILLs for Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents increasingly read repository knowledge from SKILLs --- plain \texttt{.md} files versioned alongside the code. Recent work synthesizes these files automatically, by optimizing the document against a benchmark. A bare repository comes with no benchmark, and the synthetic tasks prior work builds are small enough that a capable agent saturates them with no document at all. We mine harder tasks --- merged pull requests of the repository, reverted at a single frozen base commit; and score a candidate document by whether the same agent does better with it than without it. On three Kotlin repositories, the documents GEPA finds raise this score by $4.9$pp on average, and the ones SkillOpt finds leave it where it started, $0.1$pp above the seed. The GEPA gain matches what prior work reports with the same optimizer, and at the dataset size a single repository supplies it cannot be separated from the agent's run-to-run variance; settling that would take more tasks than one repository's history yields. The documents themselves read better than the score: a maintainer of one repository found in them knowledge one only gets by working in the project.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles automatic synthesis of repository SKILL documents (plain .md files) for coding agents, addressing the absence of benchmarks in bare repositories and the saturation of prior synthetic tasks. It mines harder tasks from merged pull requests that were reverted at a frozen base commit and scores documents by whether an agent performs better with them than without. Across three Kotlin repositories, GEPA-found documents improve the score by 4.9pp on average while SkillOpt's remain at 0.1pp above the seed, though the GEPA gain is statistically indistinguishable from run-to-run variance at single-repository dataset sizes.
AI.motivation: Coding agents increasingly rely on repository knowledge stored in SKILLs, i.e., plain .md files versioned alongside code. Recent work synthesizes these files by optimizing a document against a benchmark. However, a bare repository ships with no benchmark, and the synthetic tasks prior work constructs are small enough that a capable agent saturates them even without any document. This creates a need for harder, repository-grounded tasks and a benchmark-free way to score candidate documents.
AI.method: The authors mine harder tasks from the repository itself: merged pull requests that were later reverted, replayed at a single frozen base commit. A candidate document is then scored by whether the same agent does better with the document than without it. The approach is evaluated on three Kotlin repositories, comparing documents produced by GEPA against those from SkillOpt.
AI.result: On three Kotlin repositories, documents found by GEPA raise the score by 4.9pp on average, whereas those found by SkillOpt leave it essentially unchanged at 0.1pp above the seed. The GEPA gain matches prior work's reports with the same optimizer, but at the dataset size a single repository supplies it cannot be statistically separated from the agent's run-to-run variance; resolving this would require more tasks than one repository's history provides. Qualitatively, the documents read better than the score suggests: a maintainer of one repository found knowledge in them that one only acquires by working in the project.
AI.conclusion: Harder, repository-mined tasks (reverted merged PRs at a frozen base commit) combined with a with-versus-without document scoring scheme can produce useful repository SKILLs, as demonstrated by GEPA's 4.9pp average gain on three Kotlin repositories, while SkillOpt's documents show no meaningful improvement. However, the measured gain is not yet statistically separable from agent run-to-run variance at single-repository dataset sizes, so stronger conclusions would require far more tasks than one repository's history yields. Notably, maintainer review suggests the generated documents capture tacit, project-specific knowledge beyond what the benchmark score reflects.

title: A Robot Among People:From Social Imitation to the Social Becoming of Human Groups
summary: Robots designed to mediate human groups often fall into the solutionist trap: they are framed as sociable agents that fix problems such as conflict, disengagement, or lack of coordination. We suggest a different way of thinking. Rather than discrete agents, robots can be understood as situated elements of shared environments; catalysts and carriers of group experience whose meaning emerges through how people position, interpret, and interact with them. From this perspective, robots are not there to repair some ostensible dysfunctionality, but to enable group-level sense-making around care, norms, and identity. Our prior work on robotic street furniture suggests that this does not happen by imitating human sociality but by taking the shape of deliberately constrained, group-facing entities that happen and act for \textit{us} without being socially entangled as one of us. We thus understand robots in public spaces not in terms of autonomy or intelligence, but as a relational capacity. This implies designing robots not in our image or for our utility, but grounded in our needs in being and becoming together.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques the "solutionist" framing of social robots as fixers of group dysfunction, proposing instead that robots be understood as situated, relational elements of shared environments that foster group-level sense-making around care, norms, and identity.
AI.motivation: Robots mediating human groups are typically framed as sociable agents meant to resolve problems like conflict, disengagement, or poor coordination. The authors argue this solutionist trap mischaracterizes the role of robots and leads to flawed design assumptions, motivating an alternative conceptualization.
AI.method: Conceptual/theoretical argument grounded in the authors' prior empirical work on robotic street furniture. The paper repositions robots as catalysts and carriers of group experience whose meaning emerges through how people position, interpret, and interact with them.
AI.result: Robotic street furniture does not support group sense-making by imitating human sociality, but by adopting the form of deliberately constrained, group-facing entities that act for "us" without being socially entangled as "one of us."
AI.conclusion: Robots in public spaces should be understood not in terms of autonomy or intelligence but as a relational capacity. This implies designing robots not in our image or for our utility, but grounded in human needs for being and becoming together.

title: What Drives Recovery in Agentic Text-to-Cypher? LAST-CQ: An LLM Agent Self-Refinement Framework
comment: Accepted at REALM: The 2nd Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models at Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026), 15 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
summary: Agentic pipelines for structured-query generation are rapidly expanding, but it is unclear which part of the loop produces the gain. We use LAST-CQ -- a five-agent, training-free, execution-grounded Text-to-Cypher framework -- as an instrumented testbed, running three counterfactuals over 2,471 live-database queries and six backbones spanning three vendor scale tiers. Removing correction is worth between 3.1% aggregate execution-BLEU against the single-pass system and 12.3% against a no-refinement counterfactual (up to 80.7% for the weakest backbone). Replacing schema-grounded, LLM-synthesised feedback with raw database error strings costs almost nothing (20.9% vs. 19.9% naive exact match; <0.2% end-to-end; equivalent within $\pm 0.075$ set-F1 by two one-sided tests). Spending the same call budget on parallel sampling degrades quality by 10-11%. What works is detecting failure and routing it to a retry, not the feedback sophistication or number of samples. LAST-CQ itself recovers 91.7% of queries that fail under single-pass generation, while a query that succeeds first time still costs exactly one LLM call. We also show that n-gram overlap on serialised results is not a bound in either direction: it over-scores against set equivalence on 65.9% of results while under-scoring against judged semantics. Finally, we calibrate our LLM judge against blind human labels and find it optimistic by 9 points.

AI.tldr: Ablating a five-agent Text-to-Cypher pipeline over 2,471 queries shows the gain comes from failure detection and retry routing, not from feedback sophistication or extra sampling.
AI.motivation: Agentic pipelines for structured-query generation are proliferating, yet it is unclear which component of the loop actually drives performance gains. The paper isolates the contribution of correction, feedback type, and sampling budget.
AI.method: LAST-CQ is used as an instrumented testbed: a five-agent, training-free, execution-grounded Text-to-Cypher framework. Three counterfactuals are run over 2,471 live-database queries across six backbone LLMs spanning three vendor scale tiers: (1) removing the correction stage, (2) replacing schema-grounded, LLM-synthesised feedback with raw database error strings, and (3) reallocating the same call budget to parallel sampling. Evaluation uses execution-BLEU, exact match, set-F1, two one-sided equivalence tests, and an LLM judge calibrated against blind human labels.
AI.result: Removing correction costs 3.1% aggregate execution-BLEU versus the single-pass system and 12.3% versus a no-refinement counterfactual, reaching up to 80.7% for the weakest backbone. Swapping synthesised feedback for raw database error strings is nearly free (20.9% vs. 19.9% naive exact match; <0.2% end-to-end; equivalent within plus/minus 0.075 set-F1). Spending the same budget on parallel sampling degrades quality by 10-11%. Serialised-result n-gram overlap is not a bound in either direction: it over-scores against set equivalence on 65.9% of results while under-scoring against judged semantics. The LLM judge is optimistic by 9 points relative to blind human labels.
AI.conclusion: What matters is detecting failure and routing it to a retry, not feedback sophistication or sample count. LAST-CQ recovers 91.7% of queries that fail under single-pass generation, while a first-try success still costs exactly one LLM call.

title: Distributed Stochastic Optimal Control for Pattern-Oriented Swarms
summary: While offering significant promise for diverse applications, pattern-oriented swarms encounter multifaceted challenges in geometric control, self-organization, and safe navigation through dynamic environments. In this paper, we present a GRF-based stochastic optimal control framework to address these challenges within a unified probabilistic architecture. By extending the GRF into the temporal domain, the proposed framework casts collective coordination as a Bayesian inference task, enabling swarms to accommodate environmental uncertainty, satisfy non-convex constraints, and reconcile heterogeneous dynamics across diverse platforms. We develop an uncertainty- and safety-aware collision avoidance module for navigation in the presence of stochastic obstacle motion. The unscented transform is employed to propagate state uncertainty for both dynamic obstacles and neighboring agents, yielding principled confidence bounds for collision avoidance. In addition, density-guided pattern control is introduced, which encodes geometric patterns as implicit density fields. This representation decouples pattern specification from explicit agent-to-target assignments, thereby facilitating intrinsic self-healing and elastic reconfiguration in a distributed manner. The proposed framework is extensively evaluated through Monte Carlo simulations across diverse scenarios. Its model-agnostic nature is demonstrated on both quadrotor and fixed-wing UAV swarms, highlighting its generalizability across platforms with heterogeneous dynamics. Finally, the efficacy and robustness of the proposed method are validated through indoor experiments with a 15-quadrotor swarm and outdoor deployments involving 4 custom-built autonomous quadrotors. These experiments substantiate the proposed framework's capacity to maintain reliable geometric pattern transitions and safety-aware navigation within real-world environments.

AI.tldr: A GRF-based stochastic optimal control framework unifies geometric pattern control, self-organization, and safe navigation for swarms, validated in simulation and real-world UAV experiments.
AI.motivation: Pattern-oriented swarms promise diverse applications but face multifaceted challenges in geometric control, self-organization, and safe navigation through dynamic environments. Existing approaches typically handle these aspects separately rather than within a unified architecture.
AI.method: Extends a Gaussian Random Field (GRF) into the temporal domain, casting collective coordination as Bayesian inference to handle environmental uncertainty, non-convex constraints, and heterogeneous dynamics. Develops an uncertainty- and safety-aware collision avoidance module using the unscented transform to propagate state uncertainty for dynamic obstacles and neighbors, yielding principled confidence bounds. Introduces density-guided pattern control encoding geometric patterns as implicit density fields, decoupling pattern specification from explicit agent-to-target assignments to enable distributed intrinsic self-healing and elastic reconfiguration.
AI.result: Extensive Monte Carlo simulations across diverse scenarios, with model-agnostic demonstration on quadrotor and fixed-wing UAV swarms. Validated via indoor experiments with a 15-quadrotor swarm and outdoor deployments of 4 custom-built autonomous quadrotors.
AI.conclusion: The framework maintains reliable geometric pattern transitions and safety-aware navigation in real-world environments, showing efficacy, robustness, and generalizability across platforms with heterogeneous dynamics.

title: Assisted Spatial Cognition Through Vision-Language Models
summary: Multimodal AI, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), is transforming assistive technologies by enabling simultaneous processing of visual and textual data. This advancement holds significant promise for over 43 million visually impaired and neuro-divergent individuals worldwide who face persistent challenges in navigating indoor and outdoor environments due to limited spatial awareness and insufficient environmental cues. Existing navigation aids often lack comprehensive 3D scene understanding, relying on constrained route-based strategies that hinder user autonomy. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end framework that integrates LLMs, VLMs and digital twin technologies to deliver a spatially cognitive navigation support for visually impaired and neuro-divergent users. Our system captures video input via standard mobile phone cameras, and employs SLAM3R to generate dense 3D point clouds from monocular RGB sequences in real-time. Our custom post-processing algorithm ensures accurate point cloud alignment across multiple viewpoints without requiring predefined reference points. This enhances the capabilities of SpatialLM to produce structured 3D representations, including architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes. The enriched spatial data is then processed by a locally deployed LLM, which interprets 3D contexts to generate detailed scene descriptions and precise distance measurements between users and surrounding objects. We evaluated our approach across diverse video scenarios featuring various perspectives, looped walking views and captured in multiple environments. The evaluation results demonstrate consistent accuracy in 3D scene interpretation and object localisation, underscoring the potential of our system as a transformative assistive navigation solution that combines advanced visual perception with spatial reasoning

AI.tldr: The paper presents an end-to-end, on-device multimodal framework combining LLMs, VLMs, SLAM3R, custom point-cloud alignment, and SpatialLM to deliver real-time spatial cognitive navigation assistance for visually impaired and neuro-divergent users, evaluated across diverse video scenarios with consistent 3D scene interpretation and object localization accuracy.
AI.motivation: Over 43 million visually impaired and neuro-divergent individuals face persistent navigation challenges indoors and outdoors due to limited spatial awareness and insufficient environmental cues. Existing navigation aids lack comprehensive 3D scene understanding, relying on constrained route-based strategies that restrict user autonomy. Multimodal AI advances offer an opportunity to provide richer, spatially aware assistance.
AI.method: An end-to-end framework integrating LLMs, VLMs, and digital twin technologies. Video is captured via standard mobile phone cameras; SLAM3R generates dense 3D point clouds from monocular RGB sequences in real time. A custom post-processing algorithm achieves accurate multi-viewpoint point cloud alignment without predefined reference points. SpatialLM then produces structured 3D representations, including architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes. A locally deployed LLM interprets the enriched 3D context to generate detailed scene descriptions and precise user-to-object distance measurements.
AI.result: Evaluation across diverse video scenarios with various perspectives, looped walking views, and multiple environments showed consistent accuracy in 3D scene interpretation and object localization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system shows promise as a transformative assistive navigation solution that combines advanced visual perception with spatial reasoning, supporting autonomy for visually impaired and neuro-divergent users through spatially cognitive guidance.

title: SCQ: Stabilizing Conservative Q-Learning with Sigmoid-Bounded Entropy
summary: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning reduces interaction cost for real-world robot learning but suffers from persistent value estimation instability. Existing methods address this through pessimistic regularization, lower-bound calibration, and architectural normalization, but an overlooked source of instability lies in the entropy formulation: the standard log-entropy term can become negative, destabilizing policy updates. We introduce SCQ (Sigmoid-Bounded Conservative Q-Learning), which replaces this term with a sigmoid-bounded formulation that stays strictly positive. SCQ retains conservative Q regularization and return-based lower-bound calibration, stabilizing policy optimization without sacrificing exploration. We evaluate SCQ on D4RL (Minari) benchmarks under both single-demonstration and standard dataset settings, as well as on simulation and real-world visual tasks. SCQ matches or exceeds baseline performance while exhibiting more stable training dynamics across state-based and visual benchmarks, and transfers to four real-robot platforms including manipulation, wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid systems. A direct clipping intervention that removes negative log-probability contributions, together with gradient-matched positive-score controls, indicates that positivity rather than a particular score shape alone drives much of the improvement. Project website: https://scq-rl.github.io.

AI.tldr: SCQ replaces the standard log-entropy term with a strictly positive sigmoid-bounded entropy formulation to stabilize offline-to-online RL, matching or exceeding baselines and transferring to real robots.
AI.motivation: Offline-to-online RL lowers real-world robot interaction cost but suffers persistent value estimation instability. Prior fixes (pessimistic regularization, lower-bound calibration, architectural normalization) overlook the entropy formulation, where the standard log-entropy term can turn negative and destabilize policy updates.
AI.method: SCQ (Sigmoid-Bounded Conservative Q-Learning) replaces the log-entropy term with a sigmoid-bounded formulation that remains strictly positive, while retaining conservative Q regularization and return-based lower-bound calibration. Ablations include a direct clipping intervention removing negative log-probability contributions plus gradient-matched positive-score controls.
AI.result: On D4RL (Minari) benchmarks under single-demonstration and standard dataset settings, and on simulation and real-world visual tasks, SCQ matches or exceeds baselines with more stable training dynamics. It transfers to four real-robot platforms: manipulation, wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-term positivity, rather than a particular score shape, drives much of the stabilization gain, offering a simple principled fix for value instability in offline-to-online robot learning.

title: Comfort by Construction: Adaptive, Comfort-Bounded Action Spaces for Learned Driving Policies
summary: Data-driven driving simulators command accelerations and steering rates from a fixed grid without constraining the realized accelerations and jerks. As a result, reinforcement-learning policies inflate safety metrics through abrupt, last-second maneuvers that lie far outside the range of human driving and would be unacceptable to occupants of a real vehicle, so the metrics measure simulator permissiveness rather than policy quality. Enforcing comfort bounds naively is not enough: lateral limits shrink quadratically with speed, so clamping a static grid saturates it and destroys fine-grained control ("grid collapse"). We propose an adaptive action parameterization that rediscretizes the grid at every step to span exactly the per-step feasible control set, via closed-form inversion of the lateral-jerk constraint. We further present PufferDrive-Editor, a browser-based tool to audit realized kinematics and author kinematically challenging scenes. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset and a hand-authored slalom, our adaptive model holds comfort violations below 1% while outperforming clipped-grid and direct-jerk baselines in navigability.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that fixed-grid action parameterizations in data-driven driving simulators allow RL policies to inflate safety metrics via unrealistic abrupt maneuvers, and proposes an adaptive action parameterization that rediscretizes the control grid each step to match the feasible control set, plus an auditing tool.
AI.motivation: Fixed-grid action parameterizations decouple commanded accelerations/steering rates from realized accelerations and jerks, letting RL policies achieve inflated safety metrics through last-second maneuvers outside human driving ranges—measuring simulator permissiveness rather than policy quality. Naive comfort-bound enforcement fails because lateral limits shrink quadratically with speed, causing clamping of a static grid to saturate and destroy fine-grained control ("grid collapse").
AI.method: The authors propose an adaptive action parameterization that rediscretizes the action grid at every step to span exactly the per-step feasible control set, achieved via closed-form inversion of the lateral-jerk constraint. They also present PufferDrive-Editor, a browser-based tool for auditing realized kinematics and authoring kinematically challenging scenes.
AI.result: On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset and a hand-authored slalom scenario, the adaptive model holds comfort violations below 1% while outperforming clipped-grid and direct-jerk baselines in navigability.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, feasibility-aware action parameterization enables RL driving policies to maintain comfort constraints without sacrificing fine-grained control, yielding more realistic and meaningful policy evaluation than fixed-grid or naive-clipping approaches, supported by an auditing/authoring tool for kinematic validation.

title: Unified Agentic Video Editing Across Levels of Complexity and Creativity
summary: Editing is a core component of video production, requiring creative planning and decisions under multiple constraints. Here, we report methods for agentic tooling for automated video editing across three tasks varying in editorial goal, complexity and creativity, namely scene previews, video summaries and cinematic trailers. We evaluate the outputs and discuss implications for automation and agency.

AI.tldr: The paper presents agentic tooling methods for automated video editing, tested across three tasks of increasing creativity—scene previews, video summaries, and cinematic trailers—and evaluates the outputs while discussing implications for automation and human agency.
AI.motivation: Video editing is a core component of video production that demands creative planning and decision-making under multiple constraints, motivating the need for agentic tooling that can automate such editorial work.
AI.method: The authors develop agentic tooling approaches for automated video editing and apply them across three tasks that vary in editorial goal, complexity, and creativity: scene previews, video summaries, and cinematic trailers.
AI.result: The outputs produced by the agentic tooling are evaluated for the three editing tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work discusses implications for automation and agency in video editing, based on the evaluation of the generated outputs.

title: Global Path Planner with Multi-Model Switching
summary: This work enhances global path planning via a pure-pursuit controller with multi-model kinematic switching that sustains plan fidelity across diverse terrains. The system includes a traversability graph for terrain analysis, a Heading-Aware A* algorithm for generating feasible paths, and a multi-model Pure Pursuit controller for dynamic tracking. A core innovation is adaptive kinematic modeling, enabling real-time switching between kinematic models based on terrain features and robot states. This adaptability optimizes path efficiency and energy use in challenging scenarios. We validate the approach in simulation on different platforms, namely the Artaban quadruped and the X3 quadrotor drone, showcasing improved performance, robustness, and adaptability over standard baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a terrain-aware global path planning and tracking framework that combines a traversability graph, a Heading-Aware A* planner, and a multi-model Pure Pursuit controller with adaptive kinematic switching, validated on a quadruped and a quadrotor.
