AI.motivation: Sustaining plan fidelity across diverse terrains is difficult because a single fixed kinematic model cannot represent how different platforms behave on varying terrain. This mismatch degrades path efficiency and energy use, especially in challenging scenarios.
AI.method: The system consists of three components: (1) a traversability graph for terrain analysis, (2) a Heading-Aware A* algorithm that generates feasible paths, and (3) a multi-model Pure Pursuit controller for dynamic tracking. The core innovation is adaptive kinematic modeling, which performs real-time switching between kinematic models based on terrain features and robot states.
AI.result: Simulation experiments on two different platforms, the Artaban quadruped and the X3 quadrotor drone, show improved performance, robustness, and adaptability compared with standard baselines.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive kinematic switching within a Pure Pursuit controller preserves plan fidelity across terrains, yielding better path efficiency and energy use, and generalizes across legged and aerial platforms.

title: MPT: Missing Prototype Tracking via Barycentric Reconstruction in Vehicular Federated Learning
summary: Cross-vehicle federated learning enables vehicles to collaboratively improve perception models while keeping locally collected driving data private. However, vehicle participation is transient, and a vehicle may depart before training converges while permanently taking its local data. When this departing vehicle holds most samples of a target class, the class becomes rare in the remaining FL network, and its recognition can silently degrade as the shared backbone continues to evolve. Recovering the class is difficult since the few remaining samples provide a noisy prototype estimate, while FL privacy constraints prevent centralized access to raw data or per-sample features. This paper presents MPT, a cross-vehicle FL framework that maintains rare-class recognition by reconstructing its prototype at every round from privacy-preserving class-level statistics. MPT combines a barycentric decomposition that tracks drift shared with remaining-class prototypes, a covariance-based residual prediction that estimates out-of-span drift, and an adaptive calibration that weighs the remaining rare-class samples according to their reliability. We evaluate MPT on three vehicle classification tasks and four backbones against representative calibration and drift-compensation baselines. MPT outperforms all baselines in rare class F1, reaching 0.516 on the nuImages dataset with only 1\% of rare-class samples remaining, without raw data, per-sample features, or retraining.

AI.tldr: MPT is a cross-vehicle federated learning framework that preserves rare-class recognition when a departing vehicle takes most of a class's data, reconstructing the class prototype each round from privacy-preserving class-level statistics.
AI.motivation: In cross-vehicle federated learning, vehicle participation is transient; a vehicle may leave before convergence and permanently remove its local data. If that vehicle held most samples of a target class, the class becomes rare in the remaining network and its recognition can silently degrade as the shared backbone evolves. Recovery is hard because remaining samples yield a noisy prototype and FL privacy constraints forbid centralized access to raw data or per-sample features.
AI.method: MPT reconstructs the rare-class prototype at every round from privacy-preserving class-level statistics. It combines three components: a barycentric decomposition that tracks drift shared with remaining-class prototypes, a covariance-based residual prediction that estimates out-of-span drift, and an adaptive calibration that weights remaining rare-class samples by their reliability.
AI.result: Evaluated on three vehicle classification tasks and four backbones against representative calibration and drift-compensation baselines, MPT outperforms all baselines in rare-class F1, reaching 0.516 on nuImages with only 1% of rare-class samples remaining, without raw data, per-sample features, or retraining.

title: Dynin-Robotics: Omnimodal Unified Diffusion Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Visual goal and dynamics prediction can provide language-conditioned robot policies with both a target outcome and a representation of action-dependent scene changes. We bring these predictions into action generation and selection through a shared trajectory model. Dynin-Robotics implements this formulation on Dynin-Omni, an omnimodal masked-diffusion backbone, representing language, visual observations, goals, and actions as discrete tokens. By varying conditioning and target spans, the same model learns action prediction, action-conditioned next-observation prediction, terminal goal-state prediction, and trajectory-to-instruction reconstruction. These interfaces support test-time scaling through goal prediction, action-candidate evaluation, and joint refinement of action and future-state predictions. We continually pretrain the model on approximately 1.33 million trajectories from 48 Open X-Embodiment datasets and adapt it separately to downstream domains. On two VLABench tasks, robot pretraining improves adaptation within a fixed Stage-2 step budget, and the full objective mixture improves shifted-instruction success over Policy-only post-training under the same coupled decoder. Combining goal guidance with joint action-next-state denoising further improves shifted-instruction success over action-only decoding; the benefit depends on how the predictions are composed. Dynin-Robotics achieves competitive performance on LIBERO and zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, together with a 78.4% average success rate across four manipulation conditions on a Franka Research 3 robot. An optimized block-parallel implementation accelerates model-side action decoding by up to 29.2x relative to the base implementation under the reported profiling setup. These results support shared trajectory modeling as a common interface for learning complementary robot objectives and composing their predictions during control.

AI.tldr: Dynin-Robotics uses a shared trajectory model on an omnimodal masked-diffusion backbone to unify goal/dynamics prediction with language-conditioned robot action generation, enabling test-time composition of complementary predictions and competitive manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: Visual goal and dynamics prediction provide robot policies with a target outcome and a representation of action-dependent scene changes, but these predictions are typically separated from action generation and selection. The paper aims to bring goal and dynamics prediction into action generation and selection through a unified formulation.
AI.method: The method builds on Dynin-Omni, an omnimodal masked-diffusion backbone that tokenizes language, visual observations, goals, and actions as discrete tokens. By varying conditioning and target spans, one model learns action prediction, action-conditioned next-observation prediction, terminal goal-state prediction, and trajectory-to-instruction reconstruction. These interfaces enable test-time scaling via goal prediction, action-candidate evaluation, and joint refinement of action and future-state predictions. The model is continually pretrained on ~1.33M trajectories from 48 Open X-Embodiment datasets and adapted to downstream domains.

Combining goal guidance with joint action-next-state denoising further improves shifted-instruction success over action-only decoding, with benefits depending on prediction composition. The model achieves competitive performance on LIBERO and zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, and 78.4% average success across four manipulation conditions on a Franka Research 3. An optimized block-parallel implementation accelerates action decoding by up to 29.2x versus the base implementation.
AI.conclusion: Shared trajectory modeling serves as a common interface for learning complementary robot objectives and composing their predictions during control, supporting both effective adaptation and test-time scaling.

title: Interpreting the predictions of neural network classification based on a Taylor Coefficient Analysis (TCA)
summary: We introduce a rigid and comprehensive taxonomy and paradigm for characterizing the influence of the input feature space $X$ on the predictions $\hat{y}$ of a neural network (NN) used for event classification, based on a Taylor expansion of $\hat{y}$ in $X$. The complete process of introspection we refer to as Taylor Coefficient Analysis (TCA). Based on two simplistic example tasks, which can be easily understood and bencmarked, we illustrate the power of the TCA when it comes to revealing, what properties of $X$ have led to what value of $\hat{y}$, of a given NN model, building up intuition for the method. A more complex application is meant to represent $X$ of a typical classification task at a CERN LHC experiment. Based on this application, we play through the different levels of introspection that the TCA offers and discuss a number of practical aspects for a TCA application typical for the analysis of CERN LHC data. We conclude with a study to support the assumption that those properties of $X$ most relevant for tasks of the complexity typical for a CERN LHC experiment, are usually caught by a TCA up to the second order.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Taylor Coefficient Analysis (TCA), a rigid taxonomy and paradigm for interpreting neural network event classifiers by Taylor-expanding the output in the input feature space.
AI.motivation: Neural networks used for event classification are opaque; there is a need for a systematic, comprehensive method to reveal which properties of the input feature space drive a given prediction.
AI.method: TCA is based on a Taylor expansion of the network prediction y-hat in input features X, providing multiple levels of introspection. It is illustrated on two simple benchmark tasks and a more complex application representing a typical CERN LHC classification task, including practical aspects for LHC data analysis.
AI.result: The method reveals what properties of X lead to a given y-hat, building intuition; the CERN LHC case demonstrates the different introspection levels and practical implementation aspects; a supporting study indicates that features most relevant for LHC-complexity tasks are typically captured by TCA up to second order.
AI.conclusion: TCA offers a rigorous and practical framework for interpreting NN event classifiers, and second-order Taylor terms usually suffice for capturing the features most relevant to tasks of CERN LHC complexity.

title: K-Bench: A Benchmark for LLM Unlearning in Agentic Deployments
summary: Unlearning benchmarks such as TOFU and MUSE certify forgetting by reading the model's final answer, where a model that refuses to answer already counts as having forgotten. We show that this model-level certificate does not transfer once the model is deployed as an agent. We introduce K-Bench, a benchmark that scores LLM unlearning under agentic deployment. K-Bench inspects all six channels a ReAct agent exposes, including its chain-of-thought (CoT), tool calls and tool observations, and elicited summary. A query counts as leaked if the secret appears in any of them. Each experiment places the secret in exactly one of the agent's three sources (the weights, the prompt, or the retrieval store). The K-Score is computed separately for each source and credits forgetting only when the agent remains usable. Clearing the answer channel does not make the secret unrecoverable. On structured retrieval, the secret stays verbatim in the tool-observation channel and the aggregate leak rate is unchanged. When the secret lives in the prompt or the retrieval store, TOFU and MUSE report no leakage, while the deployed agent still leaks it on 22--86\% of queries. When the secret is in the weights, none of the twenty evaluated published methods demonstrably removes it, and only an input-corruption intervention reaches selective forgetting under the evaluated observer. The top-ranked method changes across base models. A refusal-tuning method resists the evaluated extraction without verified knowledge removal.

AI.tldr: K-Bench shows that model-level unlearning certificates (TOFU, MUSE) do not transfer to agentic deployment: secrets remain recoverable from CoT, tool calls, tool observations, or summaries even when the final answer is suppressed.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearning benchmarks certify forgetting by only inspecting the model's final answer, so a model that merely refuses to answer is scored as having forgotten. The authors argue this model-level certificate is insufficient once the model is deployed as an agent that exposes multiple output and internal channels.
AI.method: The authors introduce K-Bench, which scores LLM unlearning under agentic deployment. It inspects all six channels a ReAct agent exposes, including chain-of-thought, tool calls, tool observations, and elicited summary; a query counts as leaked if the secret appears in any channel. Each experiment places the secret in exactly one of three sources (weights, prompt, or retrieval store), computes a K-Score separately per source, and credits forgetting only when the agent remains usable. Twenty published methods are evaluated.
AI.result: Clearing the answer channel does not make the secret unrecoverable. On structured retrieval, the secret remains verbatim in the tool-observation channel and the aggregate leak rate is unchanged. With the secret in the prompt or retrieval store, TOFU and MUSE report no leakage while the deployed agent leaks it on 22-86% of queries. The top-ranked method varies across base models, and a refusal-tuning method resists the evaluated extraction without verified knowledge removal.
AI.conclusion: Model-level unlearning certificates such as TOFU and MUSE do not transfer to agentic deployment settings, where leakage persists through non-answer channels. Evaluation must inspect the full set of agent-exposed channels, and verified removal of secrets from weights remains an open problem.

title: Scaling Clinical Judgment to Evaluate Medical AI
summary: Blinded physician evaluation has been considered by many to be the gold standard for assessing clinical reasoning in large language models (LLMs). This is difficult to scale; thus, prior studies typically rely on small physician panels, often from a single institution or specialty, which both limits the scientific questions investigated and makes it unclear whether findings would be reproduced with a different set of evaluators. To more rigorously and scalably study clinical reasoning in AI models, here we introduce PrecepTron, an LLM fine-tuned for physician-level evaluation of open-ended responses. PrecepTron was trained using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) of a 32-billion-parameter model on a small number of physician examples. We also release GRAND-ROUNDS, a new large-scale physician-annotated benchmark of 9,217 scores by 11 physicians across seven studies. We show that frontier LLMs in typical "LLM-as-a-judge" approaches often disagree with physicians and with each other, but fine-tuning PrecepTron on a small number of cases enables physician-level consistent scoring across tasks. We use PrecepTron to reproduce headline findings from five influential studies assessing LLMs for clinical care in JAMA, Science, and Nature Medicine without new human grading. Using PrecepTron, we then pose new questions about how LLMs reason in medicine that would have been infeasible with human grading alone, including measuring the diagnostic accuracy of frontier LLMs when clinical cases are provided piecemeal, even token by token. Together, PrecepTron and GRAND-ROUNDS provide a foundation for reproducible, large-scale study of how LLMs reason in medicine. All code, data, and labels are made freely available for researchers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PrecepTron, an LLM fine-tuned via LoRA on a 32B model with a small number of physician examples to perform physician-level evaluation of open-ended clinical responses, along with GRAND-ROUNDS, a large-scale physician-annotated benchmark of 9,217 scores from 11 physicians across seven studies, enabling scalable and reproducible assessment of clinical reasoning in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Blinded physician evaluation is regarded as the gold standard for assessing clinical reasoning in large language models, but it is difficult to scale. Prior work therefore relies on small physician panels, often from a single institution or specialty, which limits the scientific questions that can be investigated and raises concerns about reproducibility with different evaluators. A more rigorous and scalable method is needed.
AI.method: The authors develop PrecepTron, an LLM fine-tuned for physician-level evaluation of open-ended responses, trained using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) of a 32-billion-parameter model on a small number of physician examples. They also release GRAND-ROUNDS, a large-scale physician-annotated benchmark comprising 9,217 scores from 11 physicians across seven studies. PrecepTron is then used to reproduce and extend prior evaluations.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs used in typical "LLM-as-a-judge" approaches often disagree with physicians and with each other. In contrast, fine-tuning PrecepTron on a small number of cases enables physician-level consistent scoring across tasks. PrecepTron reproduces headline findings from five influential studies assessing LLMs for clinical care in JAMA, Science, and Nature Medicine without new human grading, and supports new questions, including measuring diagnostic accuracy of frontier LLMs when clinical cases are provided piecemeal, even token by token.
AI.conclusion: PrecepTron and GRAND-ROUNDS together provide a foundation for reproducible, large-scale study of how LLMs reason in medicine. All code, data, and labels are made freely available to researchers.

title: MedRoundsQA: A Persona and Difficulty Aware Evaluation for Multi-Turn Medical Consultations
summary: Medical benchmarks are dominated by single-turn, multiple-choice clinical cases that poorly reflect real consultations. Practically, clinicians elicit evidence interactively and patient communication varies widely. We introduce MedRoundsQA, a multi-turn diagnostic benchmark derived from 1,387 board-exam cases across 17 specialties. Each case is converted into a structured 24-slot clinical record, and then instantiated as controlled doctor-patient dual-agent dialogues under varying patient personas, with the underlying clinical content held fixed. We further classify cases by difficulty using model-based uncertainty to enable easy-to-hard analysis. Evaluations of fifteen LLM doctor agents show that (i) moving from a single-turn diagnosis on the standardized records to multi-turn consultations causes large degradations of roughly 13-39 points; (ii) more turns reliably improves question relevance, but diagnostic accuracy exhibits diminishing returns and typically plateaus after 6-12 turns; and (iii) patient persona differences can shift diagnosis accuracy by about 7-8 points (lowest to highest education), highlighting equity risks that single-turn benchmarks miss.

AI.tldr: MedRoundsQA is a multi-turn, dual-agent diagnostic benchmark built from 1,387 board-exam cases (17 specialties), showing that LLM doctors degrade 13-39 points when moving from single-turn diagnosis to interactive consultations, with diminishing returns after 6-12 turns and ~7-8 point accuracy shifts across patient personas.
AI.motivation: Existing medical benchmarks rely on single-turn, multiple-choice clinical cases that fail to reflect real consultations, where clinicians interactively elicit evidence and patient communication varies widely. This gap misses diagnostic degradation, turn dynamics, and equity risks inherent to interactive settings.
AI.method: Each of 1,387 board-exam cases across 17 specialties is converted into a structured 24-slot clinical record and instantiated as controlled doctor-patient dual-agent dialogues under varying patient personas while holding clinical content fixed. Cases are classified by difficulty using model-based uncertainty to support easy-to-hard analysis. Fifteen LLM doctor agents are evaluated.
AI.result: (i) Moving from single-turn diagnosis on standardized records to multi-turn consultations causes large degradations of roughly 13-39 points; (ii) more turns reliably improve question relevance, but diagnostic accuracy shows diminishing returns and plateaus after 6-12 turns; (iii) patient persona differences shift diagnosis accuracy by about 7-8 points (lowest to highest education), revealing equity risks missed by single-turn benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: MedRoundsQA demonstrates that realistic multi-turn consultations substantially challenge LLM diagnostic performance and expose turn-related and persona-driven effects absent from single-turn benchmarks, underscoring the need for interactive, equity-aware medical evaluation.

title: Tracing and Coordinating Cross-Layer Influence for Multimodal Model Merging
summary: Multimodal model merging aims to consolidate task experts into a single model that retains their complementary capabilities. Most unimodal model merging methods combine expert updates within individual layers, and multimodal approaches largely follow this design. However, an expert update changes the representations passed to subsequent layers, allowing its influence to propagate across depth and affect how visual and textual information interact. When visual and language updates are combined, later updates act on inputs already modified by earlier ones, coupling their effects. This poses two challenges: (1) how to characterize the multimodal influence of individual expert updates across depth, and (2) how to jointly combine expert updates based on their multimodal influence. To address these challenges, we propose TAC-Merge for tracing and coordinating cross-layer influence in multimodal model merging. It contains two modules, i.e., multimodal influence mapping (MIM) and coupled merge control (CMC). MIM constructs graphs of update effects and uses Ricci curvature together with expert predictions to define a shared fusion objective. CMC models interactions among coefficient adjustments and jointly optimizes regional weights to synthesize one shared model. Experiments across diverse multimodal tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of TAC-Merge in consolidating complementary expert capabilities and supporting generalization to unseen tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TAC-Merge, a multimodal model merging method that traces and coordinates cross-layer influence of expert updates, using multimodal influence mapping (MIM) and coupled merge control (CMC) to consolidate complementary experts and generalize to unseen tasks.
AI.motivation: Most unimodal and multimodal model merging methods combine expert updates within individual layers. However, an expert update alters the representations passed to later layers, so its influence propagates across depth and affects visual-textual interaction. When visual and language updates are merged, later updates operate on inputs already modified by earlier ones, coupling their effects. This creates two challenges: (1) characterizing the multimodal influence of individual expert updates across depth, and (2) jointly combining expert updates based on that influence.
AI.method: TAC-Merge contains two modules: (1) multimodal influence mapping (MIM), which builds graphs of update effects and uses Ricci curvature together with expert predictions to define a shared fusion objective; and (2) coupled merge control (CMC), which models interactions among coefficient adjustments and jointly optimizes regional weights to synthesize one shared model.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse multimodal tasks show that TAC-Merge effectively consolidates complementary expert capabilities and supports generalization to unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: TAC-Merge addresses cross-layer, multimodal influence coupling in model merging by tracing update effects (MIM) and jointly optimizing merge coefficients (CMC), outperforming layer-wise merging and enabling generalization to unseen multimodal tasks.

title: EduFair-Bench: Evaluating Pedagogical Fairness of LLM Tutors Across Student Demographics
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as tutors, but it is unclear whether they support all students equally well. We introduce \textbf{EduFair-Bench}, a benchmark for auditing the pedagogical fairness of LLM tutors---whether tutoring quality varies systematically with student demographics. EduFair-Bench pairs a multi-domain question bank (mathematics, physics, chemistry) with a controlled simulation in which a fixed LLM student interacts with each tutor across nine demographic levels spanning four dimensions: gender, immigration background, first language, and socioeconomic status (SES). Tutoring quality is scored on five turn-level pedagogical metrics and four conversation-level dimensions, using an LLM judge validated against three-annotator consensus on 180 tutor turns. Bias is measured via paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and bootstrap effect-size confidence intervals. Two ablations (demographic cues conveyed through names; conflicting demographic information between tutor and student) disentangle tutor-driven from student-driven bias. Across five tutors, we find that model capability and demographic fairness are largely orthogonal: the smallest model is the most consistent while the four more capable tutors all exhibit wide demographic gaps with no clear capability-to-fairness ordering, pedagogy-specific RL training redistributes rather than removes bias, and language- and immigration-related cues produce larger gaps than gender- and SES-related cues.

AI.tldr: EduFair-Bench is introduced as a benchmark for auditing pedagogical fairness of LLM tutors, revealing that model capability and demographic fairness are largely orthogonal: more capable tutors show wide demographic gaps with no clear capability-to-fairness ordering, and bias is redistributed rather than removed by pedagogy-specific RL training.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as tutors, yet it remains unclear whether they support all students equally well. There is a lack of systematic tooling to audit whether tutoring quality varies with student demographics.
AI.method: EduFair-Bench pairs a multi-domain question bank (mathematics, physics, chemistry) with a controlled simulation where a fixed LLM student interacts with each tutor across nine demographic levels spanning four dimensions (gender, immigration background, first language, SES). Tutoring quality is scored on five turn-level pedagogical metrics and four conversation-level dimensions via an LLM judge validated against three-annotator consensus on 180 tutor turns. Bias is measured with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and bootstrap effect-size confidence intervals. Two ablations (demographic cues via names; conflicting tutor-student demographic information) disentangle tutor-driven from student-driven bias.
AI.result: Across five tutors, model capability and demographic fairness are largely orthogonal: the smallest model is most consistent, while the four more capable tutors exhibit wide demographic gaps with no clear capability-to-fairness ordering. Pedagogy-specific RL training redistributes rather than removes bias, and language- and immigration-related cues produce larger gaps than gender- and SES-related cues.
AI.conclusion: Pedagogical fairness of LLM tutors is not guaranteed by greater model capability, and training interventions may merely shift where bias appears. Fairness auditing across demographic dimensions is necessary before deploying LLM tutors.

title: How Good Are Frontier Models at Physics? Expert Re-Grading Reveals Broken Evaluations and Near-Saturation of Leading Benchmarks
summary: Low reported scores on leading physics benchmarks, including those featured in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (2026), suggest that frontier language models still struggle with advanced physics, a demanding test of their scientific reasoning and quantitative problem-solving abilities. Yet this impression does not always align with domain experts' experiences using these models in their work. We revisit these reported findings by evaluating frontier models on six widely used physics benchmarks and auditing them with experts, focusing on text-only problems with verifiable final answers. For each subfield of physics, faculty and graduate researchers with relevant expertise carefully review problem statements, reference solutions, and model responses to distinguish genuine model errors from grader errors, incorrect reference solutions, and ambiguous or underspecified questions. Most audited cases initially evaluated as incorrect reflect these benchmarking issues rather than errors in the models' physics reasoning. We then ask experts to address these benchmarking issues by correcting erroneous reference solutions and repairing or excluding flawed questions. We find that GPT-5.6-Sol's measured mean@4 rises from 47.3% to 78.7% on HLE-Physics and from 61.0% to 87.2% on CMT-Benchmark, while its corrected pass@4 reaches 94.4% on the 54 retained CritPt challenges. Corrected scores are computed on the retained evaluation subsets following expert review. Scores on the audited subsets of UGPhysics, PRISM-Physics, and PHYBench also rise substantially after correction. These findings suggest that current benchmarks substantially understate frontier models' ability to solve well-posed physics problems. Near-saturation on these closed-ended tasks highlights the need for more demanding, expert-validated evaluations.

AI.tldr: Frontier language models appear to underperform on physics benchmarks, but expert auditing reveals most "incorrect" responses are actually caused by benchmark flaws (grader errors, wrong reference solutions, ambiguous questions) rather than model reasoning failures; correcting these issues substantially raises scores and shows the benchmarks understate model physics ability.
AI.motivation: Low reported scores on leading physics benchmarks (e.g., those in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 2026) suggest frontier models still struggle with advanced physics, yet this conflicts with domain experts' practical experience. The authors suspect the reported results are distorted by benchmarking issues rather than genuine model limitations, and seek to investigate this discrepancy.
AI.method: Evaluate frontier models (e.g., GPT-5.6-Sol) on six widely used physics benchmarks, focusing on text-only problems with verifiable final answers. For each physics subfield, faculty and graduate researchers with relevant expertise audit problem statements, reference solutions, and model responses to distinguish genuine errors from grader errors, incorrect reference solutions, and ambiguous or underspecified questions. Experts then correct erroneous reference solutions and repair or exclude flawed questions, and scores are recomputed on the retained subsets.
AI.result: Most audited cases initially scored as incorrect were due to benchmarking issues rather than model physics errors. After correction, GPT-5.6-Sol's mean@4 rose from 47.3% to 78.7% on HLE-Physics and from 61.0% to 87.2% on CMT-Benchmark; corrected pass@4 reached 94.4% on the 54 retained CritPt challenges. Audited subsets of UGPhysics, PRISM-Physics, and PHYBench also rose substantially.
AI.conclusion: Current physics benchmarks substantially understate frontier models' ability to solve well-posed physics problems. Near-saturation on these closed-ended tasks highlights the need for more demanding, expert-validated evaluations.

title: Diffusion Models and Concept Formation
comment: Advances of Cognitive Systems 2026 Oral Presentation
summary: Humans organize knowledge into a taxonomy of concepts with nested levels of abstraction and a \emph{basic level} at which people recognize and name objects with the least cognitive effort. Cobweb is a classic cognitive account of this ability, an incremental learner that builds a probabilistic concept hierarchy by maximizing category utility. We argue that diffusion models, although designed for image synthesis, implicitly perform the same computation. The noisy marginals of a diffusion model are Gaussian smoothings of the data distribution, and the modes of these marginals form a hierarchy that corresponds to a Cobweb tree of probabilistic prototypes in four respects. Both are hierarchical density models, both are hierarchical-Bayesian models with Gaussian prototypes, both treat categorization as score-following that reduces uncertainty, and in both a basic level emerges. We locate this basic level for a diffusion model at an intermediate noise level, where recent analyses show that the reverse process commits to the class identity of a sample. The two models differ mainly in how they represent and learn the taxonomy. Cobweb learns a discrete tree incrementally, whereas a diffusion model encodes a continuous, interpolable hierarchy in a single learned score field fit to the data distribution. We test the correspondence on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST by recovering the diffusion hierarchy through mode-finding and comparing the basic levels of the two models. This reframes diffusion as a cognitive model of concept formation and offers Cobweb a continuous, scalable instantiation.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that diffusion models implicitly compute the same cognitive process as Cobweb: their noise-conditional marginals form a hierarchical prototype taxonomy with an emergent basic level, which the authors verify on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST via mode-finding.
AI.motivation: Humans organize concepts into taxonomies with nested abstraction and a basic level of least cognitive effort, classically modeled by Cobweb via category-utility maximization. The authors aim to show that diffusion models, despite being designed for image synthesis, implement the same hierarchical categorization computation.
AI.method: The authors draw a four-part correspondence: both are hierarchical density models; both are hierarchical-Bayesian models with Gaussian prototypes; both treat categorization as uncertainty-reducing score-following; and both exhibit an emergent basic level. They locate the diffusion basic level at an intermediate noise level where the reverse process commits to class identity, and empirically test the correspondence on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST by recovering the diffusion hierarchy through mode-finding and comparing basic levels.
AI.result: The two models are shown to correspond across the four claimed respects, with the diffusion basic level emerging at an intermediate noise level aligned with the commitment point of the reverse process; this is tested on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST by recovering the hierarchy via mode-finding and comparing basic levels.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models can be reframed as a cognitive model of concept formation, and the work offers Cobweb a continuous, scalable instantiation; the main difference is that Cobweb learns a discrete tree incrementally while diffusion encodes a continuous, interpolable hierarchy in a single learned score field.

title: Anchoring Clinical Events in Time: UID-Preserving Multimodal Reconstruction and Source-Grounded Adjudication
summary: Clinical timelines support treatment-window analysis and leakage-free modeling, but discharge summaries often obscure chronology and structured EHR tables describe only part of the patient course. We present a UID-preserving framework that links each narrative event occurrence to its source span and retains that identity through text-only estimation, structured-evidence retrieval, timestamped source-row grounding, and joint revision. We also present GAVEL, an LLM judge that compares two UID-aligned timelines against the narrative and structured record, to augment prior matching and temporal assessments. Across six open-weight models and 40 mixed-critical-care summaries, the GLM 5.2 multimodal revision, as compared to its text-only variant, improved temporal agreement without reducing event recovery and performed competitively with clinician annotations, while other model revisions showed smaller gains and lower overall performance. Ablations showed that UIDs primarily preserve event retention, whereas source-row linkage supports temporal placement. Blinded human review upheld most GAVEL findings, and controlled adjudication favored multimodal over text-only GLM 5.2 but did not for DeepSeek V3.2. In developing the UID and judge pipeline, we are able to demonstrate 43\% increased event recovery, a framework competitive with clinician annotations, and a system with occurrence-level provenance for both reconstruction and evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a UID-preserving framework that grounds each narrative clinical event to its source span and row-level evidence across the patient record, plus GAVEL, an LLM judge for timeline evaluation. Multimodal revision (GLM 5.2) improved temporal agreement and matched clinician annotations, with 43% higher event recovery.
AI.motivation: Clinical timeline reconstruction is needed for treatment-window analysis and leakage-free modeling, but discharge summaries obscure chronology and structured EHR tables capture only part of the patient course. Existing approaches lack occurrence-level provenance and reliable temporal grounding, hampering both reconstruction and evaluation.
AI.method: A UID-preserving framework links each narrative event occurrence to its source span and keeps that identity through text-only estimation, structured-evidence retrieval, timestamped source-row grounding, and joint revision. GAVEL, an LLM judge, compares two UID-aligned timelines against the narrative and structured record to augment prior matching and temporal assessments.
AI.result: Across six open-weight models and 40 mixed-critical-care summaries, the GLM 5.2 multimodal revision improved temporal agreement without reducing event recovery and performed competitively with clinician annotations; other model revisions showed smaller gains. Ablations showed UIDs primarily preserve event retention while source-row linkage supports temporal placement. Blinded human review upheld most GAVEL findings; controlled adjudication favored multimodal over text-only GLM 5.2 but not DeepSeek V3.2. The pipeline achieved 43% increased event recovery.
AI.conclusion: The UID and judge pipeline yields 43% increased event recovery, a framework competitive with clinician annotations, and occurrence-level provenance for both reconstruction and evaluation.

title: Autonomous Research for Open-Ended Problems: A Case Study on Telecom Ticket Retrieval
summary: Recent breakthroughs in LLM-based systems and their abilities in problem solving and coding have allowed progress in the AI for Science paradigm, potentially replacing human roles in machine learning (ML) research. However, while several frameworks of fully autonomous end-to-end ML research have been proposed, successful implementations of them are often limited to problems with narrow search spaces, like language modeling or biomedical ML benchmarks. In this paper, we explore how autonomous research can be adapted to solve open-ended, industry-grade ML problems, by considering a case study: telecom ticket retrieval, an open-ended task with degrees of freedom in representation, architecture, and training data generation. We discover that autonomous research for open-ended problems with commercial and open-source agents shows both promise and limitations: while autonomous research can excel in narrow hyperparameter optimization, it lacks human-like intuition and creativity and requires operational overhead. Even with minimal human supervision, autonomous research can reach $90\%$ of state-of-the-art performance (0.34 vs. 0.38 Recall@1) in a much shorter time period (10 weeks vs. 10 months of human work) at a modest cost (up to \$200 per Cursor campaign). Our empirical evidence recommends that human researchers and autonomous research frameworks work together for best results in ML research.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether autonomous LLM-based research agents can tackle open-ended, industry-grade ML problems, using telecom ticket retrieval as a case study, and finds that autonomous research excels at narrow hyperparameter optimization but lacks human-like intuition and creativity, recommending human-AI collaboration.
AI.motivation: Recent LLM-based autonomous research frameworks have enabled end-to-end ML research, but successful implementations are typically limited to problems with narrow search spaces (e.g., language modeling or biomedical benchmarks). It remains unclear whether autonomous research can be adapted to open-ended, industry-grade ML problems that involve many degrees of freedom in representation, architecture, and training data generation.
AI.method: The authors conduct a case study on telecom ticket retrieval, an open-ended task with degrees of freedom in representation, architecture, and training data generation. They deploy both commercial and open-source autonomous research agents and compare their performance against human researchers under conditions of minimal human supervision.
AI.result: Autonomous research reached 90% of state-of-the-art performance (0.34 vs. 0.38 Recall@1) in a much shorter time period (10 weeks vs. 10 months of human work) at a modest cost (up to $200 per Cursor campaign). However, it excelled only in narrow hyperparameter optimization, lacked human-like intuition and creativity, and required operational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous research for open-ended problems shows both promise and limitations. The empirical evidence recommends that human researchers and autonomous research frameworks work together to achieve the best results in ML research.

title: Embodied-BenchForge: A Closed-Loop Agentic Workflow for Embodied Benchmark Construction
summary: Agentic systems offer a promising way to automate embodied benchmark construction, but existing approaches typically cover isolated stages or remain specialized to predefined environments and task families. More importantly, multi-step construction produces dependent intermediate artifacts that are often passed downstream without artifact-specific verification, allowing local defects to propagate into the final benchmark. We present Embodied-BenchForge, an agentic framework that transforms user-specified evaluation intents into complete embodied benchmark artifacts. It formulates construction as Closed-Loop Benchmark Synthesis, integrating forward artifact synthesis with backward verification and repair. Skill-Orchestrated Artifact Synthesis composes typed and reusable skills into executable workflows, while an artifact dependency graph records intermediate outputs and their dependencies. Requirement-Guided Verification and Repair applies artifact-specific contracts throughout construction and uses provenance to trigger local re-execution or upstream rollback when verification fails. Embodied-BenchForge constructs six benchmarks covering diverse embodied scenarios in the Offline EQA Track, together with one interactive benchmark containing 220 executable tasks in the Interactive Embodied Track. Evaluations of representative MLLMs and embodied agents show that the benchmarks distinguish model capabilities in both observation-based understanding and closed-loop execution. Quality assessment and ablations validate benchmark quality and the effectiveness of verification and repair, while repair and skill-reuse analyses demonstrate efficient localized recovery and cross-benchmark reusability.

AI.tldr: Embodied-BenchForge is an agentic framework that turns user evaluation intents into complete embodied benchmarks via closed-loop synthesis, combining skill-orchestrated artifact synthesis with requirement-guided verification and repair, producing six Offline EQA benchmarks and one 220-task interactive benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic benchmark-construction approaches cover only isolated stages or are specialized to predefined environments and task families. Crucially, multi-step construction yields dependent intermediate artifacts passed downstream without artifact-specific verification, so local defects propagate into the final benchmark.
AI.method: Construction is formulated as Closed-Loop Benchmark Synthesis, integrating forward artifact synthesis with backward verification and repair. Skill-Orchestrated Artifact Synthesis composes typed, reusable skills into executable workflows, and an artifact dependency graph records intermediate outputs and dependencies. Requirement-Guided Verification and Repair applies artifact-specific contracts throughout construction, using provenance to trigger local re-execution or upstream rollback upon verification failure.
AI.result: The framework constructs six benchmarks spanning diverse embodied scenarios in the Offline EQA Track, plus one interactive benchmark with 220 executable tasks in the Interactive Embodied Track. Evaluations of representative MLLMs and embodied agents show the benchmarks distinguish model capabilities in observation-based understanding and closed-loop execution. Quality assessment and ablations validate benchmark quality and the effectiveness of verification and repair; repair and skill-reuse analyses show efficient localized recovery and cross-benchmark reusability.
AI.conclusion: Embodied-BenchForge demonstrates that closed-loop, artifact-verified agentic synthesis can generate complete, high-quality embodied benchmarks that discriminate model abilities and support efficient localized repair and skill reuse across benchmarks.

title: CMA-OT: Hierarchical Expert Supervision for Dance-to-Music Generation
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures, accepted by ACM MM 2026
summary: Dance-to-music (D2M) generation aims to synthesize music that is rhythmically and stylistically aligned with dance videos. A key challenge arises from the semantic mismatch between sparse dance cues, such as rhythm and style, and the dense information required for music composition, including structure, instrumentation, and expressive dynamics. Existing methods typically rely on these sparse cues and supervise only the final audio output, resulting in poorly learned music representations and generated music with limited musicality and structural coherence. To address these issues, we propose Curriculum-guided Multi-scale representation Alignment with scale-aware Optimal Transport (CMA-OT), a novel paradigm that leverages an external music expert to provide hierarchical supervision for the generator's latent features, bridging the semantic gap and enhancing representation learning. To effectively incorporate hierarchical supervision, we introduce a curriculum-guided multi-scale learning strategy that progressively transfers musical knowledge from the expert to the music generator, enabling stable and effective representation learning. Moreover, to accommodate the semantic and structural variations across different expert scales and achieve fine-grained alignment under temporal mismatch, we propose a scale-aware optimal transport alignment mechanism, which models soft correspondences between hierarchical expert representations and the generator's latent features. Extensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate that CMA-OT achieves state-of-the-art performance in rhythmic synchronization, perceptual quality, and overall music generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CMA-OT, a novel paradigm for dance-to-music (D2M) generation that uses an external music expert for hierarchical supervision and curriculum-guided multi-scale alignment with scale-aware optimal transport to bridge the semantic gap between sparse dance cues and dense music composition needs, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: D2M generation faces a semantic mismatch: dance cues are sparse (rhythm, style), while music composition requires dense information (structure, instrumentation, expressive dynamics). Existing methods rely on these sparse cues and only supervise the final audio output, resulting in poorly learned music representations and generated music with limited musicality and structural coherence.
AI.method: CMA-OT leverages an external music expert to provide hierarchical supervision for the generator's latent features, bridging the semantic gap. It introduces a curriculum-guided multi-scale learning strategy that progressively transfers musical knowledge from expert to generator for stable representation learning, and a scale-aware optimal transport alignment mechanism that models soft correspondences between hierarchical expert representations and generator latent features to handle semantic/structural variations and temporal mismatch.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate that CMA-OT achieves state-of-the-art performance in rhythmic synchronization, perceptual quality, and overall music generation.
AI.conclusion: CMA-OT effectively addresses the semantic mismatch in D2M generation by combining hierarchical expert supervision, curriculum-guided multi-scale learning, and scale-aware optimal transport alignment, yielding superior rhythmic synchronization, perceptual quality, and overall music generation performance.

title: A Hybrid LSTM-XGBoost Framework for Multi-Horizon Stock Return Prediction Across Diversified Equity Portfolios
summary: Accurate prediction of equity returns remains a major challenge in computational finance due to the non-stationary, nonlinear, and low signal-to-noise ratio nature of financial time series. This paper proposes a hybrid two-stage architecture that combines a long short-term memory (LSTM) network with an XGBoost gradient-boosted regressor for multi-horizon stock return prediction across a diversified panel of 14 U.S. equities spanning six industry sectors. The LSTM component, comprising two stacked layers with 64 hidden units, processes 60-day sliding windows of five sequential market features to produce 64-dimensional temporal embeddings that encode learned sequential market dynamics. These embeddings are concatenated with 14 hand-crafted technical indicators to form a 78-dimensional hybrid feature vector, which is subsequently passed to an XGBoost regressor tuned via 3-fold cross-validation grid search. The framework is trained on a multi-stock pooled corpus using strict chronological splits and per-stock MinMaxScaling to prevent look-ahead bias, and evaluated across four prediction horizons of 30, 90, 252, and 365 trading days. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid model achieves a test RMSE of 0.0949 on the 30-day horizon, roughly one-third that of the standalone LSTM baseline, while marginally matching or surpassing the XGBoost-Only baseline across the majority of stocks. Directional accuracy rises with horizon length, reaching 97.6% at 365 days; we show, however, that this largely tracks the high base rate of positive long-horizon returns in the sample, and we therefore benchmark directional accuracy against a naive always-positive predictor and treat the above-base-rate gap at short horizons as the more informative signal. A composite investment scoring framework derived from multi-horizon predictions is further proposed to support portfolio ranking and decision support.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a two-stage hybrid model combining an LSTM encoder with an XGBoost regressor to predict multi-horizon stock returns for 14 U.S. equities, using LSTM-derived temporal embeddings concatenated with technical indicators, trained with chronological splits to avoid look-ahead bias.
AI.motivation: Equity return prediction is difficult due to the non-stationary, nonlinear, and low signal-to-noise characteristics of financial time series, motivating a model that captures both sequential temporal dynamics and nonlinear feature interactions.
AI.method: A two-stage architecture: (1) a two-layer LSTM with 64 hidden units encodes 60-day windows of five market features into 64-dimensional temporal embeddings; (2) these embeddings are concatenated with 14 hand-crafted technical indicators into a 78-dimensional feature vector fed to an XGBoost regressor tuned by 3-fold cross-validation grid search. Training uses a multi-stock pooled corpus, strict chronological splits, and per-stock MinMaxScaling to prevent look-ahead bias. Evaluation spans horizons of 30, 90, 252, and 365 trading days.
AI.result: The hybrid model achieves a 30-day test RMSE of 0.0949, approximately one-third that of the standalone LSTM baseline, while marginally matching or exceeding the XGBoost-Only baseline on most stocks. Directional accuracy increases with horizon length, reaching 97.6% at 365 days, though this largely reflects the high base rate of positive long-horizon returns.
AI.conclusion: Directional accuracy must be benchmarked against a naive always-positive predictor, since high long-horizon accuracy mostly tracks the sample's base rate; the above-base-rate gap at short horizons is the more informative signal. A composite multi-horizon investment scoring framework is proposed for portfolio ranking and decision support.

title: Rethinking Heterogeneous System Disaggregation for Subquadratic Attention
summary:
Frontier language models are more aggressively using subquadratic attention to reduce the memory footprint and compute requirements during inference while still delivering frontier accuracy. While existing systems make dense attention-centric disaggregated serving decisions, we show that disaggregating inference around the unique arithmetic intensity and memory footprint of subquadratic attention LLMs can achieve significant throughput and energy efficiency gains on emerging DRAM-based and SRAM-only heterogeneous systems.
  We introduce SQD (SubQuadratic Disaggregation), a fine-grained heterogeneous disaggregation scheme that splits decode by quadratic and subquadratic attention rather than by operator type, and that applies across subquadratic attention variants. For sparse attention LLMs, we disaggregate decode into top-k selection, which must index through the full KV, and top-k attention plus FFN, which have static memory footprints. For linear and sliding-window attention LLMs, we disaggregate decode into dense attention layers and subquadratic attention layers plus FFN. In an adjusted 8xB200 heterogeneous system proxy, we observe average tokens/J improvements of 53% on GLM 5.2, 31% on Nemotron 3 Ultra, and 56% on Gemma 4 31B over the strongest GPU-only baselines. In an analytical model of a Rubin plus LPX system with fixed power budgets, we observe 1.2x to 1.5x tighter achievable latencies and up to 3.6x higher throughput over the best baseline of attention-FFN disaggregation. Our experiments also reveal architectural insights on chip and interconnect provisioning for next-generation heterogeneous systems serving subquadratic attention.

AI.tldr: SQD introduces subquadratic-aware heterogeneous disaggregation that splits decode by quadratic vs. subquadratic attention rather than operator type, yielding large tokens/J and throughput gains over attention-FFN disaggregation baselines.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs increasingly adopt subquadratic attention to cut inference memory and compute while preserving accuracy. Existing disaggregated serving systems, however, make dense attention-centric decisions that ignore the distinct arithmetic intensity and memory footprint of subquadratic attention, missing throughput and energy efficiency opportunities on emerging DRAM-based and SRAM-only heterogeneous hardware.
AI.method: SQD (SubQuadratic Disaggregation) is a fine-grained heterogeneous disaggregation scheme that splits decode by quadratic and subquadratic attention instead of by operator type, and generalizes across subquadratic attention variants. For sparse attention LLMs, decode is disaggregated into top-k selection (indexing the full KV) and top-k attention plus FFN (static memory footprints). For linear and sliding-window attention LLMs, decode is disaggregated into dense attention layers and subquadratic attention layers plus FFN.
AI.result: On an adjusted 8xB200 heterogeneous system proxy, SQD achieves average tokens/J improvements of 53% on GLM 5.2, 31% on Nemotron 3 Ultra, and 56% on Gemma 4 31B over the strongest GPU-only baselines. In an analytical model of a Rubin plus LPX system under fixed power budgets, it attains 1.2x-1.5x tighter achievable latencies and up to 3.6x higher throughput versus the best attention-FFN disaggregation baseline.
AI.conclusion: Disaggregating inference around the arithmetic intensity and memory footprint of subquadratic attention delivers significant throughput and energy efficiency gains on heterogeneous DRAM-based and SRAM-only systems, and yields architectural insights for chip and interconnect provisioning in next-generation serving infrastructure.
